domain.title: Chip Architecture & Co-design
domain.tag: ISA · systolic arrays · dataflow · HBM · chiplets · PPA · tapeout
domain.why: This is where 'I want to help design AI chips' stops being a dream and becomes actual arithmetic you can do on paper — how big should this piece of hardware be, is this design memory-bound or compute-bound, would a different layout be faster. Every one of those questions has a real calculable answer, and being able to do that calculation is most of what the job of a chip architect actually is.

sections.note: The contract, and what each encoding choice costs the implementer.

L0.body:
# The ISA is the only thing a compiler is allowed to know.
# RISC-V RV32I says: 32 registers, x0 hardwired to zero, 32-bit
# instructions, byte-addressed little-endian memory, and this behaviour:

  add  x5, x6, x7     # x5 <- x6 + x7, wrapping on overflow, no flags
  lw   x5, 8(x6)      # x5 <- mem[x6+8], 32-bit, must be 4-byte aligned
                      #   (misaligned: implementation may trap OR handle it)

# NOT in the contract: how many cycles, how deep the pipeline,
# whether there is a cache, whether add is even a separate unit.
L0.cloze: The ISA fixes {{c1::architectural state}} and instruction semantics; it says nothing about {{c2::cycles, pipeline depth or caches}}. In RV32I, register {{c3::x0}} is hardwired to zero.

concepts.L1: An instruction set architecture is the specification a compiler targets and a microarchitecture implements: the register file, the memory model, the instruction encodings and their observable effects. Everything about speed is deliberately outside it.
concepts.L2: The ISA is not the performance model. Two implementations of RV32I can differ by 100x in throughput and both be correct. The reason people confuse them is that ISA choices constrain what microarchitectures are cheap to build, which is influence, not specification.
concepts.L3: The contract exists so the two sides can move independently. Intel has replaced its microarchitecture roughly every two years since 1995 while keeping x86 binaries working; ARM ships in-order and out-of-order cores against one ISA. The cost of that freedom is that the contract must be conservative: once you specify that misaligned loads work, every future implementation must either handle them in hardware or trap and emulate. RISC-V leaves misaligned access implementation-defined precisely to avoid committing future silicon. Reading a spec, the question to keep asking is: what did they refuse to promise, and what did that buy the implementer?

L4.prompt_tpl: A vendor ships two chips implementing the same ISA. Chip A runs a benchmark in {a} seconds, chip B in {b} seconds. Is one of them violating the ISA?
options: No, because timing is not part of the ISA contract
Yes, because an ISA fixes the cycles-per-instruction of each opcode
Only if chip B has a different cache size, which the ISA does specify
L4.answer: No. The ISA specifies observable results, not timing, so an arbitrarily large performance gap between conformant implementations is expected.
L4.explanation: Timing is outside the contract. The ISA constrains architectural state and instruction semantics; an in-order single-issue core and a wide out-of-order core implementing the same ISA differ by an order of magnitude and are both conformant. Only a difference in results would be a violation.

L4.prompt_tpl: RISC-V leaves the behaviour of a misaligned {w}-byte load implementation-defined: it may complete, or it may trap. Explain what the implementer gains and what the compiler writer loses.
L4.answer: The implementer may omit the alignment-fixup hardware in the load path, saving area and a critical-path stage; the compiler and runtime must either guarantee alignment or supply a trap handler, and portable code cannot assume the fast path exists.
L4.explanation: Under-specification is how an ISA buys implementers freedom. Hardware misaligned support costs a splitter and a merge in the load pipeline. Leaving it open lets a microcontroller trap and a server core handle it. The bill lands on software: alignment must be guaranteed or a handler written, and performance becomes non-portable.

L0.body:
# x86-64, one instruction:
  addq  %rax, 8(%rbx,%rcx,4)   # load, add, store: 1 instruction, 5 bytes

# RV64I, same work:
  slli  t0, x12, 2             # 4 bytes
  add   t0, x11, t0            # 4
  ld    t1, 8(t0)              # 4
  add   t1, t1, x10            # 4
  sd    t1, 8(t0)              # 4   -> 5 instructions, 20 bytes

# But the x86 chip cracks that into ~4 internal uops anyway.
# The RISC/CISC argument is about the DECODER, not the execution core.
L0.cloze: x86's memory-operand arithmetic is decoded into about {{c1::4}} internal uops, so the real difference lives in the {{c2::decoder}}, not the execution core. RISC-V needs {{c3::5}} instructions and 20 bytes for the same work.

concepts.L1: RISC means fixed-length, load-store, register-register instructions with simple addressing; CISC means variable-length instructions that may fold addressing and memory access into arithmetic. Modern high-performance CISC cores translate to RISC-like internal operations before execution.
concepts.L2: The RISC victory is real but narrow: it was won in the decoder and in the compiler, not in the execution core, which converged. The remaining CISC cost is that variable-length instructions cannot be found in parallel without either a length predecoder, a uop cache, or brute-force speculative decode at every byte offset.
concepts.L3: Trace the actual cost. A fixed-width 32-bit encoding lets a decoder slice a fetch block at known offsets and decode $W$ instructions with $W$ independent decoders. A variable-length encoding does not know where instruction $i+1$ starts until $i$ is partly decoded, which is serial. Intel and AMD pay with length-marking predecode bits in the icache and uop caches that bypass decode for hot loops: silicon and energy a RISC decoder never spends. Against that, CISC wins code density, meaning icache footprint and fetch bandwidth, and RISC-V answers with the C extension. The honest total is a few percent of front-end area and energy, and almost nothing elsewhere.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {w}-wide fetch unit decodes fixed-width 32-bit instructions from a {f}-byte fetch block. How many instructions can it see per cycle, and what changes if the encoding is variable-length between 1 and 15 bytes? Answer with the number of instructions seen per cycle.
L4.answer: Fixed width: $\min(w, f/4)$ instructions, boundaries known statically. Variable length: boundaries are unknown until decode, so the decoder needs predecoded length marks or a uop cache; worst case one instruction per cycle without them.
L4.explanation: For $f=32$ and $w=4$ the fixed-width decoder sees $32/4 = 8$ candidate boundaries and decodes all 4 slots in parallel. Variable-length encoding makes boundary discovery serial, which is why x86 implementations carry length-marking bits in the instruction cache and a uop cache for hot code.

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone claims a RISC ISA gives a {n} percent performance advantage because it has fewer addressing modes. Assess the claim.
options: Wrong: execution cores converged, the difference is decoder cost and code density
Right: fewer addressing modes directly reduce cycles per instruction by that much
Right, but only for out-of-order cores, where addressing modes stall issue
L4.answer: The claim is wrong: CISC cores crack complex instructions into internal RISC-like operations, so the execution cores converged. The residual difference is front-end decode area and energy, plus code density in the other direction.
L4.explanation: Addressing modes were the 1980s argument and are largely settled: a load-op-store x86 instruction becomes about four uops and executes on the same kind of out-of-order core. The measurable modern difference is decoder complexity and energy versus code density, and both are single-digit percent effects on a large core.

concepts.t: RISC-V base ISA and the extension mechanism

L0.body:
# The name encodes the contract:
#   RV64GC  =  RV64I  +  M A F D  +  Zicsr Zifencei  +  C
#              base    G = "general"                  compressed
#
#   I  base integer (47 instructions in RV32I)
#   M  integer multiply/divide      A  atomics
#   F  single-precision float       D  double
#   C  16-bit compressed forms      V  vector
#   Zb* bit manipulation            Zk* scalar crypto
#
# Extensions are ratified separately and frozen forever once ratified.
L0.cloze: RV64GC expands to RV64I plus {{c1::M A F D}} plus Zicsr/Zifencei plus {{c2::C}}. The base integer ISA RV32I has {{c3::47}} instructions.

concepts.L1: RISC-V is a small frozen base integer ISA plus a set of independently ratified extensions, each identified by a letter or a Z-prefixed name. An implementation declares which it supports; software queries that set rather than assuming a fixed instruction repertoire.
concepts.L2: Modularity is not free: it converts a compatibility problem into a combinatorial one. There is no single RISC-V binary that runs everywhere, so the ecosystem needs profiles (RVA23 and friends) to force a common denominator. Fragmentation is the standing risk, and profiles are the mitigation, not a fix.
concepts.L3: The design point is that the base must fit in a few thousand gates for a microcontroller and must also sit under a server core. So RV32I has no multiply, no atomics and no floating point, and it fits in 47 instructions, the smallest ISA shipped commercially at scale. Everything else is opt-in, which is why one specification covers a TinyTapeout-scale core and a Linux-capable out-of-order design. The cost is that a distribution targets a profile, not the base: RVA23 mandates V, the bit-manipulation groups and hypervisor support so a distro can compile once. Extension letters freeze on ratification, so deprecated ideas get new names rather than new versions.

L4.prompt_tpl: A vendor ships a core advertising RV{bits}IMAC and no F or D. What must the toolchain do for a program using {t} arithmetic, and what is the performance consequence?
L4.answer: The compiler targets a soft-float ABI and emits library calls that implement the operations with integer instructions; each operation costs tens to hundreds of instructions instead of one, so float-heavy code slows by one to two orders of magnitude.
L4.explanation: Absent F/D there is no float register file and no float instructions, so the toolchain selects a soft-float ABI. Correctness is preserved, performance is not: an emulated double add is a multi-branch integer routine. This is exactly the fragmentation cost the profiles exist to bound.

L4.prompt_tpl: Expand the ISA string RV{bits}GC into its component extensions and say how many of them the letter G stands for.
L4.answer: RV{bits}I plus M, A, F, D, Zicsr and Zifencei (that is G, six components) plus C.
L4.explanation: G is a shorthand abbreviation covering IMAFD plus Zicsr and Zifencei, and C adds the 16-bit compressed encodings. Writing it out is worth doing once, because the ISA string is the actual contract a distribution compiles against and every letter is a separately ratified document.

L0.body:
# Fixed 32-bit (RV32I): every instruction starts at a 4-byte boundary.
#   fetch 32 bytes -> 8 instruction starts, known with zero decode work
#
# Variable (x86-64): 1 to 15 bytes.
#   fetch 32 bytes -> starts unknown until you decode left to right
#   mitigations: predecode length bits in the I-cache, or a uop cache
#
# Encoding budget arithmetic, fixed 32-bit:
#   R-type: 7 opcode + 5 rd + 3 funct3 + 5 rs1 + 5 rs2 + 7 funct7 = 32
#   every extra register bit costs 3 bits (rd, rs1, rs2) of opcode space
L0.cloze: With a fixed 32-bit encoding, widening the register file by one bit costs {{c1::3}} bits of encoding space, because {{c2::rd, rs1 and rs2}} all grow. Variable-length encoding makes instruction boundaries {{c3::serial}} to discover.

concepts.L1: Fixed-width encoding puts every instruction at a known offset, so fetch and decode parallelise trivially; variable-width buys code density at the cost of serial boundary discovery. The choice sets the shape of the entire front end.
concepts.L2: The real constraint on a fixed-width ISA is not decode, it is the encoding budget. Thirty-two bits is a scarce resource, and the reason RISC-V has 32 registers rather than 64 is that a sixth register bit would cost three bits across the three register fields, which is most of a major opcode.
concepts.L3: Count it out on the RISC-V R-type: 7 bits opcode, 5 rd, 3 funct3, 5 rs1, 5 rs2, 7 funct7, exactly 32. Now ask for 64 registers. rd, rs1 and rs2 each need 6 bits, so you spend 3 more bits and must take them from funct7 or opcode, either shrinking the space for future extensions or breaking the uniform field positions that let the decoder read register specifiers before it knows the opcode. That last property is worth a lot: RISC-V places rs1 and rs2 at fixed bit positions in every format so the register file read can start in parallel with decode. Variable-length encodings cannot do that either, which is a second, quieter reason fixed width helps a wide front end.

L4.prompt_tpl: An ISA has a fixed {w}-bit encoding, {r} architectural registers, and three register fields per instruction. How many bits remain for opcode and function fields, and what happens to that budget if the register count doubles? Answer with the bits remaining for opcode and function fields.
L4.answer: Register bits $= 3\lceil \log_{2} r \rceil$; remaining $= w - 3\lceil \log_{2} r \rceil$. Doubling $r$ costs 3 more bits. For $w=32, r=32$: $3 \times 5 = 15$ used, 17 left; at $r=64$, 18 used, 14 left.
L4.explanation: Each register specifier costs $\log_{2} r$ bits and there are three of them, so the marginal cost of doubling the register file is 3 bits taken directly out of opcode space. At 32 bits total this is the dominant pressure on the encoding and is why 32 registers is the near-universal choice.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are designing a {d} accelerator control processor and code size in on-chip ROM is the binding constraint. Fixed-width or variable-width encoding?
options: Fixed-width base plus a 16-bit compressed extension
Full variable-length encoding from 1 to 15 bytes, for maximum density
Fixed 32-bit only, since ROM size never dominates control-processor cost
L4.answer: Fixed-width base plus a compressed 16-bit extension: it keeps decode parallel and boundary discovery cheap while recovering most of the density, which is what RISC-V's C extension does.
L4.explanation: Full variable-length encoding wins raw density but forces serial boundary discovery and complicates every future widening of the front end. A fixed base with an optional 16-bit compressed form recovers most density at the cost of a two-length decoder, which is a much smaller problem than a fifteen-length one.

L0.body:
# Six formats, all 32 bits, all with rs1/rs2/rd at FIXED bit positions.
#
#  31        25 24  20 19  15 14 12 11   7 6      0
# R: funct7      rs2    rs1   funct3  rd     opcode
# I: imm[11:0]          rs1   funct3  rd     opcode
# S: imm[11:5]   rs2    rs1   funct3  imm[4:0] opcode
# B: imm[12|10:5] rs2   rs1   funct3  imm[4:1|11] opcode
# U: imm[31:12]                       rd     opcode
# J: imm[20|10:1|11|19:12]            rd     opcode
#
# B and J immediates are scrambled ON PURPOSE: each immediate bit keeps
# one wire position across formats, so sign-extension is fixed muxing.
L0.cloze: RISC-V keeps {{c1::rs1, rs2 and rd}} at fixed bit positions in every format so register read can start before decode finishes. The scrambled B and J immediate bit order exists to keep each immediate bit in a {{c2::fixed wire position}}.

concepts.L1: RISC-V defines six 32-bit instruction formats that differ only in how the non-register bits are used. Register specifiers occupy identical bit positions across all of them, and immediate fields are permuted so each immediate bit lands on the same output wire regardless of format.
concepts.L2: The apparently perverse bit ordering of the branch and jump immediates is the single most misread part of the specification. It is not an accident of history; it is a deliberate choice that trades human readability for eliminating a multiplexer layer from the immediate path, which sits on the branch-resolution critical path.
concepts.L3: Follow the hardware. The immediate generator takes 32 instruction bits and must produce a sign-extended 32-bit value for any format. If each format placed its immediate bits contiguously, output bit $k$ would have to select among several different input bits: a mux per output bit per format. RISC-V fixes the mapping instead. Bit 31 is always the sign bit, bits 30 to 25 always feed immediate bits 10 to 5, and so on, so most output bits have one source wire and the rest need a small mux. On a five-stage core that removes gates from decode; on a wide core it removes them from a path replicated per decode slot. Read the format table as a wiring diagram, not a text layout.

L4.prompt_tpl: Decode the RISC-V instruction word 0x{hexword} by hand: give the opcode field, the format, and the register numbers involved.
L4.answer: Take bits 6:0 as opcode, then bits 11:7 as rd, 19:15 as rs1, 24:20 as rs2. 0x00C58533 is opcode 0x33 (R-type OP), funct3 0, funct7 0, rd = x10, rs1 = x11, rs2 = x12, i.e. add x10, x11, x12.
L4.explanation: Field extraction is pure bit slicing because positions are format-invariant: opcode 6:0, rd 11:7, funct3 14:12, rs1 19:15, rs2 24:20, funct7 31:25. Doing one by hand is worth more than reading the table, because it makes the fixed-position property concrete.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why the B-format immediate stores bit {b} of the offset in a bit position that looks out of order, and what hardware that saves.
L4.answer: Because the encoding is chosen so each immediate output bit has one fixed source wire across formats; keeping the offset contiguous would instead require a multiplexer per output bit selecting among formats, adding a gate layer to the immediate path.
L4.explanation: The immediate generator is a wiring problem. Fixed source-to-destination mapping makes most bits a wire and the remainder a small mux, rather than a per-bit format selector. Branch offsets are also always even, so bit 0 is not encoded at all, which recovers a bit of range for free.

L0.body:
# The C extension adds 16-bit forms of the most common instructions.
# Restrictions that make it fit: 3-bit register field -> only x8..x15,
# and many forms are two-operand (rd is also rs1).
#
#   c.add   rd, rs2      -> add  rd, rd, rs2
#   c.lw    rd', off(rs1')  -> registers limited to x8..x15
#
# Density arithmetic: if a fraction p of instructions compress,
#   bytes per instruction = 4(1-p) + 2p = 4 - 2p
#   size ratio vs uncompressed = (4 - 2p)/4 = 1 - p/2
#   p = 0.60  ->  0.70    (a 30% code-size reduction)
L0.cloze: If a fraction $p$ of instructions take the 16-bit form, average bytes per instruction is {{c1::4 - 2p}} and the size ratio is {{c2::1 - p/2}}. At $p = 0.6$ the code shrinks to {{c3::70}} percent.

concepts.L1: The C extension provides 16-bit encodings for the most frequent instruction forms, chosen by restricting register fields to eight registers and folding destination into source. Compressed and uncompressed instructions interleave freely in the same stream.
concepts.L2: Compression is a fetch-bandwidth and instruction-cache win, not an execution win: the 16-bit forms expand to exactly the same base instructions in the decoder, so cycle counts do not change. It reintroduces variable length, but with two lengths distinguished by two bits, a far smaller decoder problem than x86's.
concepts.L3: It works because instruction frequency is Zipf-like. A handful of forms, small-offset loads and stores, small-immediate adds, moves and short branches, dominate real code, and they almost always use a small register subset because the ABI concentrates locals there. Restricting to x8 through x15 costs 2 bits of register field and buys 16 bits of instruction. At $p = 0.6$ the arithmetic gives $4 - 2(0.6) = 2.8$ bytes per instruction, a ratio of $0.7$: a 64 KiB icache behaves like 91 KiB. Since an icache miss on a small core costs tens of cycles the throughput win is real, though per-instruction work is identical. The cost is one extra decode length and a wider branch-target alignment problem.

L4.prompt_tpl: In a binary, {p} percent of instructions have a valid 16-bit compressed form. Compute the average bytes per instruction and the code-size ratio against a pure 32-bit encoding. Answer with the average bytes per instruction.
L4.answer: Bytes per instruction $= 4(1-p) + 2p = 4 - 2p$ with $p$ as a fraction; ratio $= 1 - p/2$. For $p = 0.55$: $4 - 1.1 = 2.9$ bytes, ratio $0.725$.
L4.explanation: Each compressed instruction saves exactly 2 bytes, so the saving is linear in the compression fraction and the best possible ratio is 0.5 at full compression. Real RISC-V binaries land near $p = 0.5$ to $0.7$, giving roughly 25 to 35 percent code-size reduction.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team reports that enabling the C extension made their {k} KiB instruction cache behave like a larger one but did not change instructions retired. Is that consistent?
options: Yes: compression changes bytes fetched, not instructions executed
No: fewer bytes must mean fewer instructions retired
No: the C extension replaces pairs of instructions with single ones
L4.answer: Yes. Compressed forms expand to the identical base instructions in decode, so retired-instruction count is unchanged; only the bytes fetched and cached shrink, which improves the instruction-cache hit rate.
L4.explanation: This is the expected signature. Compression is a front-end effect: same architectural work, fewer bytes to hold and fetch. If instruction count had changed, something else did too, most likely a different compiler optimisation level enabled alongside the extension.

concepts.t: The vector extension and length-agnostic code

L0.cloze: `vsetvli` returns the number of elements the hardware chose, which is {{c1::min(n, VLMAX)}}. Because the loop reads that back, one binary runs on any {{c2::VLEN}} and needs no {{c3::remainder loop}}.

concepts.L1: RVV is a vector-length-agnostic ISA: software requests an element count and a data type, hardware returns how many elements it will actually process this iteration, and the loop advances by that. VLEN is an implementation parameter, not an ISA constant.
concepts.L2: This is the opposite of the AVX and NEON model, where register width is baked into the opcode and every width change means a new instruction set and a recompile. The consequence people miss is that the tail is free: the same sequence handles the remainder, so the classic remainder loop does not exist.
concepts.L3: Compare the failure mode it removes. With AVX-512 you write a 16-wide main loop and a scalar or masked tail; for $n = 100$ that is six full iterations plus four elements handled separately, and the tail is a real fraction of source and icache. Under RVV, `vsetvli` returns $\min(n, \mathrm{VLMAX})$ each time, so the final iteration sets a smaller vector length and every later operation respects it. Grouping (LMUL) lets one instruction span eight vector registers, so a small VLEN part still amortises loop overhead. The cost: the compiler cannot constant-fold the vector length, so it unrolls less aggressively and vector stack frames become variable-size.

L4.prompt_tpl: An RVV implementation has VLEN = {vlen} bits. For 32-bit elements with LMUL = {lmul}, how many elements does one `vsetvli` request cover at most, and how many loop iterations does a length-{n} array take? Answer with the number of loop iterations.
L4.answer: $\mathrm{VLMAX} = \mathrm{VLEN} \times \mathrm{LMUL} / \mathrm{SEW}$ with SEW = 32; iterations $= \lceil n / \mathrm{VLMAX} \rceil$. For VLEN = 256, LMUL = 4: VLMAX = 32, and $n = 100$ takes 4 iterations, the last with vl = 4.
L4.explanation: VLMAX scales with both the hardware vector length and the register grouping factor. The last iteration simply carries a smaller vl, which is why there is no separate remainder loop; the ceiling in the iteration count is the whole story.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team ports a kernel from AVX-{w} intrinsics to RVV and finds the source shrank substantially. Explain the structural reason, and name one thing the compiler can no longer do.
L4.answer: The remainder or masked-tail handling disappears because vl is set per iteration from the remaining count, so one loop body covers full and partial iterations. The compiler loses the compile-time-constant vector length, so it cannot fully unroll to a known trip count or size vector stack slots statically.
L4.explanation: Length-agnostic execution moves the tail from software into the vl register. The cost is optimisation information: with a fixed 512-bit register the compiler knows trip counts and can unroll and schedule precisely; with RVV it must emit a loop that works for any VLEN, which occasionally leaves throughput on the table on a specific implementation.

prereqs: RISC-V base ISA and the extension mechanism
Masking, tails and the remainder loop

L0.body:
# RISC-V reserves four major opcodes for non-standard use:
#   custom-0 (0x0B), custom-1 (0x2B), custom-2 (0x5B), custom-3 (0x7B)
#
# Rocket's RoCC interface takes exactly these and routes them to your
# accelerator, with rs1/rs2 and a 7-bit funct field:
#
#   customX  rd, rs1, rs2, funct   // your unit sees rs1, rs2, funct
#                                  // returns rd, may also touch memory
#
# Rough decision rule:
#   < ~10 cycles of work per invocation   -> custom instruction
#   > ~1000 cycles                        -> MMIO accelerator + DMA
L0.cloze: RISC-V reserves {{c1::four}} major opcodes for non-standard extensions, and Rocket's {{c2::RoCC}} interface routes them to an attached unit. Work of thousands of cycles per invocation belongs behind {{c3::a memory-mapped accelerator with DMA}}, not an instruction.

concepts.L1: A custom instruction adds an opcode that dispatches to your own functional unit through the normal register file and pipeline. It is the cheapest way to attach small fixed-function logic, and it costs you a private toolchain, a private ABI and a fork of every simulator.
concepts.L2: The real decision is not whether the operation is expressible as an instruction but whether the operand traffic fits the register file. A matrix operation with a 64 KiB tile cannot pass through two 64-bit source registers, so it needs architectural state of its own, which is why matrix extensions define separate tile registers.
concepts.L3: Work it out from the interface cost. A custom instruction gives two sources and one destination: at most 24 bytes of operand per issue on RV64. A $16 \times 16$ int8 tile is 256 bytes; a useful matmul tile is kilobytes. Once operands exceed register-file bandwidth you either add architectural registers, as Arm's SME does with ZA tiles and Intel's AMX with eight 1 KiB tiles, or move data through memory and reduce the instruction to a command, an MMIO accelerator wearing an opcode. That is the fork. Architectural state is expensive forever: it must be saved and restored on context switch, which is why AMX ships a tile-configure and release protocol gated behind an OS state-enable request.

L4.prompt_tpl: You want hardware acceleration for an operation that consumes {b} bytes of input per invocation and takes {c} cycles. Custom instruction or memory-mapped accelerator?
options: Register-fit and short latency favour a custom instruction; kilobyte operands and long latency favour a memory-mapped accelerator
Always a custom instruction, since it avoids the memory system entirely
Always memory-mapped, since custom opcodes break binary compatibility
L4.answer: If operands fit in two source registers and the latency is a few cycles, use a custom instruction; once the operand is kilobytes or the latency is thousands of cycles, use a memory-mapped block with DMA, because the register file cannot supply the data and the pipeline should not stall on it.
L4.explanation: The register file is the bottleneck, not the opcode space. Two 64-bit sources cap you at 16 bytes of operand per issue. Kilobyte operands force either new architectural state, with its context-switch cost, or a memory interface. Long latency additionally argues for decoupling so the core can run ahead.

L4.prompt_tpl: Adding {n} new architectural registers to hold matrix tiles has a cost that has nothing to do with the datapath. Name it and explain who pays.
L4.answer: Context-switch state: the kernel must save and restore that state on every thread switch and signal delivery, and the size directly enlarges the thread control block, so operating systems gate such extensions behind an explicit enable and lazy save protocol.
L4.explanation: Intel's AMX carries eight 1 KiB tiles, which is 8 KiB per thread of extra context. That is why AMX requires an explicit request to the kernel before use and defines a tile-release instruction to mark state dead. Architectural state is a permanent tax on every context switch, paid by the OS, not the accelerator.

prereqs: RISC-V base ISA and the extension mechanism

sections.note: Not what the chip does, but what each structure costs the person building it.

concepts.t: Pipeline depth as a design variable

L0.body:
# Logic depth is measured in FO4 (fan-out-of-4 inverter delays), not ns,
# because FO4 is roughly process-independent.
#
#   total combinational path  T = 20 FO4
#   flip-flop overhead        L =  3 FO4  (clk-to-Q + setup + skew)
#
#   k stages -> cycle = T/k + L,  f = 1/(T/k + L)
#
#   k= 4 : cycle = 5+3 = 8 FO4   f_rel = 1.00
#   k=10 : cycle = 2+3 = 5 FO4   f_rel = 1.60
#   k=20 : cycle = 1+3 = 4 FO4   f_rel = 2.00
#   k=inf: cycle =   3 FO4       f_rel = 2.67   <- the hard ceiling is L
L0.cloze: Cycle time is {{c1::T/k + L}}, so frequency saturates at {{c2::1/L}} no matter how deep you pipeline. Going from k=10 to k=20 buys only {{c3::1.25x}} frequency for twice the flip-flops.

concepts.L1: Pipeline depth is chosen, not given. Deeper stages shorten the cycle toward the flip-flop overhead $L$ and no further, so frequency gain per added stage falls off sharply while flip-flop count, clock power and misprediction penalty all rise linearly.
concepts.L2: The diminishing return is not the main argument against depth. The main argument is that the misprediction penalty is proportional to depth, so at a fixed branch-prediction accuracy, deepening the pipeline costs IPC at exactly the rate it gains frequency, and past some point the product falls.
concepts.L3: Do the product. Let $f(k) = 1/(T/k + L)$ and let IPC degrade as $\mathrm{IPC}(k) = \mathrm{IPC}_{0}/(1 + m k \beta)$, with $m$ mispredictions per instruction and $\beta$ the fraction of depth refilled. Performance is $f \cdot \mathrm{IPC}$. Take $T = 20$, $L = 3$, $m = 0.005$, $\beta = 1$: at $k = 10$, $f_{\mathrm{rel}} = 1.60$ and the IPC factor $1/1.05 = 0.952$, product $1.52$; at $k = 20$, $2.00 \times 0.909 = 1.82$; at $k = 40$, $2.29 \times 0.833 = 1.90$. The curve is flat by 20 while energy per instruction still climbs linearly in $k$. That is the whole Pentium 4 story from two lines of algebra.

L4.prompt_tpl: A combinational path of {T} FO4 is pipelined into {k} stages with {L} FO4 of flip-flop overhead per boundary. Give the cycle time, the relative frequency against a 4-stage version, and the ceiling frequency as depth goes to infinity. Answer with the cycle time in FO4.
L4.answer: Cycle $= T/k + L$; $f \propto 1/(T/k+L)$; ceiling $= 1/L$. For $T=20, k=10, L=3$: cycle 5 FO4, versus 8 FO4 at $k=4$, so $1.6\times$; the ceiling is $1/3$ per FO4, i.e. $2.67\times$ the 4-stage design.
L4.explanation: Frequency is bounded by the flip-flop overhead alone, since $T/k$ vanishes. This is why FO4 is the useful unit: it makes the ceiling visible without reference to a process node. Every added stage also adds flip-flops, clock load and misprediction depth.

L4.prompt_tpl: With mispredictions per instruction $m = {m}$ and a full pipeline refill on each, show how the product of relative frequency and relative IPC behaves between $k = 10$ and $k = {k2}$, for $T = 20$ and $L = 3$ FO4.
L4.answer: $f(k) = 1/(20/k+3)$ and $\mathrm{IPC}(k) \propto 1/(1+mk)$. At $m=0.005$: $k=10$ gives $0.200 \times 0.952 = 0.190$; $k=20$ gives $0.250 \times 0.909 = 0.227$; $k=40$ gives $0.286 \times 0.833 = 0.238$. The curve flattens while energy keeps rising linearly in $k$.
L4.explanation: The product of a saturating frequency curve and a linearly degrading IPC curve peaks and then decays. Where the peak sits depends entirely on $m$: better branch prediction moves the optimum deeper, which is exactly why predictor research and frequency ambition rose together in the 1990s.

concepts.t: The energy cost of a pipeline stage

L0.body:
# Every stage boundary you add is a rank of flip-flops on the clock tree.
#
#   datapath width      64 bits
#   control+tags        ~40 bits
#   flops per boundary  ~104
#
# A flip-flop's clock input toggles EVERY cycle whether or not data
# changes. So each added stage adds ~104 unconditional switching nodes
# plus their share of clock-tree buffers.
#
# In big cores the clock network is commonly quoted at 20-35% of total
# dynamic power. Deeper pipeline -> more clock load -> more of that 30%.
L0.cloze: A flip-flop's clock input toggles {{c1::every cycle}} regardless of whether the data changes, so added pipeline stages raise power even when idle. The clock network is typically quoted at {{c2::20-35}} percent of core dynamic power.

concepts.L1: Adding a pipeline stage adds a full rank of flip-flops whose clock pins switch unconditionally, plus the clock-tree buffering to drive them. Depth therefore raises dynamic power roughly linearly, independent of whether the extra frequency is used.
concepts.L2: The usual mental model, that pipelining is free because the same work is done, ignores that clocking is not data-dependent. Data activity factors sit around 0.1 to 0.2 on a datapath; a clock pin's activity factor is 1.0 by construction, and the clock tree is the largest single net in the chip.
concepts.L3: Put it in the power equation. Dynamic power is $P = \alpha C V^{2} f$. For a datapath node $\alpha$ is perhaps $0.15$: it toggles when the data changes. For a clock node $\alpha = 1$ by definition, since it rises and falls every cycle. A stage adds roughly a hundred flip-flops, each with a clock pin, a share of local buffering and internal power, all at $\alpha = 1$. Then the frequency the deeper pipeline enables multiplies the whole chip's power again. Hence clock gating, forcing $\alpha$ to zero on idle regions, is the highest-leverage power technique in digital design, and hence ML accelerators use shallow pipelines and wide datapaths: equal throughput, a fraction of the clocked state.

L4.prompt_tpl: A stage boundary adds {n} flip-flops. Compare the dynamic energy contributed per cycle by those clock pins against {m} datapath nodes with activity factor {a}, assuming equal per-node capacitance. Answer with the clock-pin energy contribution in node-equivalents.
L4.answer: Clock contribution $\propto n \times 1.0$; datapath $\propto m \times a$. For $n = 104$, $m = 500$, $a = 0.15$: $104$ versus $75$, so the added clock pins alone exceed the switching energy of five times as many data nodes.
L4.explanation: Activity factor is the whole argument. Clock nets switch with $\alpha = 1$; data nets typically $0.1$ to $0.2$. A modest number of unconditionally toggling nodes therefore rivals a much larger set of data nodes, which is why clock gating pays and why pipeline depth is a power decision as much as a timing one.

L4.prompt_tpl: An accelerator designer runs a {w}-wide MAC datapath at {f} MHz rather than a narrow one at {g} times the frequency for the same throughput. Give the energy argument.
L4.answer: Same arithmetic throughput, but the wide-and-slow version has far fewer clocked stage boundaries per unit of work and can run at a lower supply voltage, so both the clock energy and the $V^{2}$ term fall. Frequency buys nothing that width does not, and costs voltage.
L4.explanation: Throughput is width times frequency, so it can be bought either way, but energy is not symmetric: frequency forces a higher supply voltage to meet timing, and $P$ depends on $V^{2}$, while width scales energy only linearly. Wide and slow is the standard accelerator answer, and it is why a TPU-class array runs below 1 GHz.

prereqs: Pipeline depth as a design variable

L0.body:
# Wasted work per committed instruction:
#
#   m = mispredictions per instruction
#   W = instructions squashed per misprediction (~ window occupancy)
#
#   wasted issued instructions per committed instruction = m * W
#
#   m = 0.005 (99.5% accurate), W =  60  ->  0.30   (30% waste)
#   m = 0.010,                  W = 100  ->  1.00   (as much wasted as useful)
#   m = 0.020,                  W = 100  ->  2.00   (2 wasted per useful)
#
# A systolic array: m = 0, W = 0. There is nothing to predict.
L0.cloze: Wasted issue energy per committed instruction is {{c1::m times W}}. At 99 percent accuracy with a 100-instruction window, you issue {{c2::one}} wasted instruction for every useful one. An accelerator with a static schedule has {{c3::zero}} speculative waste.

concepts.L1: Speculative execution issues work that may be discarded. The discarded work still charges the register file, the issue queue, the functional units and often the caches, so the energy is spent whether or not the prediction was right.
concepts.L2: The standard framing treats misprediction as a latency cost in refill cycles. The energy cost is separate and larger in aggregate: even correctly predicted paths spend energy on wakeup, select and rename logic a statically scheduled machine does not need, and that overhead is paid every cycle, not only on mispredictions.
concepts.L3: Two costs compose. The first is squashed work, $mW$ per committed instruction: at $m = 0.01$ and a window of 100 you throw away one instruction's worth of issue energy for every one you keep. The second is the machinery itself. Out-of-order issue broadcasts each result tag to every waiting operand, a comparator array growing with issue width times queue depth, toggling every cycle regardless of prediction accuracy. So domain-specific accelerators abandon speculation rather than predict better: with a static schedule there is no inner-loop branch to predict, no rename table and no reorder buffer, and the energy a CPU spends deciding what to do next goes to arithmetic.

L4.prompt_tpl: A core sustains {ipc} IPC with a {w}-instruction window and a branch every {b} instructions predicted at {pacc} percent accuracy. Compute wasted issued instructions per committed instruction. Answer with the wasted instructions per committed instruction.
L4.answer: $m = (1-\mathrm{acc})/b$ mispredictions per instruction; waste $= mW$. For acc = 99, $b = 5$, $W = 192$: $m = 0.002$, waste $= 0.384$ instructions squashed per committed one.
L4.explanation: Note that IPC does not enter the waste ratio directly: what matters is how often you are wrong and how much work is in flight when you find out. A wider window improves latency hiding and simultaneously enlarges the blast radius of every misprediction. Both effects are real and they pull opposite ways on energy.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team proposes adding a {n}-entry reorder buffer to an ML inference accelerator whose inner loop is a static matmul schedule. Assess.
options: Reject: static schedules leave nothing to speculate on, so it is pure overhead
Accept: reorder buffers always improve throughput by hiding memory latency
Accept, but only if the accelerator has a branch predictor to feed it
L4.answer: Reject: the inner loop has no unpredictable control flow, so there is nothing to speculate on, and the reorder buffer would add area and per-cycle energy for no throughput. The scheduling problem belongs to the compiler.
L4.explanation: Speculation pays where control flow is data-dependent and unpredictable. A matmul loop nest has statically known trip counts, so a compiler can produce the schedule at build time. Adding out-of-order machinery would spend area and clocked energy every cycle to rediscover a schedule that is already known.

prereqs: Speculative execution and its security cost

concepts.t: Issue width and the quadratic wakeup problem

L0.body:
# Out-of-order wakeup: every result tag must be compared against every
# waiting source operand in the issue queue.
#
#   Q = issue queue entries, W = issue width, 2 sources per entry
#   comparators = 2 * Q * W
#
#   Q=32, W=2  ->  128 comparators
#   Q=64, W=4  ->  512
#   Q=128, W=8 -> 2048        16x the comparators for 4x the width
#
# And the select logic is a priority encoder over Q entries, whose delay
# grows as ~log Q, on a path that must close in ONE cycle for
# back-to-back dependent issue.
L0.cloze: Wakeup needs {{c1::2 Q W}} tag comparators, so doubling both queue depth and issue width multiplies them by {{c2::4}}. The wakeup-select loop must close in {{c3::one cycle}} for dependent instructions to issue back to back.

concepts.L1: Superscalar issue requires waking every dependent operand when a result is produced and then selecting up to $W$ ready instructions. The comparator count grows as the product of queue size and width, and the whole loop must complete within one cycle.
concepts.L2: Width is limited not by execution units, which are cheap, but by the wakeup-select loop, a single-cycle feedback path that cannot be pipelined without losing back-to-back dependent issue. That is the structural reason mainstream cores stalled at 4 to 8 wide for two decades while accelerators went to thousands of MACs.
concepts.L3: Palacharla, Jouppi and Smith named the three complexity-critical structures in 1997: rename map, wakeup-select loop and operand bypass network, all scaling worse than linearly in issue width. Wakeup is $O(QW)$ in comparators and its wire delay grows because the tag must reach every entry. Bypass is worse: a full network among $W$ units needs $O(W^{2})$ paths, each crossing the datapath. Select is a priority encoder over $Q$. Because the loop is feedback, pipelining it inserts a bubble between dependent instructions, costing IPC on exactly the chains that limit performance. Accelerators delete the problem: a static schedule needs no wakeup, select or bypass, only fixed neighbour wiring.

L4.prompt_tpl: An issue queue holds {q} entries with two source operands each and the machine issues {w} instructions per cycle. Compute the tag comparators required, and the factor by which it grows if both are doubled. Answer with the number of tag comparators.
L4.answer: Comparators $= 2QW$. For $Q = 64$, $W = 4$: $512$. Doubling both gives $2 \times 128 \times 8 = 2048$, a factor of 4.
L4.explanation: The comparator array is the visible cost; the hidden cost is the wire that carries each result tag to every queue entry, whose delay grows with the physical size of the array. Both effects push against width, which is why issue widths plateaued while transistor budgets kept growing.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why the wakeup-select loop cannot simply be pipelined over {n} cycles to relieve its timing pressure.
L4.answer: Because it is a feedback loop: an instruction's result must wake its dependents in time for them to be selected the very next cycle. Pipelining it inserts that many bubbles between every pair of dependent instructions, which directly lengthens the critical dependence chain that limits IPC.
L4.explanation: Back-to-back dependent issue is the property that makes out-of-order execution worth its cost. Splitting wakeup and select across cycles preserves throughput on independent instructions and destroys it on chains, and chains are what out-of-order machines exist to shorten. Some designs pipeline it anyway and speculatively wake, which reintroduces recovery logic.

prereqs: Superscalar issue width and execution ports
Register renaming and the physical register file

concepts.t: In-order versus out-of-order: the area and energy bill

L0.body:
# What out-of-order execution adds that in-order does not have:
#
#   rename map + free list          physical register file (2-4x arch regs)
#   reorder buffer                  load/store queue with address CAM
#   issue queue + wakeup CAM        checkpoint/recovery state
#   branch predictor (large)        memory dependence predictor
#
# Rough shape from published core areas (same node, excluding caches):
#   a small in-order RV64 core      ~0.02-0.05 mm^2
#   a wide out-of-order RV64 core   ~0.5-1.5 mm^2
#   ratio roughly 10-30x for maybe 3-5x the single-thread performance
L0.cloze: Out-of-order adds rename, a {{c1::reorder buffer}}, an issue queue with a wakeup CAM, and a load/store queue with an address CAM. The area ratio against a small in-order core is roughly {{c2::10-30x}} for about {{c3::3-5x}} the single-thread performance.

concepts.L1: Out-of-order execution buys latency tolerance by adding renaming, a reorder buffer, an issue queue and a load-store queue with associative search. Every one of those is content-addressable memory, which is dense in transistors and hot in operation.
concepts.L2: The area ratio is worse than the performance ratio, which is why throughput-oriented designs use many small in-order cores or accelerators rather than few big ones. The conclusion is not that out-of-order is bad: it buys single-thread latency, and single-thread latency is the one thing parallelism cannot buy back.
concepts.L3: Reason about where each structure earns its keep. The reorder buffer exists to make exceptions precise, a correctness requirement, not a performance one. The issue queue and rename find independent work across a cache miss: at 200 cycles and 4 IPC that needs 800 instructions of lookahead, far beyond any real window, so out-of-order hides tens of cycles, not hundreds. The load-store queue lets loads pass stores safely, and its address CAM is the least scalable part of the machine. Accelerators avoid all of it by making memory latency statically known through scratchpads and DMA. That is the co-design move: remove the uncertainty rather than build hardware to discover a schedule at runtime.

L4.prompt_tpl: A core sustains {ipc} IPC and takes a last-level cache miss costing {lat} cycles. How many instructions of independent work must the window hold to fully hide it, and what does that say about a {w}-entry reorder buffer? Answer with the instructions of independent work needed.
L4.answer: Instructions needed $= \mathrm{IPC} \times \mathrm{latency}$. For 4 IPC and 350 cycles: 1400 instructions, far beyond a 512-entry reorder buffer, so a DRAM miss is only partly hidden however wide the window.
L4.explanation: This is Little's law applied to the instruction window. It explains why window sizes grew far more slowly than memory latency and why memory-level parallelism, overlapping several misses, matters more than window size: covering one miss is hopeless, overlapping four of them is not.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a fixed silicon area you can build one wide out-of-order core or roughly {n} small in-order cores. Which is right for an inference serving workload dominated by matrix multiplication?
options: Neither: dense matmul has a static schedule, so a systolic array beats both on performance per watt
One wide out-of-order core, because matrix multiplication is latency sensitive
The small in-order cores, because they have better aggregate branch prediction
L4.answer: Neither, in the limit: the right answer for dense matmul is a systolic array, because the work has no unpredictable control flow and no need for latency tolerance, so both CPU designs spend most of their area on machinery the workload does not use.
L4.explanation: The question is a trap in a useful way. Many small cores beat one big core on throughput workloads, but a matmul kernel has a static schedule and enormous data reuse, so an array of MACs with a fixed interconnect beats both by an order of magnitude in performance per watt. Recognising when the CPU question is the wrong question is the co-design skill.

prereqs: The reorder buffer and precise exceptions

concepts.t: Register file ports and the wire cost of width

L0.body:
# An SRAM-style register cell with R read and W write ports needs
# R+W wordlines and roughly (R+W) bitline pairs crossing the cell.
# Cell area is wire-pitch limited in both directions:
#
#   area per bit  ~  (R + W)^2   (both dimensions grow with port count)
#
#   2R 1W  (in-order scalar)     -> (3)^2  =   9  units
#   8R 4W  (4-wide OoO)          -> (12)^2 = 144  units   (16x)
#  16R 8W  (8-wide OoO)          -> (24)^2 = 576  units   (64x)
#
# Mitigations: banking, clustering, operand bypass, and in accelerators,
# not having a shared register file at all.
L0.cloze: Register-cell area scales roughly as {{c1::(R+W) squared}} because both wordlines and bitlines grow with port count. Going from 2R1W to 16R8W is about a {{c2::64x}} area increase per bit.

concepts.L1: A multiported register file's cell area grows with the square of total port count, because read and write ports each add a wordline in one dimension and a bitline pair in the other. Ports, not capacity, dominate register-file cost in wide machines.
concepts.L2: This is why issue width is expensive even before you consider the issue queue: an $N$-wide machine needs $2N$ read ports and $N$ write ports, so the register file alone grows quadratically. It is also why vector and matrix units keep separate register files rather than widening the scalar one.
concepts.L3: The quadratic comes from geometry, not transistor count. Each read port adds a horizontal wordline and a vertical bitline pair through every cell; each write port does the same. The cell must be at least as tall as its wordline pitch and as wide as its bitline pitch, so both dimensions grow linearly in $(R+W)$ and area as the square. Access time grows too: the bitline is longer and more heavily loaded. Real designs escape by banking the file, clustering execution units around private copies, or bypassing so operands never read the file at all. An accelerator escapes more cheaply: PEs hold operands in local registers wired to neighbours, with no shared multiported structure.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare register-file cell area for a machine with {r1} read and {w1} write ports against one with {r2} read and {w2} write ports, using the $(R+W)^{{2}}$ rule.
L4.explanation: The rule is approximate but the exponent is right and it is the number that matters: port count, not entry count, is what makes a register file expensive. Doubling issue width roughly doubles port count and therefore quadruples cell area, before any change to the number of architectural registers.

L4.prompt_tpl: An accelerator with {n} MAC units has no shared register file at all. Explain what replaces it and why that is cheaper than a file with enough ports to feed {n} units.
L4.answer: Each PE holds its operands in a few local flip-flops or a tiny local register file and receives new values from fixed wires to its immediate neighbours. A shared file feeding that many units would need thousands of ports, whose area grows as the square, and global wires whose delay would set the clock.
L4.explanation: The systolic answer is to make communication local and static. Neighbour-to-neighbour wires are short, have constant fanout and cost no arbitration, so the structure scales linearly in PE count. A centralised multiported file for the same units is quadratic in area and would not close timing at any useful frequency.

prereqs: Issue width and the quadratic wakeup problem

concepts.t: Choosing a design point for a known workload

L0.body:
# The co-design question is never "what is the best core?" It is:
#
#   given this workload mix, this power budget and this area budget,
#   which structure maximises the metric I am actually paid for?
#
# Worked example: 200 mm^2 and 300 W for LLM inference.
#   option A  32 wide OoO cores          ~ 3 TFLOP/s   fp16
#   option B  1 large systolic array     ~ 300 TFLOP/s fp16
#   option C  A + B, small host + array  ~ 300 TFLOP/s + control
#
# C wins, and that is why every accelerator has a wimpy control core.
# The interesting question is only: how big does the host need to be?
L0.cloze: The design question is not the best core but the best structure for {{c1::a given workload, power budget and area budget}}. Every real accelerator pairs a large array with a {{c2::small control core}}.

concepts.L1: Architecture is a constrained optimisation, not a search for the fastest machine. The inputs are a workload characterisation, an area budget, a power budget and a target metric, and the output is a partition of the die among structures.
concepts.L2: The common mistake is optimising the accelerator in isolation. Every real workload has a serial or irregular fraction, and Amdahl's law applies to the whole chip: an array 100 times faster on 90 percent of the work yields a total speedup of 9.2, not 100, so host core size is a first-order decision.
concepts.L3: Compute the Amdahl bound before designing anything. With parallelisable fraction $p$ and array speedup $s$, overall speedup is $1/((1-p) + p/s)$. At $p = 0.9$, $s = 100$: $1/(0.1 + 0.009) = 9.2$. At $p = 0.99$: $1/(0.01+0.0099) = 50.3$. The difference between 90 and 99 percent coverage is a factor of 5 in delivered performance, which usually dominates any choice about the array itself. That is why accelerator teams spend so much effort on operator coverage and on a host fast enough for the residue: layout transforms, softmax, normalisation, sampling. It is also why performance modelling exists as a job; the chip's value is decided by workload analysis long before any RTL.

L4.prompt_tpl: An accelerator is {s}x faster than the host on the {p} percent of work it covers. Compute overall speedup, and the speedup if coverage rises to {p2} percent. Answer with the overall speedup at coverage p.
L4.answer: Speedup $= 1/((1-p) + p/s)$. For $s = 100$, $p = 0.90$: $9.17$. At $p = 0.99$: $50.25$. Coverage dominates array speed once $s$ is large.
L4.explanation: Once $s$ is large the $p/s$ term is negligible and the answer is set almost entirely by the uncovered fraction $1-p$. This is why adding operators to a compiler often beats making the array bigger, and it is the single most useful piece of arithmetic in accelerator planning.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your array is idle {idle} percent of the time waiting for the host to run unsupported operators. You have budget for one change. Which do you make?
options: Improve operator coverage or host speed, since the uncovered fraction bounds total speedup
Double the array width, since peak throughput is the headline metric
Add HBM bandwidth, since idle time is always a bandwidth symptom
L4.answer: Increase operator coverage or host throughput, not array size: by Amdahl's law the uncovered fraction bounds achievable speedup, and enlarging an already-idle array moves nothing.
L4.explanation: An idle array is a coverage problem wearing a hardware costume. Doubling array width changes only the covered fraction's runtime, which is already the small term. The measurement to demand first is the split of wall-clock time between array and host, because it identifies which term of the Amdahl expression you are actually optimising.

L0.body:
# Three stable states per cache block, per cache.
#
#   I  Invalid   : not present
#   S  Shared    : present, clean, other caches may also have it
#   M  Modified  : present, dirty, THIS cache is the only copy
#
# Transitions (snooping, bus-ordered):
#   local read,  I -> S     : issue GetS
#   local write, I -> M     : issue GetM
#   local write, S -> M     : issue Upgrade (must invalidate other sharers)
#   see GetS  while M       : write back, M -> S
#   see GetM  while M or S  : invalidate, -> I
#
# Invariants: at most one M anywhere; if any M exists, no S exists.
L0.cloze: MSI's two invariants are: at most {{c1::one M}} copy exists anywhere, and if an M copy exists there are {{c2::no S}} copies. A write to a block in S must issue an {{c3::Upgrade}} to invalidate other sharers.

concepts.L1: MSI is the smallest protocol that keeps caches coherent: one writer or many readers, enforced by invalidating every other copy before a write. Every other protocol in use is MSI plus states that remove a specific message from the common case.
concepts.L2: The state you should learn first is not M but the transition $S \rightarrow M$, because it is the one that costs. A processor that reads then writes a block it alone will ever touch still pays a full bus transaction to upgrade, and that single wasted transaction is the entire reason MESI exists.
concepts.L3: State the invariant precisely: for every block, either exactly one cache holds M and none holds S, or no cache holds M and any number hold S. Every transition must preserve that. A write from I must invalidate all sharers and any M holder, so it needs a global operation. A write from S needs the same invalidation but not the data, hence a separate Upgrade message. This is where the single-writer-multiple-reader property software depends on comes from: not emergent behaviour but the protocol's induction hypothesis. The three stable states are also a fiction, since a real implementation needs a transient state for every window between issuing a request and receiving its response.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two cores, MSI, block starts Invalid everywhere. Core 0 reads, core 1 reads, core 0 writes, core 1 reads. Give the state in each cache after each of the {n} steps and the bus transactions issued.
L4.answer: 1) C0 GetS: C0 = S, C1 = I. 2) C1 GetS: both S. 3) C0 Upgrade, invalidating C1: C0 = M, C1 = I. 4) C1 GetS forces C0 to write back and downgrade: both S, memory updated.
L4.explanation: Trace it against the invariant after each step: never two writers, never a writer alongside a reader. Step 3 is the interesting one, because C0 already had the data and still needed a bus transaction purely to revoke C1's copy. That transaction is what MESI's Exclusive state removes when no other cache has a copy.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why MSI needs a distinct Upgrade transaction rather than reusing GetM when a core writes a block it already holds in {st}.
L4.answer: Because the cache already has valid data; it needs only permission. GetM would return a data payload the requester does not need, wasting interconnect bandwidth equal to a full cache block on every read-modify sequence.
L4.explanation: The distinction is bandwidth, not correctness. On a 64-byte block, treating an upgrade as a full GetM moves 64 bytes for a transaction that logically carries zero bytes of data. On a shared bus with many cores doing read-modify-write on the same structure, that difference is most of the traffic.
