L0.body:
# MESI = MSI + E (Exclusive: present, CLEAN, and the only copy).
#
#   read miss, no other cache has it  -> E   (not S)
#   read miss, others have it         -> S
#   write while in E                  -> M, SILENTLY. No bus transaction.
#   see GetS while in E               -> S (no writeback: it is clean)
#
# Requires a shared-line signal on the bus (or a directory) so the
# requester can tell whether anyone else responded.
#
# Payoff: for private data, read-then-write costs ONE transaction, not two.
L0.cloze: The E state means present, {{c1::clean}}, and the only copy. A write from E goes to M {{c2::silently}}, with no bus transaction. Detecting E requires a {{c3::shared-line signal}} telling the requester whether any other cache responded.

concepts.L1: MESI adds a clean-exclusive state so that a cache that loaded a block nobody else has can later write it without any bus transaction. It exists entirely to make the read-then-write pattern on private data cost one transaction instead of two.
concepts.L2: E is not a performance nicety on the margins: most data in most programs is private, so the read-then-write sequence covers stack slots, freshly allocated objects and thread-local state. Without E, every one of those pays an Upgrade broadcast. That is why essentially no shipping protocol is plain MSI.
concepts.L3: The cost of E is interconnect signalling people forget when reading the state diagram: at the moment of the read response the requester must learn whether any other cache also had the line. On a snooping bus that is a wired-OR shared line every cache asserts if it holds the block; in a directory the home node knows the sharer set and answers directly. Either way E is implementable only if the fabric can distinguish nobody-else-has-it from somebody-does. Note too that E to M is silent, observed by no other agent, which is why a directory must treat E and M identically for invalidation: it cannot know whether the holder has written.

L4.prompt_tpl: A thread performs {n} read-then-write sequences on private data, each on a distinct cache block. Compare the number of coherence transactions under MSI and MESI. Answer with the number of MESI coherence transactions.
L4.answer: MSI: $2n$ (GetS then Upgrade). MESI: $n$ (GetS returns E, the write is silent). For $n = 100000$: 200000 versus 100000, a 2x reduction in coherence traffic.
L4.explanation: Private data is the common case, which is why this halving matters. It also explains an observable effect: on MESI machines a first-touch write to freshly allocated memory generates no visible coherence traffic at all, which can make coherence look cheaper in microbenchmarks than it is for genuinely shared data.

L4.prompt_tpl: A directory-based system must decide how to handle an invalidation for a block one cache holds in {st}. What does it do and why?
options: Treat E like M, because the silent E to M upgrade is invisible to the directory
Treat E like S, because E is defined as clean and therefore needs no writeback
Refuse the request, because E blocks cannot be invalidated without a downgrade first
L4.answer: Treat it exactly like Modified: send an invalidation and expect a possible dirty writeback, because the E to M transition is silent and the directory cannot know whether the holder wrote the block.
L4.explanation: Silence is the price of E. The whole point of the state is that the upgrade to M generates no message, so no other agent can distinguish a clean exclusive copy from a dirty one. The directory must therefore assume the worst and accept a writeback that may not come.

L0.body:
# MOESI = MESI + O (Owned: dirty, shared, and I am responsible for it).
#
#   In MESI, M + someone else reads  -> write back to memory, both go S.
#   In MOESI, M + someone else reads -> M -> O, requester -> S.
#                                       NO writeback. Memory stays stale.
#   The O holder supplies data to future readers and must write back on
#   eviction.
#
# Invariant change: memory is no longer guaranteed up to date when the
# block is Shared. Exactly one cache may be in O; others are S.
#
# Used by: AMD (Opteron onward), ARM AMBA ACE (SharedDirty).
L0.cloze: The O state means dirty, shared, and responsible for {{c1::writing back on eviction}}. Under MOESI, a read of a Modified block causes {{c2::no writeback}} to memory, so memory may be stale while the block is shared. Exactly {{c3::one}} cache may hold O.

concepts.L1: MOESI lets a dirty block be shared without writing it back to memory. The former writer becomes the Owner: it keeps the dirty data, supplies it to other readers, and is obliged to write it back when it evicts.
concepts.L2: The invariant that breaks is the one most people are actually relying on: under MESI, a block in S is guaranteed identical to memory, and under MOESI it is not. Anything that reads memory without participating in coherence, a naive DMA engine or a debug port, becomes incorrect rather than merely slow.
concepts.L3: The traffic argument is direct. Take a producer-consumer pattern: one core writes a block, several then read it. Under MESI each M to S transition forces a writeback, so the block crosses the memory interface once per store epoch even though no reader wanted it in memory. Under MOESI the data travels cache to cache and memory is touched only when the owner evicts. With a remote memory controller that is the difference between a local transfer and a full round trip. The costs are an extra state in every tag, a rule that the owner must respond, and loss of the clean-shared guarantee, which is why non-coherent agents on MOESI need explicit cache maintenance.

L4.prompt_tpl: One core writes a block, then {r} other cores read it in turn, repeated {k} times. Count memory writebacks under MESI and under MOESI, assuming no eviction occurs. Answer with the number of MESI writebacks.
L4.answer: MESI: one writeback per M-to-S downgrade, so $k$ writebacks. MOESI: zero, since the owner supplies data and only writes back on eviction. For $k = 1000$: 1000 versus 0.
L4.explanation: The readers get their data from a cache either way; the difference is whether memory is also updated each time. MOESI defers that indefinitely, which is why it suits multi-socket systems where the memory controller may be an interconnect hop away and the writeback would be the expensive part.

L4.prompt_tpl: A DMA engine on a MOESI system reads {n} KiB directly from DRAM without issuing coherence requests. What can go wrong and what is the fix?
L4.answer: It can read stale data, because a block held in O is dirty in a cache while memory holds an older value. The fix is either to make the DMA engine coherent, issuing snoop or directory requests, or to require software cache maintenance, cleaning the range before the transfer.
L4.explanation: Under MESI a Shared block always matched memory, so non-coherent readers happened to work. MOESI removes that accident. This is a genuine source of silent data corruption in SoC bring-up, and it is why ARM systems distinguish coherent and non-coherent masters explicitly and why drivers carry explicit cache clean and invalidate calls.

L0.body:
# Problem MESIF solves: in MESI with several S copies, who answers a
# read? If all of them answer you get N redundant data messages; if none
# does, you go to memory and pay full latency.
#
# MESIF = MESI + F (Forward: clean, shared, and the designated responder).
#
#   at most one cache in F; all other sharers in S
#   only the F cache supplies data cache-to-cache
#   the MOST RECENT requester becomes F (so F migrates to the hot core)
#
# F is CLEAN, unlike MOESI's O: memory stays up to date, so a writeback
# is still needed when the line leaves the caches dirty.
#
# Used by: Intel QPI/UPI.
L0.cloze: F designates {{c1::one}} sharer as the responder, so a read gets {{c2::exactly one}} cache-to-cache data reply instead of N or zero. Unlike MOESI's O state, F is {{c3::clean}}, so memory stays up to date.

concepts.L1: MESIF adds a Forward state that elects a single clean sharer to answer read requests. It removes the ambiguity in MESI about which of several S copies should supply data, without allowing dirty sharing.
concepts.L2: MESIF and MOESI are often presented as rival letters when they solve different problems. MOESI is about avoiding writebacks by permitting dirty sharing; MESIF is about avoiding duplicate responses while keeping memory clean. A protocol can and sometimes does have both.
concepts.L3: The design pressure comes from point-to-point interconnects. On a shared bus a wired-OR signal plus a fixed priority rule picks a responder cheaply. On a mesh or ring there is no broadcast medium and no natural arbiter, so either every sharer replies, wasting bandwidth proportional to sharer count, or the protocol names one. F names one. Migrating F to the most recent requester is a locality heuristic: the newest sharer is often physically near the next requester. The software consequence is real: on MESIF machines the latency of read-sharing a hot line depends on which core holds F, so cache-to-cache latency is not symmetric across a socket.

L4.prompt_tpl: A design has {n} sharers of a hot read-only block on a ring interconnect. Which protocol feature most directly reduces the interconnect traffic on each new read?
options: A Forward state, which elects exactly one cache to supply the data
An Owned state, which lets the dirty holder answer without a writeback
A larger directory, since responder choice is a directory-capacity problem
L4.answer: A Forward state, because it elects exactly one responder; without it either every sharer replies, costing $n$ data messages, or none does and the read goes to memory.
L4.explanation: MOESI's Owned state does not help here: the block is clean, so there is nothing to avoid writing back. The problem is responder selection on a fabric with no broadcast arbiter, and that is precisely what F is for. Recognising which of the two extra states applies to a given symptom is the point.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why cache-to-cache transfer latency measured between core pairs on a MESIF machine is often {a}symmetric, and what that means for a benchmark.
L4.answer: Because the F state migrates to the most recent requester, so which cache answers depends on access history, and the physical distance from that cache to the requester varies across the die. A benchmark that measures pairwise latency therefore measures a history-dependent path, and results shift with warm-up order.
L4.explanation: This is a real hazard in core-to-core latency matrices: the number reported depends on which cache holds F when the measurement runs, which depends on the previous iteration. Interpreting such a matrix requires knowing the protocol, otherwise the asymmetry gets attributed to topology alone.

L0.body:
# Snooping's correctness argument in one sentence:
#   the shared medium serialises requests, so all caches observe the same
#   order, so a global order of coherence events exists for free.
#
#   cycle 0: C0 broadcasts GetM(A)
#   cycle 0: every cache tag array looks up A, in parallel
#   cycle 1: C1 (had A in M) responds, writes back, invalidates
#
# Cost per request:
#   reaches ALL N caches            O(N) messages
#   ALL N tag arrays do a lookup    O(N) tag bandwidth
#   total = N * (misses/s) * N      O(N^2)
#
# Duplicate tag arrays exist so snoops do not steal L1 tag ports.
L0.cloze: Snooping gets a global order for free because the {{c1::shared medium serialises}} requests. Its cost is that every request touches all N tag arrays, so total tag lookup demand grows as {{c2::N squared}}. Caches carry {{c3::duplicate tag arrays}} so snoops do not steal ports from the core.

concepts.L1: Snooping broadcasts every coherence request to every cache, which each check against their tags. The broadcast medium supplies a total order on requests, which is what makes the protocol's correctness argument short.
concepts.L2: The reason snooping dies at scale is not the wires but the tag-array bandwidth. Each cache must look up every request from every other cache, so the aggregate lookup rate grows quadratically in core count against a per-cache tag bandwidth that is fixed.
concepts.L3: Quantify it. Suppose each of $N$ cores generates $r$ coherence requests per second. Every request is snooped by all $N$ caches, so each cache absorbs $Nr$ lookups per second and the system performs $N^{2}r$. With $N = 8$ and $r = 10^{7}$, each tag array sees $8 \times 10^{7}$ lookups per second, which a duplicated tag array handles. At $N = 64$ it is $6.4 \times 10^{8}$ per cache, stolen from the core's own accesses unless duplicated. At $N = 256$ it is hopeless. The broadcast medium fails first in practice, but even with unlimited broadcast bandwidth the tag arrays impose the same quadratic. Snooping survives only by layering a snoop filter or directory at the cluster boundary.

L4.prompt_tpl: Each of {n} cores issues {r} million coherence requests per second on a snooping fabric. Compute the tag lookups per second each cache must absorb and the system total. Answer with the tag lookups per second each cache absorbs.
L4.answer: Per cache $= N r$; total $= N^{2} r$. For $N = 64$, $r = 20$ million: each cache absorbs $1.28 \times 10^{9}$ lookups per second and the system performs $8.19 \times 10^{10}$.
L4.explanation: Per-cache load grows linearly in $N$ while the number of caches also grows, giving the quadratic total. Since a tag array's lookup rate is fixed by its design, the per-cache figure is what actually breaks first, and it breaks whether or not the interconnect can carry the broadcasts.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why high-performance cores keep a duplicate copy of their L1 tag array, and what a {n}-core design pays for it.
L4.answer: Because snoop lookups would otherwise contend with the core's own accesses for tag ports, stalling the pipeline on other cores' traffic. The cost is a second tag array per cache in area and power, plus the requirement to keep the two exactly consistent on every fill and eviction.
L4.explanation: The duplicate exists to decouple snoop bandwidth from core bandwidth. Getting it wrong is a classic silicon bug class: the shadow tags must be updated atomically with the real ones or the protocol observes a state the cache is not actually in, producing a coherence violation that appears only under precise timing.

concepts.t: Directory coherence and the sharer vector

L0.body:
# The directory replaces broadcast with a per-block record at a home node.
#
#   entry = { state, owner, sharer set }
#
# Full bit-vector sharer set: N bits per memory block.
#   64B block = 512 bits of data
#   N =   64 cores ->   64/512 = 12.5% storage overhead
#   N =  256 cores ->  256/512 = 50%
#   N = 1024 cores -> 1024/512 = 200%   <- directory bigger than DRAM data
#
# Compressed alternatives: coarse vectors (1 bit per cluster of k cores),
# limited pointers (store the first p sharers, then broadcast), and
# sparse/cache-like directories that only track cached blocks.
L0.cloze: A full bit-vector directory costs {{c1::N bits}} per block, which against a 64-byte block is {{c2::12.5}} percent at 64 cores and {{c3::200}} percent at 1024. Compressions include coarse vectors, limited pointers and sparse directories.

concepts.L1: A directory keeps, for every memory block, which caches hold it and in what state, so a coherence request goes to one home node instead of to everyone. Messages become point-to-point and proportional to actual sharers, not to core count.
concepts.L2: The naive full bit-vector directory does not scale either: its storage grows as cores times memory, so at high core counts the directory exceeds the data it describes. The scaling win comes from the message count, and it has to be paid for by giving up exact sharer knowledge.
concepts.L3: Set the costs side by side. Snooping sends $O(N)$ messages per request and uses $O(1)$ storage. A full-vector directory sends $O(1 + s)$ messages, $s$ the actual sharer count, usually one or two, and uses $O(N)$ storage per block. Real systems are neither. They size a sparse directory to cache capacity rather than DRAM, since only cached blocks need entries, and compress the sharer set: coarse vectors give one bit per cluster of $k$ cores, cutting storage by $k$ at the price of cluster-wide spurious invalidations; limited pointers keep $p$ sharers exactly and broadcast beyond. Every compression trades exactness for storage and becomes needless traffic when a workload breaks its assumption.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compute full-bit-vector directory storage overhead for {n} cores with a {b}-byte block, and the overhead if a coarse vector with one bit per {k} cores is used instead. Answer with the full-vector directory overhead as a fraction.
L4.answer: Full: $N/(8b)$. Coarse: $N/(k \cdot 8b)$. For $N = 1024$, $b = 64$: full $= 1024/512 = 200$ percent; with $k = 8$, $128/512 = 25$ percent, at the cost of invalidating whole clusters.
L4.explanation: The full vector is linear in core count against a fixed block size, which is why it becomes absurd past a few hundred cores. Coarse vectors divide storage by the cluster size and multiply spurious invalidations by roughly the same factor, so the exchange rate is explicit and workload-dependent.

L4.prompt_tpl: A sparse directory sized to total cache capacity rather than DRAM capacity can run out of entries. Describe what must happen when a new block needs an entry and all {w} ways of the directory set are used.
L4.answer: The directory must evict an existing entry, and because the entry is the only record of who holds the block, eviction forces invalidation of every cached copy that entry describes. That is a directory-induced cache miss with no corresponding capacity pressure in the caches themselves.
L4.explanation: This effect surprises people because the invalidation has no visible cause in the cache hierarchy: the data still fits, but its coherence metadata did not. It is why sparse directories are over-provisioned relative to cache capacity and why their associativity matters as much as their size.

concepts.t: Snooping versus directory: the scaling argument

L0.body:
#                     snooping            directory
#   messages/request   O(N) broadcast      O(1 + s), s = real sharers
#   storage            O(1)                O(N)/block (full vector)
#   latency, 2 cores   lower (no home hop) higher (req -> home -> owner)
#   ordering           free (bus order)    built at the home node
#   scales to          ~8-32 cores         hundreds, with compression
#
# Real machines hybridise: snoop in a cluster, directory between.
#
# Accelerators do neither. A TPU has no coherence protocol at all:
# scratchpads plus explicit DMA make the question not arise.
L0.cloze: Snooping costs {{c1::O(N)}} messages and O(1) storage; a full directory costs O(1+s) messages and {{c2::O(N)}} storage per block. Real machines {{c3::snoop within a cluster and use a directory between clusters}}. Accelerators avoid the question entirely with scratchpads and DMA.

concepts.L1: The two protocols trade message count against storage and add a latency hop. Snooping wins at small core counts because it needs no home-node indirection; directories win at large counts because broadcast bandwidth and snoop tag bandwidth both grow quadratically.
concepts.L2: The conclusion an accelerator architect should draw is not which protocol to pick, but that coherence is optional. A TPU-class design has no coherence protocol at all: memory is software-managed scratchpad moved by explicit DMA, so the hardware never needs to discover who holds what.
concepts.L3: Follow the crossover. A two-hop directory request costs home lookup plus forward plus response, roughly 1.5 to 2 times a snoop's cache-to-cache latency on a small die, so at four or eight cores snooping is simply faster. As $N$ grows, snoop tag bandwidth per cache grows as $N$ and broadcast bandwidth as $N^{2}$, while directory message count stays flat because sharing degree does not grow with core count. The crossover in shipped designs sits between 8 and 32 cores, exactly the cluster size in multi-socket server parts. Accelerators sidestep the curve: if the compiler knows which tile each PE needs and when, it issues a DMA, and the protocol, its transients and its traffic all disappear.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given cache-to-cache latency {t1} ns under snooping, a directory home hop of {th} ns, and snoop tag bandwidth of {bw} billion lookups per second per cache, find roughly where directory coherence becomes preferable as core count grows.
L4.answer: Directory latency is about $t_{1} + t_{h}$, a fixed penalty. Snooping's per-cache lookup load is $Nr$, so it stays viable while $Nr < bw$. With $r = 2 \times 10^{7}$ per core and $bw = 10^{9}$, snooping saturates near $N = 50$; the practical crossover comes earlier because tag ports are shared with the core.
L4.explanation: The comparison is a fixed latency penalty against a load that grows linearly in $N$. Directories always cost an extra hop and always win eventually. Where the crossing happens depends on miss rate, so a workload with high sharing pushes it earlier and a workload of independent threads pushes it later.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are designing a {n}-PE ML accelerator. Which coherence approach do you specify?
options: No coherence: software-managed scratchpads and explicit DMA
Full-vector directory coherence, for programmability across all PEs
Snooping, since PE counts are small enough for a broadcast fabric
L4.answer: None: use software-managed scratchpads with explicit DMA. The dataflow is statically known, so there is nothing for a coherence protocol to discover, and omitting it removes area, energy, latency variance and an enormous verification burden.
L4.explanation: This is the answer the whole section builds to. Coherence exists to handle sharing patterns unknown until runtime. A matmul loop nest's data movement is known at compile time, so the protocol would spend area and energy rediscovering it. Every major ML accelerator makes this choice.

prereqs: Directory coherence and the sharer vector

concepts.t: Transient states: why the textbook protocol is a lie

L0.body:
# Textbook MSI: 3 states. A real implementation of MSI:
#
#   stable:    I, S, M
#   transient: IS_D  (I, issued GetS, awaiting Data)
#              IM_AD (I, issued GetM, awaiting Ack and Data)
#              IM_A  (data arrived, still awaiting invalidation acks)
#              SM_AD, SM_A  (upgrading from S)
#              MI_A  (evicting M, awaiting writeback ack)
#              SI_A, II_A   (evictions)
#
# Sorin, Hill & Wood's MSI directory tables run to dozens of states,
# because every message in flight is a state. The verification burden
# is in the transients, not the stable states.
L0.cloze: Every request in flight is a {{c1::transient state}}, so a three-state protocol becomes a dozen or more once implemented. The verification burden lives in the {{c2::transients}}, not the stable states.

concepts.L1: Between issuing a coherence request and receiving all its responses, a block is in neither its old state nor its new one. Implementations encode each such window as a distinct state, and the resulting table is many times larger than the textbook diagram.
concepts.L2: The bugs are never in the stable transitions. They are in what happens when a request arrives while you are mid-transaction on the same block: your invalidation for a block you are simultaneously trying to acquire, or a response arriving out of order relative to the request that triggered it.
concepts.L3: Consider a concrete race. Core 0 in S issues an Upgrade for block A. Before its acknowledgement returns, core 1's GetM for A arrives at core 0, which is in SM_AD: it has requested exclusivity and not yet got it. It cannot simply invalidate, because its own upgrade is outstanding and will return acknowledgements that must be counted. It cannot ignore the request, because core 1 would wait forever. The protocol must define the behaviour, typically by invalidating into IM_AD so the outstanding request is reinterpreted, or by ordering both at the home. Every such pair of concurrent events is a table entry, and the table is quadratic in message types. Hence model checkers rather than tests.

L4.prompt_tpl: A designer implements MSI with only the {n} stable states and handles an incoming GetM during an outstanding Upgrade by invalidating immediately. What breaks?
L4.answer: The outstanding Upgrade's acknowledgements still arrive and are counted against a block the cache no longer holds, so the cache either transitions to M without valid data or leaks an acknowledgement count. Correct handling requires a transient state that remembers a request is in flight.
L4.explanation: A stable-state-only implementation has nowhere to record that a transaction is outstanding, which is exactly the information needed to resolve the race. This is the canonical bug class in coherence implementations, and it appears only under precise timing, which is why formal model checking rather than directed testing is the standard method.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a coherence protocol table grows roughly as states times {m} message types, and what that implies about how these designs are verified.
L4.answer: Every state must define behaviour for every incoming message, so the table is the product of the two, and adding a state or a message type multiplies rather than adds. The size and the timing sensitivity make exhaustive simulation infeasible, so protocols are specified formally and checked with model checkers such as Murphi or TLA-based tools.
L4.explanation: The combinatorial growth is why coherence is one of the few areas of commercial hardware design where formal methods are routine rather than exotic. Sorin, Hill and Wood publish full Murphi models alongside their protocol tables for exactly this reason.

prereqs: Directory coherence and the sharer vector

L0.body:
# A store buffer is a small FIFO of {address, data, size, valid} entries
# between the pipeline and L1. Typical depth 40-80.
#
# Store path: retire -> allocate entry -> drain to L1 once it owns the line
# Load path:  probe store buffer AND L1 in parallel
#             if any older entry matches -> forward from the buffer
#
# The matching hardware is the expensive part:
#   address CAM across all entries
#   partial-overlap detection (8-byte load over two 4-byte stores)
#   on partial overlap most designs STALL and replay, they do not merge
#
# Every 'forwarding failure' stall is this.
L0.cloze: A store buffer is a FIFO probed by loads through an {{c1::address CAM}}, so a load can be forwarded from an older store that has not reached L1. On a {{c2::partial overlap}} most designs stall and replay rather than merging.

concepts.L1: The store buffer holds retired stores that have not yet reached the cache, letting the pipeline retire stores without waiting for write permission. Loads search it associatively so a thread always sees its own most recent stores.
concepts.L2: The store buffer is not a performance optimisation bolted onto a sequentially consistent machine; it is the mechanism that creates the relaxed memory model. Total Store Order is precisely the model you get when stores are buffered in FIFO order and loads may bypass them.
concepts.L3: Follow the ordering consequence. A store retires into the buffer and the pipeline continues; a later load to a different address probes L1 and can complete while the earlier store is still buffered. The load has moved ahead of the store, which is store-to-load reordering, the only reordering TSO permits, and it is permitted because it is what the buffer does. A load to the same address must not see stale data, so it forwards from the buffer, which is why a thread always observes its own stores in order. A fence is implemented as a drain. This is where memory models stop being arbitrary: sequential consistency would drain before every load, paying full store latency each time.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two threads on a TSO machine: T0 does `x = 1; r1 = y;` and T1 does `y = 1; r2 = x;`, with x and y initially 0. Can `r1 == {v} && r2 == {v}` be observed, and which hardware structure is responsible?
L4.answer: Yes. Both stores sit in their cores' store buffers while both loads read the other variable from cache, so both loads see 0. The store buffer is responsible; it is the only reordering TSO allows, and it is why this litmus test requires a fence to forbid.
L4.explanation: This is Dekker's litmus test, and it is the standard demonstration that TSO is not sequential consistency. On x86 the fix is an mfence or a locked instruction between store and load in each thread, which drains the buffer. Under sequential consistency the outcome would be impossible, which is exactly why sequential consistency is expensive.

L4.prompt_tpl: A store buffer has {n} entries and a load must be compared against every valid older entry. How many address comparators does the forwarding path need, and what happens to the load's critical path as {n} grows? Answer with the number of address comparators.
L4.answer: One comparator per entry, so $n$ of them, plus age-ordering and partial-overlap logic. For $n = 56$: 56 comparators whose results feed a priority select for the youngest older match, and that select sits on the load-to-use path, so deeper buffers directly threaten L1 latency.
L4.explanation: The forwarding CAM is on the load critical path, which is why store buffers do not simply grow to hide all store latency. Some designs restrict forwarding to exactly-matching addresses and sizes, stalling otherwise, precisely to keep this logic small and fast.

concepts.t: Memory consistency at the hardware level

L0.body:
# Consistency is ORDER BETWEEN DIFFERENT addresses.
# Coherence is a SINGLE address. Separate problems.
#
# What each model permits to be reordered:
#              St->Ld  St->St  Ld->Ld  Ld->St
#   SC            no      no      no      no
#   x86-TSO      YES      no      no      no
#   ARMv8/RVWMO  YES     YES     YES     YES  (subject to dependencies)
#
# RVWMO fences name the sets explicitly:
#   fence rw, rw   # all prior loads+stores before all later ones
#   fence r, rw    # acquire-like
#   fence rw, w    # release-like
#
# Weak models are cheaper to build; the cost moves to software.
L0.cloze: Coherence concerns a {{c1::single address}}; consistency concerns order {{c2::between different addresses}}. x86-TSO permits only {{c3::store-to-load}} reordering, while RVWMO and ARMv8 permit all four.

concepts.L1: A memory consistency model specifies which reorderings of accesses to different addresses a program may observe. It is a hardware-software contract distinct from coherence, and it determines what fences a compiler must emit.
concepts.L2: Weak models are not sloppy versions of strong ones; they are a deliberate transfer of cost from hardware to software. A weakly ordered machine needs no store-buffer drain on ordinary loads, but every lock, every atomic and every publication of initialised data now requires an explicit fence that the compiler must get right.
concepts.L3: Models differ in which structures may reorder. TSO arises from a FIFO store buffer with load bypass and nothing else; forbid the bypass and you have sequential consistency, at the cost of stalling every load behind every pending store. Weak models additionally let the memory system complete accesses out of order, permitting non-blocking caches, multiple outstanding misses and write coalescing without tracking program order globally. RVWMO makes this explicit: fences carry predecessor and successor sets, so `fence r, rw` is an acquire and `fence rw, w` a release. The rule: a stronger model costs hardware on every access, a weaker one costs correctness risk at every synchronisation site.

L4.prompt_tpl: Under {model}, thread T0 executes `data = 42; flag = 1;` and T1 executes `while (flag == 0) ; r = data;`. Can T1 read r == 0, and what fence fixes it?
L4.answer: Under x86-TSO, no: store-to-store order is preserved, so flag cannot become visible before data. Under RVWMO, yes: stores may be reordered, so T0 needs `fence w, w` (or a release store) between them, and T1 needs `fence r, r` (or an acquire load) after the loop.
L4.explanation: This is the message-passing litmus test, and it is the clearest demonstration that portable lock-free code cannot rely on x86 behaviour. Code that is correct by accident on TSO breaks on ARM and RISC-V, which is why the C++ and Rust memory models exist and why acquire and release must be written even when a given machine would not need them.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team proposes implementing sequential consistency in hardware for a {n}-core design to simplify software. What is the main hardware cost?
options: Loads must stall until prior stores are globally visible, negating the store buffer
The coherence protocol needs additional states to track ordering per address
The directory must be replaced with snooping, since only a bus provides a total order
L4.answer: Every load must wait for all prior stores of that thread to become globally visible, which means draining the store buffer before each load, adding full store-completion latency to the load path and largely eliminating the benefit of the store buffer.
L4.explanation: Sequential consistency is implementable and some research designs use speculation to recover most of the performance, but the naive implementation stalls loads behind stores. The cost is paid on every access, not only at synchronisation points, which is why commercial architectures expose weaker models and let software pay only where it must.

concepts.t: Buses and why they stopped scaling

L0.body:
# A shared bus: one set of wires, one transaction at a time.
#
#   aggregate bandwidth = width * frequency, INDEPENDENT of node count
#   per-node bandwidth  = width * frequency / N        -> falls as 1/N
#
#   64 bits @ 1 GHz = 8 GB/s total
#     4 nodes -> 2.0 GB/s each
#    16 nodes -> 0.5 GB/s each
#    64 nodes -> 0.125 GB/s each
#
# Electrical limit: every added node adds capacitance to the same wire,
# so frequency FALLS as N rises. Bandwidth does not stay flat, it drops.
#
# What a bus gives you for free: a total order on all transactions.
L0.cloze: A bus's aggregate bandwidth is {{c1::independent of node count}}, so per-node bandwidth falls as {{c2::1/N}}. Worse, each added node adds {{c3::capacitance}}, so achievable frequency falls too. What it gives free is a total order.

concepts.L1: A bus is a shared set of wires with arbitration: exactly one transaction occupies it at a time. Its total bandwidth is fixed by width and frequency, so per-node bandwidth falls inversely with the number of attached agents.
concepts.L2: The reason buses vanished is electrical, not architectural. Each additional connected agent loads the shared wire with more capacitance and stub inductance, so achievable frequency degrades as nodes are added. Aggregate bandwidth therefore falls with $N$ rather than merely being divided by it.
concepts.L3: What kept buses alive long past their bandwidth usefulness is the free total order. Exactly one transaction is on the wire at a time and every agent sees it, so the bus supplies a global serialisation that snooping coherence uses directly as its correctness argument. Give that up and the protocol must construct an order explicitly at a home node, which is the whole complexity of directory coherence. The migration to point-to-point fabrics was therefore not a wiring change but a protocol change. Modern fabrics keep a vestige: AXI and CHI define ordering rules per channel and per ID precisely because the fabric supplies none for free, and getting those rules wrong is a common integration bug.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {w}-bit bus runs at {f} MHz. Give total and per-node bandwidth for {n} attached agents, and state what actually happens to $f$ as agents are added. Answer with the per-node bandwidth in bytes per second.
L4.answer: Total $= wf/8$ bytes per second; per node $=$ total$/N$. For 64 bits at 1000 MHz: 8 GB/s total, 0.125 GB/s each at 64 nodes. In reality $f$ falls with $N$ because each agent adds capacitive load, so total bandwidth degrades rather than staying flat.
L4.explanation: The idealised division by $N$ is already bad; the electrical effect makes it worse. This is why every fabric past a handful of agents is point-to-point and why the bus survives only as a low-frequency configuration interface such as APB.

L4.prompt_tpl: Replacing a bus with a point-to-point fabric in a {n}-core design removes a property the coherence protocol was relying on. Name it and say what must replace it.
L4.answer: The free total order on transactions. Snooping used bus serialisation as its global order; a point-to-point fabric has none, so the protocol must construct an order explicitly, typically by serialising each block's requests at a home node, which is directory coherence.
L4.explanation: This is the causal link between interconnect choice and protocol choice that gets lost when the two are taught separately. You cannot swap the fabric and keep the protocol: the protocol's correctness argument was an argument about the fabric.

L0.body:
# An N x N crossbar connects any input to any free output simultaneously.
#
#   crosspoints = N^2
#   N =  16 ->    256
#   N =  64 ->  4,096
#   N = 256 -> 65,536
#
# Area scales as N^2. Worse, the wires that must span the array grow as
# N in each dimension, so the longest wire grows as N and delay with it.
#
#   aggregate bandwidth = N * b     (b = per-port bandwidth)
#   per-node bandwidth  = b         <- CONSTANT. This is the appeal.
#
# Practical ceiling: crossbars top out around 16-64 ports on chip.
L0.cloze: A crossbar has {{c1::N squared}} crosspoints and delivers {{c2::constant}} per-node bandwidth, which is why it is the ideal. Its practical on-chip ceiling is roughly {{c3::16-64}} ports, set by area and wire delay.

concepts.L1: A crossbar gives every input a simultaneous path to any free output, so per-node bandwidth is independent of node count. It pays for this with area quadratic in port count and a longest wire linear in it.
concepts.L2: The binding constraint is wire delay, not crosspoint area. Transistors shrank with each node; wires did not get proportionally faster, so a crossbar that was timing-clean at 32 ports on an old process is not automatically clean at 32 ports on a new one at higher frequency.
concepts.L3: The quadratic is easy to see: each of $N$ inputs needs a possible connection to each of $N$ outputs. Less obvious is the geometry. The array must be at least $N$ tracks tall and $N$ wide, so a signal crossing it travels a distance proportional to $N$, and on-chip wire delay grows superlinearly with length once repeaters and RC effects count. Arbitration compounds it: an $N$-port crossbar needs an allocator matching requests to outputs every cycle, and good allocators are themselves $O(N^{2})$ in comparators. The answer is hierarchy: small 4- to 8-port crossbars connected by a topology. Every network-on-chip topology approximates a large crossbar from small ones at subquadratic cost.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare a {n1}-port and a {n2}-port crossbar on crosspoint count and aggregate bandwidth with {b} GB/s per port. State the per-node bandwidth in each case. Answer with the crosspoint count of the larger crossbar.
L4.answer: Crosspoints $= N^{2}$; aggregate $= Nb$; per node $= b$, constant. For 16 versus 256 ports: 256 versus 65536 crosspoints, a 256x area growth, for 16x the aggregate bandwidth.
L4.explanation: Per-node bandwidth staying constant is precisely what makes a crossbar the reference point for every other topology. The cost is that area grows 16 times faster than bandwidth in this comparison, which is why nobody builds a 256-port on-chip crossbar and everyone builds hierarchies of small ones.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {n}-port crossbar met timing on a 28 nm process and fails on a newer node at higher frequency despite smaller transistors. Explain.
L4.answer: Because the limiting path is wire delay across the array, and wire RC delay per unit length has not improved with scaling the way gate delay has. Shrinking transistors makes the array physically smaller but the higher target frequency shrinks the cycle budget faster, so the long traversal no longer fits.
L4.explanation: This is the general shape of modern physical design: gates got faster, wires did not, so global structures became the limiters. It is also why floorplanning matters to architects. A structure whose delay is set by distance cannot be fixed by synthesis effort.

L0.body:
# N = 64 nodes, per-link bandwidth b = 128 GB/s each direction.
#
#   topology     degree  diameter    bisection links  bisection BW
#   ring           2      N/2 = 32         2            256 GB/s
#   2D mesh 8x8    4    2(k-1) = 14        k = 8       1024 GB/s
#   2D torus 8x8   4      k = 8           2k = 16      2048 GB/s
#   crossbar      N-1        1              N/2        4096 GB/s
#
#   mesh bisection/node = k*b/N = b/sqrt(N)  -> falls as 1/sqrt(N)
#   ring bisection/node = 2b/N               -> falls as 1/N
#
# Intel used rings to ~10 cores, then meshes: the diameter term.
L0.cloze: A $k \times k$ mesh has bisection {{c1::k}} links, so per-node bisection bandwidth falls as {{c2::1/sqrt(N)}}. A ring's falls as {{c3::1/N}}, which is why ring-based designs stopped around ten cores.

concepts.L1: Ring, mesh and torus are the practical on-chip topologies. They differ in node degree, diameter and bisection bandwidth, and the choice is a trade between router cost, worst-case latency and cross-chip bandwidth.
concepts.L2: Rings are chosen for a reason people rarely state: they need only two ports per router and no routing decision beyond direction, so the router is tiny and fast. Meshes cost a five-port router with allocation at every node, which is real area and a per-hop latency penalty the ring does not pay.
concepts.L3: Work the numbers for 64 nodes at 128 GB/s per link direction. A ring is cut by two links, so bisection is 256 GB/s, 4 GB/s per node, and average hop count is $N/4 = 16$. An $8 \times 8$ mesh is cut by $k = 8$ links: 1024 GB/s, 16 GB/s per node, average hops about 5.3. A torus wraps the edges, doubling the cut to 16 links and halving the diameter, at the cost of long wrap-around wires unless folded. The scaling laws matter more than any number: mesh per-node bisection falls as $1/\sqrt{N}$, ring as $1/N$, so the gap widens with size. That is the arithmetic behind Intel's ring-to-mesh move and behind a 3-D torus for TPU pods, where the third dimension gives $N^{-1/3}$.

L4.prompt_tpl: For {n} nodes with {b} GB/s per link direction, compute bisection bandwidth and per-node bisection bandwidth for a ring, a square 2-D mesh and a 2-D torus. Answer with the torus bisection bandwidth in GB/s.
L4.answer: Ring: $2b$ total, $2b/N$ per node. Mesh: $\sqrt{N} b$ total, $b/\sqrt{N}$ per node. Torus: $2\sqrt{N} b$, $2b/\sqrt{N}$. For $N=64$, $b=128$: ring 256 and 4; mesh 1024 and 16; torus 2048 and 32 GB/s.
L4.explanation: Bisection bandwidth is the standard first-order figure of merit because any all-to-all traffic pattern must cross the cut. The per-node form is the one to quote, since it says what each core actually gets and makes the scaling exponent visible.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {n}-core server die currently uses a ring. Performance analysis shows average memory latency dominated by hop count. What topology change do you propose and what does it cost?
options: A 2-D mesh: diameter falls to $O(\sqrt{N})$, at the cost of a five-port router per node
A larger ring with wider links, since bisection scales with link width
A full crossbar, since on-chip crossbars scale comfortably past a hundred ports
L4.answer: Move to a 2-D mesh: diameter drops from $O(N)$ to $O(\sqrt{N})$ and bisection improves by a factor of $\sqrt{N}/2$. The cost is a five-port router with allocation at every node, more area and typically one extra cycle of per-hop latency.
L4.explanation: The ring's problem is diameter growing linearly, so hop latency dominates once core counts pass roughly ten. A mesh fixes the exponent at the price of a real router at every node. That per-hop cost is why small designs keep rings: fewer, cheaper hops beats more, better-connected ones when $N$ is small.

L0.body:
# Dimension-order routing (DOR) on a 2-D mesh: all the way in X,
# then all the way in Y. Deadlock-free, and here is why.
#
# Deadlock needs a CYCLE in the channel dependency graph.
#   X-then-Y: an X channel can only wait on an X or a Y channel;
#   a Y channel can only wait on a Y channel.
#   No edge from Y back to X, so no cycle.
#
# Break the rule (sometimes Y-then-X) and you get:
#   A holds X, wants Y ; B holds Y, wants X  -> deadlock, forever
#
# Cost of DOR: it is oblivious. It cannot route around congestion, and
# adversarial patterns (transpose, bit-reverse) hit it hard.
L0.cloze: Dimension-order routing is deadlock-free because the channel dependency graph has no edge from {{c1::Y back to X}}, so no cycle exists. Its cost is being {{c2::oblivious}}: it cannot route around congestion.

concepts.L1: A routing algorithm decides the path each packet takes. Deadlock freedom is proved by showing the channel dependency graph is acyclic, and dimension-order routing achieves this by forbidding turns that would close a cycle.
concepts.L2: Deadlock is not a rare corner case to be handled by timeouts; it is a permanent, unrecoverable state that a correct network must make structurally impossible. That is why routing algorithms come with proofs rather than tests, and why adding an apparently harmless shortcut path can break a network that worked for years.
concepts.L3: The technique is Dally and Seitz's: build a graph whose nodes are channels and whose edges are the waits-for relations induced by the routing function, then show it is acyclic. Under X-then-Y a packet in an X channel may next need an X or a Y channel, but a packet in a Y channel can only next need a Y channel, having finished its X movement. Edges run X to X, X to Y and Y to Y, never Y to X, so there is no cycle. The turn model generalises it: of the eight turns in a 2-D mesh, forbidding a well-chosen two suffices, giving west-first and north-last more freedom while keeping the proof. Any optimisation that adds a path, an express link or an escape route, must be re-proved, not assumed safe.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineer adds an adaptive rule to a {k}x{k} mesh: packets may switch from Y to X to avoid a congested link. Latency improves in simulation, then the network hangs under heavy load. Diagnose it.
L4.answer: Allowing a Y-to-X turn creates an edge from Y channels back to X channels in the channel dependency graph, closing a cycle. Under light load the cycle is never fully occupied so nothing hangs; under heavy load a set of packets each holds one channel and waits on the next, which is deadlock. The fix is a turn restriction or an escape virtual channel with dimension-order routing.
L4.explanation: The load dependence is the diagnostic signature: deadlock requires all channels in the cycle to be simultaneously occupied, which only happens when buffers are full. This is why interconnect bugs surface late, in system-level stress testing rather than in unit simulation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show that dimension-order routing on a {k}-ary 2-mesh is deadlock-free by describing the channel dependency graph, then say what breaks if wrap-around links are added to make it a torus.
L4.answer: Edges go X-to-X, X-to-Y and Y-to-Y only, so the graph is acyclic and no deadlock is possible. Adding wrap-around links creates cycles within a single dimension, since a ring of channels can wait on itself, so a torus needs at least two virtual channels per physical channel with a dateline rule to break them.
L4.explanation: The torus case is the standard illustration of why virtual channels exist. The topology change alone reintroduces cycles that the routing function cannot remove, so the fix has to come from splitting each physical channel into independent buffer classes.

L0.body:
# One physical link, several independent buffer queues sharing it.
#
#   no VCs:     a blocked packet at the head of the input buffer stops
#               every packet behind it (head-of-line blocking)
#   with V VCs: V queues; the arbiter picks any non-blocked VC each
#               cycle. A blocked flow costs one VC, not the link.
#
# Two uses:
#   1. performance: remove head-of-line blocking
#   2. correctness: break deadlock cycles (dateline VCs on a torus;
#      separate request and response VCs so responses always drain)
#
# Cost: V x buffer area per input, plus a V-way arbiter.
L0.cloze: Virtual channels give one physical link {{c1::several independent buffer queues}}. They serve two purposes: removing {{c2::head-of-line blocking}} and breaking {{c3::deadlock cycles}}, for example by separating requests from responses.

concepts.L1: Virtual channels multiplex several independent packet queues over one physical link, so a stalled packet blocks only its own queue. They are the standard mechanism for both performance isolation and deadlock avoidance in on-chip networks.
concepts.L2: The correctness use is the one that is non-negotiable. Protocol-level deadlock, where every request buffer is full of requests whose responses cannot get through, is possible even in a topologically deadlock-free network, and no amount of buffering fixes it. Separate request and response virtual channels do.
concepts.L3: Distinguish the two deadlocks, because they need the same mechanism for different reasons. Network-level deadlock is a cycle in the channel dependency graph, fixed by routing restrictions or dateline virtual channels. Protocol-level deadlock is a cycle in the message dependency graph: a cache cannot free the buffer holding a request until it sends a response, but every buffer on the path is full of requests. The network is acyclic and the system still stops. The fix is a virtual channel for responses that requests can never occupy. Hence coherence specifications state a required number of independent virtual networks, and getting that count wrong is a hang that appears only under saturation.

L4.prompt_tpl: An SoC integrator merges coherence requests and responses onto a single virtual channel to save {n} percent of router buffer area. The system passes all directed tests and hangs under saturating load. Explain.
L4.answer: Protocol-level deadlock: caches cannot free request buffers until they emit responses, but every buffer is full of requests, so no response can be delivered and nothing drains. The network topology is irrelevant; the fix is to restore an independent virtual channel for responses.
L4.explanation: Directed tests never fill the buffers, so the cycle is never fully occupied and the bug is invisible. This is a real and expensive class of silicon bug, and it is why coherence protocol specifications state a minimum number of independent virtual networks as a hard requirement rather than a recommendation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A router input port has {b} flit buffers. Compare head-of-line blocking behaviour with 1 virtual channel against {v} virtual channels sharing the same total buffering, and state the arbiter cost.
L4.answer: With 1 VC, a blocked head flit stalls all $b$ buffered flits. With $v$ VCs of $b/v$ flits each, a blocked flow stalls only its own queue, so $(v-1)/v$ of the buffered traffic can still proceed. The cost is a $v$-way arbiter in the router critical path and $v$ sets of control state per port.
L4.explanation: Splitting buffers reduces the depth available to any single flow, so very deep single-flow bursts do slightly worse. In practice the isolation dominates, because on-chip traffic is many independent flows rather than one long stream, and $v$ of 2 to 4 is the common choice.

concepts.t: Flow control and the buffer-bandwidth product

L0.body:
# Credit-based flow control: a sender may transmit only if it holds a
# credit for a free buffer downstream. Credits return on buffer release.
#
# The round trip sets the minimum buffering for full throughput:
#
#   buffers_needed >= credit round-trip latency (cycles) * flits per cycle
#
#   link 1 flit/cycle, round trip 6 cycles -> need >= 6 flits of buffer
#   under-buffer it and the link idles waiting for credits:
#     4 buffers, 6-cycle round trip -> throughput = 4/6 = 67% of the link
#
# This is Little's law again: occupancy = rate * latency.
L0.cloze: Credit-based flow control needs at least {{c1::round-trip latency times rate}} buffers to keep a link busy. With 4 buffers and a 6-cycle credit round trip, throughput is {{c2::67}} percent of the link. This is {{c3::Little's law}}.

concepts.L1: Flow control decides when a packet may advance. Credit-based schemes track downstream buffer availability exactly, and the buffering required to sustain full link throughput equals the credit round-trip time multiplied by the link rate.
concepts.L2: Under-buffering does not merely reduce burst tolerance; it caps steady-state throughput at the ratio of buffers to round-trip time. A link that looks fine in a latency test can be permanently limited to a fraction of its wire bandwidth, and no amount of offered load fixes it.
concepts.L3: This is Little's law on a link: flits in flight equal rate times the time each occupies a buffer, and a sender cannot exceed its credits. With $R$ cycles of credit round trip at one flit per cycle, you need $R$ buffers. Cut them to $B < R$ and the sender stalls after $B$ flits until the first credit returns: throughput $B/R$. The same arithmetic governs wormhole versus virtual-cut-through. Wormhole lets a packet span several routers, so a blocked packet holds channels it is not using; virtual-cut-through requires the whole packet to fit one buffer, needing more storage but freeing channels sooner. Both show up in the buffer budget, usually the largest part of router area.

L4.prompt_tpl: A link carries {r} flits per cycle with a credit round-trip latency of {c} cycles. Compute the buffers needed for full throughput and the throughput achieved with only {b} buffers. Answer with the buffers needed for full throughput.
L4.answer: Buffers needed $= rc$. Achieved throughput $= \min(r, b/c)$ flits per cycle. For $r = 1$, $c = 10$, $b = 4$: need 10, achieve 0.4 flits per cycle, i.e. 40 percent of the link.
L4.explanation: The formula is Little's law with occupancy as the unknown. It is worth internalising because the same shape governs memory-level parallelism, outstanding DRAM requests, and network-attached storage queues: to keep a pipe full you must have rate times latency of work in flight.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain the difference between wormhole and virtual-cut-through flow control for a {n}-flit packet, and which one needs more buffer storage.
L4.answer: Wormhole lets the packet's flits span several routers, so a blocked head stalls the whole worm and holds channels along its path; buffers need only be a few flits deep. Virtual-cut-through requires a full packet to fit in one router's buffer before forwarding, so buffers must be at least packet-sized, but a blocked packet occupies exactly one router.
L4.explanation: The trade is buffer area against channel hoarding. Wormhole is the on-chip default because buffer area is precious and packets are short; virtual-cut-through is more common off-chip where buffering is cheap relative to link cost and blocking is more expensive.

prereqs: Bandwidth versus latency: Little's law for memory

L0.body:
# Bisection bandwidth = bandwidth across the worst-case cut splitting
# the network into two equal halves. It bounds all-to-all traffic.
#
# All-to-all (all-reduce, transpose, MoE dispatch):
#   each of N nodes sends D bytes to every other node
#   bytes that MUST cross the bisection = (N/2)*(N/2)*D = N^2 D / 4
#   time >= N^2 D / (4 * bisection_BW)
#
# Worked: N=64, D=1 MB, 8x8 mesh, b=128 GB/s links
#   bisection = 8 * 128 = 1024 GB/s
#   bytes across = 64^2 * 1e6 / 4 = 1.024e9
#   time >= 1.024e9 / 1.024e12 = 1.0 ms
# Crossbar (bisection 32*128 = 4096 GB/s): 0.25 ms.
L0.cloze: All-to-all forces {{c1::N squared D / 4}} bytes across the bisection, so the time is at least that divided by {{c2::bisection bandwidth}}. For 64 nodes exchanging 1 MB each on an 8x8 mesh at 1024 GB/s, the floor is {{c3::1.0}} ms.

concepts.L1: Bisection bandwidth is the aggregate bandwidth across the narrowest cut into two equal halves. It gives a hard lower bound on the time for any traffic pattern in which half the nodes must communicate with the other half.
concepts.L2: The number is only useful when paired with a traffic pattern. Nearest-neighbour stencils never approach the bisection and are limited by local link bandwidth instead; all-to-all and transposes hit it exactly. Quoting bisection bandwidth without saying which collective you mean is how accelerator marketing works.
concepts.L3: Derive the all-to-all bound. Split $N$ nodes in half. Each of the $N/2$ nodes on one side must send $D$ bytes to each of the $N/2$ on the other, so $(N/2)^{2} D = N^{2}D/4$ bytes cross the cut, and elapsed time cannot be less than that over the bisection bandwidth. For 64 nodes, 1 MB each, an $8 \times 8$ mesh with 128 GB/s links, the cut carries 1024 GB/s and $1.024$ GB must cross: a 1.0 ms floor however clever the collective. Ring all-reduce clarifies the point by contrast: each node sends only to its neighbour, consuming local link bandwidth rather than bisection, moving $2D(N-1)/N$ bytes per node in $2(N-1)$ steps. Hence topology and collective algorithm must be chosen together.

L4.prompt_tpl: {n} nodes each send {d} MB to every other node. On a square 2-D mesh with {b} GB/s links, compute the bisection bandwidth and the minimum possible completion time. Answer with the minimum completion time in seconds.
L4.answer: Bisection $= \sqrt{N} b$; bytes across $= N^{2}D/4$; time $\geq N^{2}D/(4\sqrt{N}b)$. For $N=64$, $D=1$ MB, $b=128$ GB/s: bisection 1024 GB/s, 1.024 GB across, 1.0 ms.
L4.explanation: The bound scales as $N^{2}/\sqrt{N} = N^{1.5}$ for a 2-D mesh, so all-to-all gets rapidly worse with scale. That exponent is the reason large training clusters use higher-dimensional topologies and why mixture-of-experts dispatch, which is an all-to-all, is the hardest collective to scale.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your {n}-node fabric has poor bisection bandwidth but good nearest-neighbour links. Which collective algorithm do you use for an all-reduce of {d} MB?
options: Ring all-reduce, which uses only neighbour links and avoids the bisection
Recursive halving and doubling, which is optimal on any topology
Direct all-to-all exchange, since it minimises the number of steps
L4.answer: Ring all-reduce: it communicates only between neighbours, so it consumes local link bandwidth rather than bisection, moving $2D(N-1)/N$ bytes per node in $2(N-1)$ steps.
L4.explanation: Ring all-reduce is bandwidth-optimal in bytes moved per node and needs no bisection at all, at the cost of a step count linear in $N$, which hurts latency for small messages. Recursive halving and doubling is the opposite trade: logarithmic steps, but it crosses the bisection.

concepts.t: Deriving the systolic array from the loop nest

L0.body:
# The matmul, C = A*B, A is MxK, B is KxN:
#
#   for m in range(M):
#     for n in range(N):
#       for k in range(K):
#         C[m][n] += A[m][k] * B[k][n]
#
# Reuse:
#   A[m][k] needed by every n -> reuse along n
#   B[k][n] needed by every m -> reuse along m
#   C[m][n] sums over k       -> reduction along k
#
# Now MAP indices to space, not time:
#   place a PE at (m, n)
#   stream A rows LEFT to RIGHT  (visits every n)
#   stream B cols TOP to BOTTOM  (visits every m)
#   accumulate C in place at (m, n)
#
# Each operand is read from memory ONCE and used N times as it walks.
L0.cloze: Mapping loop index m to array rows and n to columns turns {{c1::reuse}} into physical propagation: a value fetched once is used {{c2::N}} times as it walks across the array. The k loop becomes {{c3::accumulation}} in place.

concepts.L1: A systolic array is the matmul loop nest with two of its loops unrolled into space rather than time. Each processing element holds one output position, operands flow between neighbours, and every value fetched from memory is consumed by an entire row or column.
concepts.L2: The array is not a clever circuit that happens to do matmul; it is the direct spatial image of the loop nest's reuse pattern. That is why it is the right shape: the structure of the computation says each operand is needed by a whole line of outputs, and neighbour wiring is the cheapest way to deliver a value to a line.
concepts.L3: The derivation generalises. Take any loop nest, choose which loops map to space and which to time: reuse along a spatially mapped loop becomes a broadcast or propagation, reuse along a temporally mapped loop becomes a local register hold. Matmul has two pure-reuse loops, $m$ and $n$, and one reduction loop $k$, so a 2-D array with in-place accumulation over $k$ falls out. Convolution has more loops, which is why convolution accelerators have richer mapping choices and why row-stationary exists. The payoff is in wires: a value moving one hop travels a fixed short distance regardless of array size, so an $N \times N$ array has $O(N^{2})$ short wires rather than global buses.

L4.prompt_tpl: Starting from the three-deep matmul loop nest with dimensions {M}, {N}, {K}, show which loops map to array rows and columns, which becomes accumulation, and how many times each element of A is read from memory.
L4.answer: Map m to rows and n to columns; k becomes accumulation in time within each PE. Each element of A is fetched once and reused across all N columns as it propagates, so memory reads of A total $MK$ rather than $MKN$, a reduction by a factor of $N$.
L4.explanation: The whole value of the structure is in that last ratio. A naive implementation reads $MKN$ elements of A; the array reads $MK$. The reuse factor equals the size of the spatially mapped dimension, which is why array width and energy efficiency are the same design knob.

L4.prompt_tpl: A colleague proposes a {n}-lane SIMD unit instead of an {n}x{n} systolic array, arguing both do multiply-accumulate. What is the structural difference that matters?
options: Operand delivery: SIMD needs register-file bandwidth proportional to lanes, the array uses neighbour propagation
Precision: systolic arrays can only do integer arithmetic, SIMD can do floating point
Latency: the systolic array completes each MAC in fewer cycles than a SIMD lane
L4.answer: The SIMD unit reads all its operands from a register file every cycle, so operand bandwidth scales with lane count; the array passes operands between neighbours, so a value read once serves an entire row or column and register-file bandwidth does not scale with array size.
L4.explanation: Both perform multiply-accumulate; they differ entirely in where operands come from. SIMD needs a register file with bandwidth proportional to lanes, which is the quadratic port problem. The array converts operand delivery into short neighbour wires, which is what lets MAC counts reach tens of thousands.

concepts.t: Sizing the matmul unit: three independent budgets

L0.body:
# Three ceilings; take the minimum.
#
# 1. AREA.  int8 MAC + registers ~ 300 um^2, mature node (ESTIMATE)
#      100 mm^2 = 1e8 um^2 / 300 = 333,333 MACs
#      -> N = sqrt(333333) = 577.  A 512x512 array fits.
#
# 2. POWER. ~0.2 pJ per int8 MAC (ESTIMATE, node-dependent)
#      512x512 = 262,144 MACs @ 1 GHz
#      P = 262144 * 1e9 * 0.2e-12 = 52.4 W  <- arithmetic only
#
# 3. BANDWIDTH. Weight-stationary NxN int8 at f Hz needs N bytes/cycle
#      in and N out: 512 GB/s each way from SRAM. DRAM: impossible.
#
# The binding constraint is almost always 3, then 2, then 1.
L0.cloze: Array size is bounded by area, power and {{c1::operand bandwidth}}, and the binding constraint is usually {{c2::bandwidth}}. A 512x512 int8 array at 1 GHz needs {{c3::512}} GB/s in and the same out.

concepts.L1: The size of a matmul unit is set by whichever of area, power and operand bandwidth runs out first. Each gives a separate ceiling, and the design point is the minimum of the three, not the area budget alone.
concepts.L2: People size arrays from the area budget because area is the easiest number to get. In practice the array is feeding-limited: an $N \times N$ array consumes $N$ operands per cycle per side, so bandwidth demand grows linearly in $N$ while compute grows as $N^{2}$, and the SRAM that can supply it caps the design.
concepts.L3: Run all three. At roughly 300 square micrometres per int8 MAC with registers, 100 square millimetres holds about 333 thousand MACs, so $N = 577$ and a 512 by 512 array fits. At roughly 0.2 pJ per int8 MAC that array at 1 GHz burns 52 watts on arithmetic alone, before any memory traffic, a large slice of a 300 watt part. Feeding it needs 512 bytes per cycle in and 512 out: 512 GB/s each way, which must come from on-chip SRAM, since no DRAM interface offers that with the latency determinism required. So the design question becomes how much SRAM you can afford and at what bandwidth, with the array sized to what it feeds. The per-MAC figures are order-of-magnitude estimates.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given {a} mm^2 of array area at {u} um^2 per int8 MAC, and {e} pJ per MAC at {f} GHz, compute the largest square array that fits, its arithmetic power, and its operand bandwidth requirement. Answer with the array side N.
L4.answer: MACs $= a \times 10^{6}/u$; $N = \lfloor\sqrt{\mathrm{MACs}}\rfloor$; power $= \mathrm{MACs} \times f \times e$; bandwidth $= N f$ bytes per second each way. For $a=100$, $u=300$, $e=0.2$, $f=1$: 333333 MACs, $N=577$, 66.7 W, 577 GB/s each way.
L4.explanation: The three ceilings scale differently: area and power scale with $N^{2}$, bandwidth with $N$. That asymmetry is why very large arrays are power-limited and why the practical fix is lower precision, which reduces both the area and the energy per MAC.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your {n}x{n} array is area-feasible and power-feasible but the SRAM can only supply half the required operand bandwidth. What do you change?
options: Increase reuse through dataflow and tiling, or reduce the effective array width
Double the array size so more work is available to hide the shortfall
Increase the clock frequency so operands arrive sooner
L4.answer: Change the dataflow or the tiling to increase reuse per fetched byte, or halve the array's effective width; adding SRAM ports is the expensive answer and enlarging the array makes the imbalance worse.
L4.explanation: Bandwidth shortfall is a mapping problem before it is a memory problem. Holding operands longer in the array, deeper accumulation over k or a stationary dimension with more reuse, reduces bytes per MAC without changing any hardware. That is exactly what dataflow choice is for.
