concepts.t: Fill, drain and why small batches waste the array

L0.body:
# An NxN systolic array is a pipeline N deep in each dimension.
# A value entering at (0,0) reaches (N-1,N-1) after 2N-2 hops.
#
#   cycles for M passes = M + 2N - 2
#   utilisation         = M / (M + 2N - 2)
#
#   N=256:
#     M=  256 -> 256/766  = 33.4%
#     M= 1024 -> 1024/1534 = 66.8%
#     M= 4096 -> 4096/4606 = 88.9%
#     M=16384 -> 16384/16894 = 97.0%
#
# This is why TPU v1's paper reports low utilisation on latency-bound
# inference: the matrices are not tall enough to amortise the fill.
# It is also why batch size is a HARDWARE parameter in disguise.
L0.cloze: An NxN array needs {{c1::2N-2}} cycles to fill and drain, so utilisation is {{c2::M/(M+2N-2)}} for M passes. At N=256, a 256-column pass achieves only {{c3::33.4}} percent utilisation.

concepts.L1: A systolic array is a deep pipeline in two dimensions: operands take $2N-2$ cycles to traverse it. Utilisation is the ratio of useful passes to total cycles, so short work is dominated by fill and drain overhead.
concepts.L2: This is the real reason batch size matters for accelerator efficiency, and it is a hardware property, not a framework one. A larger array is more efficient per MAC only when the workload is tall enough to amortise a fill cost that grows linearly with array size while capability grows quadratically.
concepts.L3: The tension is sharp. Doubling $N$ quadruples peak throughput and doubles the fill cost, so for a fixed workload shape bigger arrays reach lower utilisation and the effective gain is less than fourfold. At $N = 256$ with $M = 256$ passes, utilisation is 33.4 percent; at $N = 512$ on the same work it is $256/(256+1022) = 20$ percent, so going from 65 thousand to 262 thousand MACs delivers only $4 \times 0.20/0.334 = 2.4$ times the throughput. Batch-one LLM decoding is the extreme case: each token's matmul has a batch dimension of one, so the array is almost all fill and drain. Hence batching, continuous batching and speculative decoding, all of which exist to give the array taller matrices.

L4.prompt_tpl: An {n}x{n} systolic array processes a matmul with {m} columns of streaming operand. Compute cycles, utilisation, and the utilisation if the array is doubled to {n2}x{n2} for the same work. Answer with the utilisation of the n-by-n array.
L4.answer: Cycles $= M + 2N - 2$; utilisation $= M/(M+2N-2)$. For $N=256$, $M=1024$: 1534 cycles, 66.8 percent. Doubling to $N=512$: $1024/2046 = 50.0$ percent, so peak quadruples but delivered throughput rises by only $4 \times 0.50/0.668 = 3.0$ times.
L4.explanation: Fill cost grows linearly while peak grows quadratically, so utilisation always falls as the array grows for fixed work. Quoting a delivered-throughput number therefore requires stating the matrix shape, which is exactly what accelerator marketing tends to omit.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain, in hardware terms, why batch-{b} LLM decoding achieves a small fraction of an accelerator's peak, and name two software techniques that address it.
L4.answer: Each decode step multiplies a weight matrix by a single activation vector, so the streaming dimension is one and the array spends $2N-2$ cycles filling and draining for one column of useful work; it is also memory bound, since every weight is read once and used once. Continuous batching and speculative decoding both raise the effective batch dimension.
L4.explanation: Both effects, pipeline fill and arithmetic intensity, point the same way and compound. Speculative decoding is particularly instructive as co-design: it turns a latency problem into a throughput problem specifically because the hardware is far better at the latter.

prereqs: Sizing the matmul unit: three independent budgets

L0.body:
# Weight stationary: each PE holds one weight in a register for the
# whole pass. Activations stream through; partial sums accumulate along
# a column.
#
# NxN array, weights loaded once, M activation columns streamed:
#   weight bytes read   = N*N
#   activation in       = N*M
#   partial sums out    = N*M
#   MACs performed      = N*N*M
#
#   MACs per byte = N*N*M / (N*N + 2*N*M)
#
#   N=256, M=1024: 67,108,864 MACs / 589,824 bytes = 113.8 MACs/byte
#   N=256, M= 256: 16,777,216 / 196,608           =  85.3 MACs/byte
#
# Used by: Google TPU, NVDLA. Optimises WEIGHT reads specifically.
L0.cloze: Weight stationary holds one weight per PE for the whole pass, so weight bytes read is {{c1::N times N}} regardless of M. At N=256 and M=1024 the array does {{c2::113.8}} MACs per byte moved. It optimises {{c3::weight}} reads.

concepts.L1: In a weight-stationary dataflow each processing element holds a single weight in a local register for an entire pass, while activations stream in one direction and partial sums accumulate in the other. Weight traffic becomes independent of the number of activations processed.
concepts.L2: Weight stationary is chosen when weights are large relative to activations, which is the datacentre inference case. It is the wrong choice when the weight matrix changes every few cycles, because reloading the array costs $N$ cycles during which no useful work happens unless the design double-buffers the weight registers.
concepts.L3: The arithmetic shows where it wins and loses. Total memory traffic is $N^{2}$ weight bytes plus $2NM$ activation and partial-sum bytes, against $N^{2}M$ MACs. As $M$ grows the weight term vanishes and the ratio approaches $N/2$ MACs per byte, so a 256-wide array asymptotes at 128 MACs per byte. As $M$ shrinks toward $N$ the weight load dominates and efficiency collapses. Hence TPU-class designs pair weight-stationary arrays with a weight FIFO and double-buffered registers: the next layer's weights load into shadow registers while the current layer streams. The forgotten term is partial-sum output traffic, as large as activation input traffic, and the reason output-stationary exists.

L4.prompt_tpl: For an {n}x{n} weight-stationary array processing {m} activation columns in int8, compute total bytes moved, MACs performed and MACs per byte. Answer with the MACs per byte.
L4.answer: Bytes $= N^{2} + 2NM$; MACs $= N^{2}M$; ratio $= N^{2}M/(N^{2}+2NM)$. For $N=256$, $M=1024$: 589824 bytes, 67108864 MACs, 113.8 MACs per byte, asymptoting to $N/2 = 128$.
L4.explanation: The asymptote $N/2$ is the number to remember: a weight-stationary array's best possible arithmetic intensity is half its width, set by the two streams of activations in and partial sums out. Everything else is amortising the one-off weight load.

L4.prompt_tpl: A weight-stationary array must switch to a new {n}x{n} weight tile every {m} columns. Explain the cost and the standard hardware fix.
L4.answer: Loading the tile takes about N cycles during which the array does no useful work, costing roughly $N/(M+N)$ of throughput. The fix is a shadow set of weight registers in each PE plus a weight FIFO, so the next tile loads while the current one computes and the switch costs one cycle.
L4.explanation: Double buffering weight registers roughly doubles the weight-register area in each PE, which on a large array is a real cost, and it is paid precisely to hide a load that would otherwise be visible whenever layers are small. TPU v1 describes exactly this structure.

prereqs: Deriving the systolic array from the loop nest

L0.body:
# Output stationary: each PE owns one output element C[m][n] and keeps
# the accumulator in place for the whole K reduction. Weights AND
# activations stream.
#
# NxN array computing an NxN output tile, reduction depth K:
#   activation bytes in = N*K
#   weight bytes in     = N*K
#   output bytes out    = N*N        <- written ONCE, not K times
#   MACs                = N*N*K
#
#   MACs per byte = N*N*K / (2*N*K + N*N)
#   N=256, K=1024: 67,108,864 / (524,288+65,536) = 113.8
#
# Same ratio as weight-stationary by symmetry. It removes DIFFERENT
# traffic: partial sums never leave the PE.
L0.cloze: Output stationary keeps the {{c1::accumulator}} in the PE for the whole K reduction, so each output is written {{c2::once}} instead of K times. Partial sums {{c3::never leave the PE}}.

concepts.L1: In an output-stationary dataflow each processing element owns one output element and holds its accumulator locally across the entire reduction. Weights and activations both stream; partial sums never move.
concepts.L2: The comparison with weight stationary is a symmetry, not a hierarchy: each eliminates one of the three traffic streams and both reach the same MACs-per-byte ratio for matched shapes. The choice depends on which stream is expensive in your memory system and on the layer's aspect ratio.
concepts.L3: Partial sums are wider than the inputs, and that is the practical asymmetry. Accumulating int8 products needs 24 to 32 bits over a deep reduction, so a partial sum is three to four times an activation's width, and a dataflow that moves partial sums moves three to four times the bytes per element. Output stationary removes that stream entirely, at the cost of a wide accumulator in every PE. Weight stationary keeps narrow weight registers but pushes wide partial sums down each column. Deep reduction with a small output tile favours output stationary; a wide shallow layer favours weight stationary. This is exactly what Timeloop answers numerically rather than by argument.

L4.prompt_tpl: An {n}x{n} output-stationary array computes an output tile with reduction depth {k}, int8 inputs and {w}-bit accumulators. Compute bytes moved and MACs per byte, then compare against weight stationary moving partial sums at the same width. Answer with the output-stationary MACs per byte.
L4.answer: Output stationary: bytes $= 2NK + N^{2}(w/8)$; MACs $= N^{2}K$. For $N=256$, $K=1024$, $w=32$: $524288 + 262144 = 786432$ bytes, 67108864 MACs, 85.3 MACs per byte. Weight stationary at the same shape moves $N^{2} + NK + NK(w/8)$, which is larger because every partial sum leaves at 4 bytes.
L4.explanation: Accumulator width is the term that decides between the two dataflows and it is the one omitted from most diagrams. Once you count partial sums at 4 bytes rather than 1, output stationary's advantage on deep reductions becomes obvious.

L4.prompt_tpl: A layer has a small output tile and a reduction depth of {k}. Which dataflow do you pick and why?
options: Output stationary, because a deep reduction means each output is touched many times
Weight stationary, because deep reductions always favour holding weights
Input stationary, because reduction depth affects only the activation stream
L4.answer: Output stationary: the deep reduction means partial sums would otherwise be written and re-read many times, and holding the accumulator in place eliminates that traffic entirely at the cost of one wide register per PE.
L4.explanation: The rule of thumb follows from the loop structure: keep stationary whichever tensor is reused most along the temporally mapped loop. A deep k loop means the output element is touched K times, so it is the one to pin. A wide n loop with shallow k means the weight is the reused one.

L0.body:
# Input stationary (IS): the PE holds an activation; weights stream,
#   partial sums stream. Optimises ACTIVATION reads.
#   Good when activations dwarf weights: early conv, high-res feature
#   maps, depthwise convolution.
#
# No local reuse (NLR): PEs have NO registers; everything comes from a
#   large global buffer every cycle.
#   Area per PE minimal    -> more PEs per mm^2
#   Buffer traffic maximal -> worst energy per MAC. DianNao (2014).
#
# The four choices are exactly 'which of the three tensors do I pin':
#   WS -> weights   OS -> partial sums   IS -> activations   NLR -> none
L0.cloze: The dataflow taxonomy is simply which tensor you {{c1::pin in the PE}}: weights, partial sums, activations, or {{c2::nothing}}. No-local-reuse minimises {{c3::PE area}} and maximises buffer traffic and energy per MAC.

concepts.L1: Input-stationary pins the activation in the processing element so weights and partial sums stream past it. No-local-reuse pins nothing: every operand comes from a global buffer each cycle, minimising PE area at the cost of maximal buffer traffic.
concepts.L2: No-local-reuse looks like a straw man and is not. It maximises MACs per square millimetre, which is the right objective if your bottleneck is area and your buffer bandwidth is abundant. DianNao chose it deliberately, and the field moved away only once energy, not area, became the binding constraint.
concepts.L3: The taxonomy is a partition of one design decision. Each of the three tensors, weights, activations and partial sums, is reused along some loop, and pinning one in a PE register turns its reuse along the innermost temporal loop into zero memory traffic. You can pin at most one per PE without adding registers, so the options are three single pins plus the empty choice; row-stationary breaks the frame by pinning a slice of the computation instead. The consequence is that dataflow choice is layer-dependent, so a fixed-dataflow accelerator is always wrong for some layer. That argues for flexible interconnects such as Eyeriss v2 and MAERI.

L4.prompt_tpl: A layer has {w} thousand weights and a {a} MB activation tensor. Which stationary dataflow minimises memory traffic?
options: Input stationary, because the activation tensor dominates the traffic
Weight stationary, because weights are always the expensive tensor to fetch
No local reuse, because it has the smallest PEs and therefore the most parallelism
L4.answer: Input stationary: the activation tensor dominates traffic, so pinning activations in the PEs and streaming the small weight set past them minimises bytes moved.
L4.explanation: The rule is to pin the largest tensor relative to its reuse. Early convolution layers have few weights and enormous feature maps, which is exactly the input-stationary case; late fully connected layers are the reverse. Since a real network contains both, one fixed dataflow is necessarily suboptimal somewhere.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why a no-local-reuse design might still be the right choice when the design is limited by {c}, and what it costs.
L4.answer: Removing per-PE registers shrinks each PE substantially, so more MACs fit in the same area and peak throughput rises. The cost is that every operand is fetched from the global buffer every cycle, so buffer bandwidth and energy per MAC are the worst of any dataflow, which is fatal once energy rather than area is the binding constraint.
L4.explanation: This is a useful reminder that dataflow choice follows from which resource is scarce. DianNao was designed when the interesting question was how many MACs you could fit; the field's shift to energy-first design is what made row-stationary and Eyeriss the reference point instead.

L0.body:
# Every other dataflow pins ONE tensor. Row stationary pins a SLICE OF
# THE COMPUTATION: one PE holds one row of filter weights and computes
# one row of the 1-D convolution primitive.
#
#   PE(i,j) holds filter row i, processes input row i+j,
#           produces partial sums for output row j
#
#   -> filter row reused ACROSS the row     (weight reuse)
#   -> input row reused along the DIAGONAL  (activation reuse)
#   -> partial sums accumulate UP the column (psum reuse)
#
# All three tensors get reuse from ONE mapping.
# Eyeriss (Chen, Krishna, Emer, Sze, ISSCC 2016): 168 PEs, 65nm.
L0.cloze: Row stationary pins {{c1::a slice of the computation}}, not a tensor, so filter rows, input rows and partial sums all get reuse from {{c2::one}} mapping. Eyeriss used {{c3::168}} PEs at 65nm.

concepts.L1: Row-stationary maps a one-dimensional convolution primitive onto each processing element: a filter row against an input row producing a partial output row. Reuse of all three tensors emerges from a single spatial mapping rather than from pinning one of them.
concepts.L2: The insight is that optimising any single tensor's traffic is the wrong objective. Total energy is the weighted sum over all three, weighted by how expensive each level of the hierarchy is, and the mapping that minimises that sum is generally not the one that minimises any single term.
concepts.L3: Eyeriss's method was to make the objective explicit. Chen, Krishna, Emer and Sze weighted each access by the energy of the level it came from: a register roughly 1 unit, a neighbour transfer 2, a global buffer 6, DRAM 200. Under that weighting the winner is not the dataflow minimising DRAM accesses for one tensor, but the one keeping the largest share of all accesses in registers and neighbour links. Row stationary does it because diagonal propagation of input rows and vertical accumulation of partial sums both use neighbour links, while filter rows are reused horizontally in registers. The lesson outlives the dataflow: state the energy model first, then search mappings against it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Using a relative energy model of register {r}, neighbour {nb}, global buffer {g}, DRAM {d} per access, compare a mapping with {a} percent register accesses against one with {b} percent, both with 1 percent DRAM. Answer with the weighted cost per access for the first mapping.
L4.answer: Weighted cost per access $= \sum p_{i} e_{i}$. With 80 percent register, 19 percent buffer, 1 percent DRAM: $0.8(1) + 0.19(6) + 0.01(200) = 3.94$. With 50 percent register, 49 percent buffer, 1 percent DRAM: $0.5 + 2.94 + 2 = 5.44$, about 38 percent worse.
L4.explanation: The DRAM term dominates even at 1 percent of accesses, which is the whole reason accelerators are built around keeping data on chip. Notice also that shifting accesses from buffer to register matters, which is why per-PE registers exist at all and why no-local-reuse designs lose on energy.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain what row-stationary pins in each PE and why that gives reuse of all {n} tensors simultaneously, unlike weight or output stationary.
L4.answer: It pins a one-dimensional convolution primitive: a filter row and its corresponding input row, producing a partial output row. Filter rows are then reused horizontally across a PE row, input rows diagonally, and partial sums vertically, so each of the three tensors gets reuse from a different direction of the same mapping.
L4.explanation: The distinction is that the other dataflows choose a tensor and the mapping follows; row-stationary chooses a computation primitive and reuse of all three tensors falls out of the geometry. It only works because convolution has that primitive; a plain matmul does not, which is why TPU-class designs stay weight stationary.

concepts.t: Reuse arithmetic: bytes moved per MAC

L0.body:
# The number that decides an accelerator's energy: bytes moved from
# each memory level, per MAC.
#
# Energy per access, 45nm, Horowitz ISSCC 2014:
#   32-bit int add        0.1 pJ
#   32-bit float add      0.9 pJ
#   32-bit int multiply   3.1 pJ
#   8 KB SRAM read        5 pJ
#   32-bit DRAM read    640 pJ    <- 6400x the int add
#
# energy = MACs*E_mac + bytes_sram*E_sram + bytes_dram*E_dram
#   1e9 MACs at 0.2 pJ                    = 0.2 mJ
#   0.1 B DRAM/MAC, 640pJ/4B: 1e8*160 pJ  = 16 mJ  (80x)
#
# You are designing a data-movement engine that happens to multiply.
L0.cloze: At 45nm a 32-bit DRAM read costs {{c1::640}} pJ against {{c2::0.1}} pJ for an int add, a ratio of about 6400. At 0.1 DRAM bytes per MAC, data movement costs roughly {{c3::80}} times the arithmetic.

concepts.L1: Bytes moved per MAC, evaluated separately at each level of the memory hierarchy, is the figure that determines an accelerator's energy. Arithmetic energy is a small and usually negligible term once any DRAM traffic is present.
concepts.L2: The consequence is that peak TOPS is nearly meaningless as a design metric. Two designs with identical MAC counts can differ by an order of magnitude in energy purely through how many times each byte crosses each level, and that is a mapping property, not a circuit property.
concepts.L3: Horowitz's ISSCC 2014 numbers are the ones the field quotes, and their shape matters more than their exact values. Arithmetic is essentially free, local SRAM roughly fifty times an add, DRAM thousands. Optimisation is entirely about pushing accesses down the hierarchy. Total energy is $E = \mathrm{MACs} \cdot E_{\mathrm{mac}} + \sum_{\ell} B_{\ell} E_{\ell}$, with $B_{\ell}$ the bytes moved at level $\ell$. A billion MACs at 0.2 pJ costs 0.2 mJ; move 0.1 bytes of DRAM per MAC and at 640 pJ per 4 bytes that is 16 mJ, eighty times more. Every dataflow argument here is an argument about $B_{\ell}$, and the first question about any accelerator claim is bytes per MAC at each level.

L4.prompt_tpl: A workload performs {g} billion MACs at {e} pJ each and moves {b} DRAM bytes per MAC at {d} pJ per 32-bit access. Compute arithmetic energy, DRAM energy and their ratio. Answer with the ratio of DRAM energy to arithmetic energy.
L4.answer: Arithmetic $= G \times 10^{9} \times e$ pJ; DRAM $= G \times 10^{9} \times b \times (d/4)$ pJ. For $G=1$, $e=0.2$, $b=0.1$: 0.2 mJ versus 16 mJ, a ratio of 80.
L4.explanation: The ratio is the design's report card. Anything above a few means the design is a data-movement engine and the mapping, not the MAC count, is what to optimise. Getting bytes per MAC below 0.01 is the actual goal of tiling and dataflow selection.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two accelerators both claim {t} TOPS. Design A moves {a} bytes per MAC from DRAM, design B moves {b}. What do you need to know to compare them, and which is better?
options: Design A: ten times less DRAM traffic per MAC means roughly ten times better performance per watt
Design B: more DRAM traffic indicates a larger effective memory bandwidth
They are equivalent, since peak TOPS fully determines delivered performance
L4.answer: Design A, by roughly ten times on energy: identical peak throughput with ten times less DRAM traffic per MAC means an order of magnitude better performance per watt, which is the metric that actually constrains deployment.
L4.explanation: Peak TOPS is set by MAC count and clock and says nothing about deliverable performance or energy. Bytes per MAC at each hierarchy level is the discriminating number, and it is a property of the dataflow and tiling, which is why two chips with the same array can differ enormously.

concepts.t: Loop nests, tiling and the mapspace

L0.body:
# A tiled matmul: same computation, loops split by level.
#
#   for m2 in range(M//Tm):      # DRAM level
#     for n2 in range(N//Tn):
#       for k2 in range(K//Tk):
#         for m1 in range(Tm):   # SRAM level
#           for n1 in range(Tn):
#             for k1 in range(Tk):  # PE / register level
#               C[...] += A[...] * B[...]
#
# MAPPING = tile sizes per level + loop ORDER per level + which loops
#   are spatial vs temporal.
#
# Mapspace, 7-deep nest, 3 levels: 5040^3 = 1.28e11 orderings, times
#   every factorisation of each dimension. Not a by-hand problem.
L0.cloze: A mapping is the {{c1::tile sizes, loop order and spatial-versus-temporal assignment}} at every memory level. For a 7-deep nest across 3 levels the orderings alone number about {{c2::1.28e11}}, which is why the search is {{c3::automated}}.

concepts.L1: Tiling splits each loop into a per-level hierarchy so that the working set at each level fits its capacity. The full set of tile sizes, loop orders and spatial assignments across all levels is the mapspace, and choosing a point in it is the mapping problem.
concepts.L2: The mapspace, not the hardware, is usually where the performance is. Two mappings of the same network onto the same accelerator routinely differ by an order of magnitude in energy, so an architecture evaluated with a bad mapping is being slandered rather than measured.
concepts.L3: Parashar and colleagues formalised this in Timeloop, and the formalisation is the useful part. A mapping assigns a tile factor per dimension and level, a loop permutation per level, and a split into spatially unrolled and temporally iterated loops. Given one, the tool computes exactly how many accesses each level sees, because the loop structure determines it: a tensor is re-fetched at a level whenever a loop it does not depend on sits outside a loop it does. Access counts plus an energy model give total energy without simulation, so $10^{11}$ candidates are searchable with pruning. Always report which mapping produced a number.

L4.prompt_tpl: A matmul with M={M}, N={N}, K={K} is tiled to fit an on-chip buffer of {s} KB holding int8 operands and 4-byte partial sums. If the tile is Tm x Tk for A, Tk x Tn for B and Tm x Tn for C, give the capacity constraint and one feasible tile.
L4.answer: Constraint: $T_{m}T_{k} + T_{k}T_{n} + 4T_{m}T_{n} \leq S$. For $S = 256$ KB = 262144 bytes, $T_{m}=T_{n}=T_{k}=128$ gives $16384+16384+65536 = 98304$ bytes, feasible; $T=256$ gives $65536+65536+262144 = 393216$, which does not fit.
L4.explanation: The partial-sum term carries a factor of 4 for accumulator width and therefore dominates the capacity constraint, which pushes tiles toward being deep in K and modest in M and N. Working one constraint by hand once makes every later Timeloop result legible.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why reporting an accelerator's energy per inference without stating the mapping is close to meaningless, using a mapspace of roughly {n} candidates as the reason.
L4.answer: Because mappings of the same network onto the same hardware differ by an order of magnitude in memory traffic, so the reported number describes the mapping search as much as the architecture. A fair comparison requires each architecture to be evaluated under its own best mapping found by the same search effort.
L4.explanation: This is the standard methodological failure in accelerator papers and the reason Timeloop's mapper is as important as its model. Comparing two architectures under a mapping tuned for one of them measures the tuning, not the hardware.

concepts.t: The TPU line, generation by generation

L0.body:
# TPU v1 (ISCA 2017, arXiv 1704.04760): 256x256 int8 systolic array,
#   700 MHz, 92 TOPS peak. Inference only. 24 MiB unified buffer =
#   29% of die; MAC array 24%. SRAM > compute.
#
# v2/v3 (CACM 2020): training, bfloat16, HBM, 2-D torus, several
#   smaller MXUs rather than one big one.
#
# v4 (ISCA 2023): optical circuit switching, so pod topology is
#   RECONFIGURED per job. Embedding hardware.
#
# v7 'Ironwood', Google Cloud docs, checked 3 Sept 2026: 2307 TFLOP/s
#   BF16, 4614 FP8, 192 GB HBM, ~7.37 TB/s/chip, two chiplets, 3-D
#   torus, 9216-chip pod. No architecture paper.
L0.cloze: TPU v1's 256x256 int8 array at 700 MHz gives {{c1::91.75}} TOPS, and its unified buffer occupied {{c2::29}} percent of the die against 24 percent for the array. TPU v7 Ironwood is documented at {{c3::4614}} TFLOP/s FP8 with 192 GB of HBM at 7.37 TB/s.

concepts.L1: The TPU line is the best-documented accelerator lineage in the field: a single large int8 inference array, then bfloat16 training parts with HBM and a torus interconnect, then optical reconfiguration, then chiplet-based designs at multi-petaflop scale.
concepts.L2: The generations are not a story about bigger arrays. Peak compute per chip grew by roughly 50 times from v1 to v7 while the array structure changed relatively little; almost all of the gain came from number format, memory bandwidth, chip count and interconnect. That is the field's actual growth mechanism.
concepts.L3: Track what changed at each step. v1 to v2 was inference to training, forcing a wider format: bfloat16 exists because fp16's five exponent bits are too few for training gradients while its ten mantissa bits are more than needed, so bfloat16 keeps fp32's eight exponent bits and truncates the mantissa to seven, making conversion a truncation. v2 to v4 was overwhelmingly scale-out: the torus, then optical circuit switching so pod topology matches a job's collective pattern. v4 to v7 added chiplets and far more HBM bandwidth. The lesson is Dally's: representation and specialisation, not process shrinks, produced most of the gain.

L4.prompt_tpl: Verify TPU v1's peak: a {n}x{n} int8 systolic array at {f} MHz, counting a multiply-accumulate as two operations. Then compute the ratio to Ironwood's documented {i} TFLOP/s FP8. Answer with the peak in operations per second.
L4.answer: Peak $= n^{2} \times 2 \times f = 65536 \times 2 \times 7 \times 10^{8} = 9.175 \times 10^{13}$, i.e. 91.75 TOPS. Ironwood at 4614 TFLOP/s FP8 is about 50 times that.
L4.explanation: Doing this multiplication once fixes the shape of every accelerator peak figure: MAC count times two times clock. It also shows how modest v1's clock was, which is the wide-and-slow energy argument in practice, and how much of the 50x gain came from format and scale rather than array size.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why bfloat16 replaced fp16 for training, in terms of the {b}-bit field allocation, and what it costs in precision.
L4.answer: bfloat16 keeps fp32's 8 exponent bits and truncates the mantissa to 7, whereas fp16 has 5 exponent and 10 mantissa bits. Training gradients span a huge dynamic range and underflow in fp16 without loss scaling; bfloat16 matches fp32's range so conversion is a truncation and no scaling is needed. The cost is about three fewer mantissa bits of precision.
L4.explanation: This is a clean example of co-design: the number format was chosen from a property of the workload, gradient dynamic range, rather than from circuit convenience. It also simplifies hardware, since fp32 to bfloat16 conversion is a shift and round rather than a full renormalisation.

L0.body:
# A cache: address -> tag lookup -> hit or miss -> maybe DRAM.
#   Hardware picks residency; latency is data-dependent; needs
#   tags, comparators, replacement state, coherence if shared.
#
# A scratchpad: flat, directly addressed SRAM, no tags.
#   Software picks what is resident; latency is constant; data
#   arrives by explicit DMA ahead of use.
#
# A scratchpad deletes the tag array (~10% of SRAM area), comparators,
#   replacement policy, MSHRs, coherence and all timing variance.
#   It costs: the compiler schedules every transfer, and a missing
#   prefetch is a stall, not a slow path.
L0.cloze: A scratchpad is directly addressed SRAM with {{c1::no tags}}, so latency is {{c2::constant}} and software issues explicit DMA. It deletes the tag array, replacement state and the whole {{c3::coherence protocol}}.

concepts.L1: Accelerators overwhelmingly use software-managed scratchpad memory with explicit DMA rather than hardware caches. The compiler decides residency, transfers are issued ahead of use, and access latency becomes a compile-time constant.
concepts.L2: The decisive advantage is not area, though tags cost about ten percent of an SRAM array. It is determinism: a systolic array must receive an operand on an exact cycle, and a structure that sometimes takes 4 cycles and sometimes 300 cannot be scheduled statically at all.
concepts.L3: Follow the requirement backwards. A statically scheduled array has no mechanism to stall a single PE, so every operand must be present when the schedule says it will be. A cache cannot promise that; it promises an average. So either you add stall logic and back-pressure through the whole array, destroying its simplicity and energy advantage, or you make latency known. Scratchpads make it known. The cost lands on software: the compiler must compute tile sizes, issue DMA far enough ahead to cover DRAM latency, and double-buffer so transfers overlap compute. That is why an accelerator without a good compiler is worthless.

L4.prompt_tpl: An accelerator team proposes replacing its {s} KB scratchpad with a cache of the same capacity to simplify the compiler. Assess.
options: Reject: static scheduling requires deterministic latency, which a cache cannot provide
Accept: caches are strictly better since they adapt to access patterns automatically
Accept, provided the cache is made coherent with the host CPU's caches
L4.answer: Reject: the array is statically scheduled and has no per-PE stall mechanism, so data-dependent latency would require adding back-pressure throughout the array, costing area, energy and the timing determinism the design depends on.
L4.explanation: The compiler burden is real but it is the price of a structure that has no dynamic control at all. Adding a cache means adding the ability to stall, which means adding valid bits and back-pressure to every PE. That is a different, much larger and less efficient machine.

L4.prompt_tpl: A DMA must cover {lat} ns of DRAM latency at {gbs} GB/s while the array consumes a tile every {t} microseconds. How far ahead must the transfer be issued and how much buffering does double buffering require for a {ktile} KB tile? Answer with how far ahead the transfer must be issued, in nanoseconds.
L4.answer: Issue at least $\mathrm{latency} + \mathrm{tile}/\mathrm{bw}$ ahead of use. For 400 ns latency, 64 KB at 400 GB/s: transfer takes 160 ns, so issue at least 560 ns ahead. Double buffering needs $2 \times 64 = 128$ KB of scratchpad.
L4.explanation: Double buffering is what converts a latency problem into a bandwidth problem: while the array consumes buffer A, the DMA fills buffer B. The scratchpad must therefore be sized to twice the working tile, which is a direct and often surprising doubling of the most expensive resource on the die.

concepts.t: On-chip SRAM is what actually eats the die

L0.body:
# TPU v1 die area breakdown (Jouppi et al., ISCA 2017):
#   unified buffer (24 MiB SRAM)   29%
#   matrix multiply unit           24%
#   accumulators                    6%
#   everything else                41%
#
#   SRAM / MAC-array area ratio = 29/24 = 1.21
#
# Why: a 6T SRAM cell is 6 transistors but is WIRE-PITCH limited, and
# SRAM has scaled far more slowly than logic across recent nodes
# (widely reported; treat per-node figures with suspicion).
#
# So you do not size the array then add SRAM. You decide the SRAM
# budget, then size the array to what it can feed.
L0.cloze: In TPU v1 the 24 MiB unified buffer took {{c1::29}} percent of the die against {{c2::24}} percent for the MAC array. The design order is therefore: choose the {{c3::SRAM budget}} first, then size the array to what it can feed.

concepts.L1: On-chip SRAM typically occupies more die area than the arithmetic it feeds. SRAM density has improved far more slowly than logic density across recent process nodes, so the imbalance has grown rather than shrunk.
concepts.L2: The instinct to treat memory as support infrastructure for the compute is backwards. In an accelerator the buffer is the primary structure: it determines achievable reuse, which determines DRAM traffic, which determines energy, and the MAC array is sized to whatever the buffer can sustain.
concepts.L3: Two forces make this true. First, SRAM cells are limited by wire pitch and by read-margin requirements, so they have not tracked logic scaling: each recent node has delivered substantially better logic density than SRAM density. Second, the buffer must grow with the tile size that gives the reuse you need, and reuse is what suppresses DRAM energy, so as arithmetic gets cheaper the buffer takes a larger share of area and cost. This drives the chiplet strategy too: since SRAM scales poorly there is little reason to fabricate buffers on the most advanced node, which argues for putting memory-heavy dies on a cheaper process behind a die-to-die interface.

L4.prompt_tpl: An accelerator budget is {a} mm^2. If SRAM costs {s} mm^2 per MiB and an int8 MAC costs {m} um^2, and you want an SRAM-to-array area ratio of {r}, how much SRAM and how many MACs do you get? Answer with the SRAM area in mm^2.
L4.answer: Let array area $= a/(1+r)$ and SRAM $= ar/(1+r)$. For $a=200$, $r=1.2$, $s=0.6$, $m=300$: array 90.9 mm^2 giving 303 thousand MACs ($N=550$), SRAM 109.1 mm^2 giving 182 MiB.
L4.explanation: Doing the split explicitly forces the real decision into the open: every square millimetre of buffer is a square millimetre not spent on MACs, and the right ratio depends entirely on how much reuse the extra buffer buys for your workload. That is a Timeloop question, not a guess.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why poor SRAM density scaling on advanced nodes is an argument for {t}, and name the packaging technology that enables it.

t: disaggregating cache onto a separate die

L4.answer: If SRAM barely shrinks on the newest node, paying that node's much higher cost per square millimetre for SRAM area buys almost nothing, whereas logic does shrink. So it is economically rational to fabricate memory-heavy dies on an older, cheaper process and connect them to a leading-edge logic die with a high-bandwidth die-to-die link, using 2.5D interposers or 3D stacking.
L4.explanation: AMD's stacked cache products are the visible instance of this reasoning. The general principle is that heterogeneous integration lets each function sit on the node where its cost per unit of value is lowest, which is only possible once die-to-die bandwidth is cheap enough.

concepts.t: Quantised datapaths and the quadratic multiplier

L0.body:
# A b-bit array multiplier is roughly b^2 partial-product cells.
# A b-bit adder is roughly b cells. So:
#
#   multiplier area, energy ~ O(b^2)
#   adder      area, energy ~ O(b)
#
#   fp16 -> fp8 : (16/8)^2 = 4x smaller multiplier
#   int8 -> int4: (8/4)^2  = 4x smaller
#
# Halving precision is NOT a 2x win. It is close to 4x on the array.
# Plus half the bytes moved, so memory energy halves too.
#
# The catch: accumulators do NOT shrink. Summing K int8 products needs
#   ceil(log2(K)) + 16 bits; K=1024 -> 26 bits.
# A 4x smaller multiplier sits next to an unchanged 32-bit adder.
L0.cloze: Multiplier cost scales as {{c1::b squared}} and adder cost as b, so halving precision is close to a {{c2::4x}} win on the multiply array. Accumulators do not shrink: summing K int8 products overflow-free needs {{c3::ceil(log2 K) + 16}} bits.

concepts.L1: Multiplier area and energy scale roughly with the square of operand width because the partial-product array is two-dimensional. Reducing precision therefore buys a quadratic improvement in the arithmetic and a linear one in memory traffic.
concepts.L2: The accumulator is the part that refuses to shrink, and it is why low-precision arrays are less of a win than the multiplier arithmetic suggests. A design at int4 has multipliers sixteen times smaller than int16 but the same wide accumulators, so accumulation becomes a large share of both PE area and PE energy.
concepts.L3: Compute the accumulator width properly, because getting it wrong is a silent correctness bug. The product of two int8 values fits in 16 bits. Summing $K$ such products needs $\lceil \log_{2} K \rceil$ extra bits to be overflow-free, so depth 1024 needs $16 + 10 = 26$ bits and designs round to 32. That accumulator sits in every PE and gains nothing from the precision reduction. This is the structural reason the industry chased formats rather than raw width: fp8 in its E4M3 and E5M2 variants, and microscaling formats that share an exponent across a block so the mantissa can be tiny while per-block dynamic range survives. Each format tries to shrink the multiplier without breaking accumulation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare multiplier and adder cost between {b1}-bit and {b2}-bit operands using the $O(b^{{2}})$ and $O(b)$ rules, then give the overflow-free accumulator width for a reduction of depth {k}. Answer with the overflow-free accumulator width in bits.
L4.answer: Multiplier ratio $= (b_{1}/b_{2})^{2}$; adder ratio $= b_{1}/b_{2}$. Accumulator $= 2b_{2} + \lceil\log_{2} k\rceil$. For 16 to 8 bits with $k=1024$: multiplier 4x smaller, adder 2x, accumulator $16+10=26$ bits, rounded to 32.
L4.explanation: The two exponents are what make precision reduction attractive and the fixed accumulator is what caps the benefit. A real PE's area is multiplier plus accumulator plus registers, so the delivered improvement is always less than the multiplier ratio, and increasingly so as precision falls.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain what a block-scaled or microscaling format buys over plain fp{b}, in terms of what each stored value must encode.
L4.answer: A shared exponent is stored once per block of values, so each element carries only a small mantissa and sign while dynamic range is preserved at block granularity. That lets the per-element width shrink further than a self-contained float allows, shrinking the multiplier array quadratically, at the cost of accuracy when a block contains values of very different magnitude.
L4.explanation: This is a co-design move: the format exploits the empirical fact that neural network tensors have locally similar magnitudes. It fails exactly where that assumption fails, which is why outlier handling is a standing topic in low-precision inference.

L0.body:
# Unstructured sparsity: any weight may be zero.
#   -> irregular gather, PE load imbalance, index overhead
#   -> 90% sparsity often yields <2x real speedup
#
# 2:4 structured sparsity (NVIDIA Ampere on): in EVERY group of 4
# contiguous weights, exactly 2 must be zero.
#   -> static pattern: 2 MACs per 4 weights
#   -> a small mux selects activations. 2x MAC throughput.
#
# Storage, int8, per group:
#   dense: 4 * 8                 = 32 bits
#   2:4:   2 * 8 + 2 * 2 (index) = 20 bits -> 1.6x, NOT 2x
#
# Co-design at its purest: the ALGORITHM was constrained to fit
# silicon.
L0.cloze: In 2:4 sparsity exactly {{c1::2}} of every 4 contiguous weights are zero, giving {{c2::2x}} MAC throughput but only {{c3::1.6x}} storage compression, because 2-bit indices must be stored.

concepts.L1: Structured sparsity constrains where zeros may appear so hardware can exploit them with a fixed, statically known pattern. NVIDIA's 2:4 scheme requires exactly two zeros in every group of four weights, letting a multiplexer select the surviving operands.
concepts.L2: The gap between the throughput gain and the storage gain is the part that gets misquoted. Skipping half the multiplies doubles arithmetic throughput, but the index metadata means memory traffic falls by only 1.6 times, so a memory-bound layer sees far less than a 2x speedup.
concepts.L3: Understand why unstructured sparsity fails on regular hardware, because that is what the structure answers. With arbitrary zeros each PE's workload depends on its slice of the weights, so PEs finish at different times and the array runs at the speed of the slowest, destroying most of the theoretical saving. Indexing costs grow too: a sparse format needs an index per non-zero, which at high sparsity approaches the value's own size. Two-in-four makes work per group constant, so there is no imbalance, and the index is two bits per selected position. The price falls on the algorithm, which must be retrained under the constraint with no automatic accuracy recovery.

L4.prompt_tpl: For int{b} weights under 2:4 structured sparsity with {i}-bit indices, compute bits per group of four, the compression ratio, and the speedup on a layer that is {m} percent memory bound. Answer with the compression ratio.
L4.answer: Bits per group $= 2b + 2i$ versus $4b$ dense; ratio $= 4b/(2b+2i)$. For $b=8$, $i=2$: $20$ versus $32$, ratio 1.6. A fully compute-bound layer gets up to 2x; a fully memory-bound layer gets at most 1.6x.
L4.explanation: Two different ratios govern two different regimes, which is why a single sparsity speedup number is never right for a whole network. Checking which regime each layer is in, via arithmetic intensity, is the necessary step before predicting any gain.

L4.prompt_tpl: A researcher reports {s} percent unstructured weight sparsity and predicts a proportional speedup on a systolic array. What is wrong?
options: Load imbalance across PEs and index overhead absorb most of the theoretical saving
Nothing: sparsity speedup is proportional to zero fraction on any array
Unstructured sparsity cannot be represented in int8, so the figure is meaningless
L4.answer: Arbitrary zero placement gives each PE a different amount of work, so the array runs at the pace of the busiest PE, and index overhead grows with sparsity. Real speedup on regular hardware is usually a small factor, which is why hardware exploits structured patterns instead.
L4.explanation: The theoretical saving assumes work can be redistributed freely, which a spatially fixed array cannot do. Load imbalance and indexing are the two costs that eat it. Designs that do exploit unstructured sparsity, such as EIE and SCNN, add substantial routing and queuing hardware precisely to attack those two problems.

concepts.t: The memory wall as a number

L0.body:
# Three ways to state the same gap:
#
# 1. LATENCY. DRAM ~80-100 ns; a 3 GHz cycle is 0.33 ns.
#    -> ~250-300 cycles of nothing.
#
# 2. ENERGY. Horowitz 2014, 45nm: 32-bit DRAM read 640 pJ vs int add
#    0.1 pJ -> 6400x. Against a 0.2 pJ int8 MAC, 160 pJ/byte -> 800x.
#
# 3. RIDGE POINT = peak compute / peak bandwidth, FLOP per byte.
#    TPU v7 Ironwood, Google Cloud docs, checked 3 Sept 2026:
#      4614e12 / 7.37e12 = 626 FLOP/byte at FP8
#    RISEN every generation. That is the wall, quantified.
#
# Bandwidth is bought with pins and power, compute with area.
# Area scaled. Pins did not.
L0.cloze: The memory wall can be stated as {{c1::250-300}} wasted cycles per DRAM access, as an energy ratio of about {{c2::6400x}} between a DRAM read and an integer add, or as a ridge point that {{c3::rises}} every generation.

concepts.L1: The memory wall is the growing gap between arithmetic capability and the ability to supply operands. It is measurable three ways: latency in cycles, energy per byte against energy per operation, and the roofline ridge point in operations per byte.
concepts.L2: The ridge-point framing is the one that matters for accelerator design, because it is the only one that gets worse by design rather than by accident. Bandwidth is bought with package pins and interface power, both of which scale poorly, while compute is bought with area, which has scaled well.
concepts.L3: Understand why the two scale differently. Adding MACs costs die area, and area per MAC has fallen with every node and every precision reduction. Adding bandwidth costs either more pins, limited by package and interposer physics, or higher per-pin rates, which cost power superlinearly and demand elaborate equalisation. HBM's answer, a wide slow interface on an interposer, buys bandwidth with width rather than frequency; it works, but stacks per die are bounded by interposer size and thermals. So the ridge point rises. The design responses follow: more on-chip SRAM to raise reuse, lower precision to halve bytes, sparsity to skip bytes, near-memory compute to avoid the crossing.

L4.prompt_tpl: A part has {c} TFLOP/s peak and {b} TB/s bandwidth; its predecessor had {c2} TFLOP/s and {b2} TB/s. Compute both ridge points and state whether the memory wall got better or worse. Answer with the new part's ridge point.
L4.answer: Ridge $= c/b$. New: $4614/7.37 = 626$ FLOP per byte. Old: $989/3.35 = 295$. The ridge more than doubled, so a kernel unchanged between generations moves further into the memory-bound region: the wall got worse.
L4.explanation: This is the honest way to compare two accelerator generations. Compute grew 4.7 times and bandwidth 2.2 times, so the balance point moved and workloads that were compute bound may no longer be. Peak FLOPs alone would have suggested a straightforward improvement.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why adding {n} TB/s of memory bandwidth is structurally harder than adding an equivalent amount of peak compute.
L4.answer: Compute is bought with die area, which shrinks per operation at each node and with each precision reduction. Bandwidth is bought with pin count, limited by package and interposer geometry, or with per-pin signalling rate, whose power cost grows superlinearly and which needs increasingly elaborate equalisation. Neither scales like area.
L4.explanation: The asymmetry is physical rather than economic, which is why it has persisted through many generations and why architectural responses, reuse, quantisation, sparsity and near-memory compute, all aim at reducing demand rather than raising supply.

#   [ DRAM die 8 ]      <- 4, 8, 12 or 16 dies high
#   [ DRAM die ... ]       joined by THROUGH-SILICON VIAS
#   [ DRAM die 1 ]
#   [ base/logic die ]  <- PHY, test, buffering
#         |||||||  microbumps
#   [ silicon interposer ]  <- ~1024 (HBM4: ~2048) wires to the
#         |||||||             compute die a few mm away
#   [ package substrate ]
#
# WIDE and SLOW, not narrow and fast: short traces run 1024+ wires at
# modest per-pin rates, far more energy-efficient per bit.
#
# Cost: co-assembled, not socketable, capacity fixed at build.
L0.cloze: An HBM stack is DRAM dies connected by {{c1::through-silicon vias}} over a base die, joined to the compute die through a {{c2::silicon interposer}}. The interface is deliberately {{c3::wide and slow}} rather than narrow and fast.

concepts.L1: HBM is a vertical stack of DRAM dies bonded to a base die and connected to the processor through a silicon interposer carrying a thousand or more parallel wires over a distance of millimetres.
concepts.L2: The reason HBM wins is geometry, not DRAM technology: the dies are ordinary DRAM. Putting them millimetres away on an interposer instead of centimetres away on a board is what allows a very wide interface at low per-pin rates, and energy per bit falls roughly with the square of the distance-driven signalling requirement.
concepts.L3: The consequences follow from the assembly. Because the stack is co-assembled with the logic die on an interposer, capacity is fixed at manufacture, which is why accelerator SKUs are defined by their memory. Because the interposer is itself a silicon die, its area is bounded by the lithographic reticle, historically about 858 square millimetres, and multi-reticle interposers are specialised and expensive; that bounds how many stacks can surround a compute die. Because the assembly is one part, yields multiply: a bad stack ruins a good logic die unless known-good-die testing is thorough. And since DRAM refresh worsens with temperature, thermal design is a memory-reliability problem too.

L4.prompt_tpl: An HBM stack presents a {w}-bit interface at {r} Gb/s per pin. Compute per-stack bandwidth, and how many stacks are needed to reach {t} TB/s. Answer with the per-stack bandwidth in GB/s.
L4.answer: Bandwidth $= w \times r / 8$ bytes per second. For $w=1024$, $r=9.6$: $1228.8$ GB/s per stack, so reaching 7.37 TB/s needs $7370/1228.8 = 6.0$ stacks.
L4.explanation: The formula is the whole of HBM bandwidth: width times per-pin rate over eight. Width is set by the standard, per-pin rate by the generation, and stack count by how many fit around the die on the interposer. Verify per-pin rates against the current JEDEC standard rather than trusting a remembered figure.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why HBM capacity on an accelerator cannot be upgraded after purchase, and one reliability consequence of the stack sitting beside a {p}-watt compute die.
L4.answer: The stacks are bonded to the same interposer as the logic die during packaging, so the assembly is a single inseparable part. Thermally, DRAM retention time falls as temperature rises, so a hot neighbour forces more frequent refresh, which consumes bandwidth and power and can become a performance limit under sustained load.
L4.explanation: The refresh coupling is the non-obvious one and it is a genuine design constraint: refresh steals bandwidth from the interface, so thermal design and achievable memory bandwidth are linked. It is also why accelerator throttling behaviour is memory-dependent rather than purely compute-dependent.

L0.body:
# The controller sits between the request stream and DRAM timing.
# Its job: reorder requests to maximise row-buffer hits.
#
# FR-FCFS (first-ready, first-come-first-served):
#   1. prefer requests hitting an OPEN row buffer
#   2. among those, the oldest
#   3. otherwise, the oldest ready request
#
# Representative DDR-class timings:
#   row-buffer HIT  : tCL only          ~ 15 ns
#   row-buffer MISS : tRP + tRCD + tCL  ~ 45 ns
#   ~3x, and the miss burns activation energy too
#
# For an accelerator this matters less: DMA streams are long and
# sequential, so hit rates are high.
L0.cloze: FR-FCFS prioritises requests that hit an {{c1::open row buffer}}, then the oldest. A row-buffer miss costs roughly {{c2::3x}} a hit. For accelerators, long sequential {{c3::DMA}} streams make hit rates high by construction.

concepts.L1: The memory controller reorders requests subject to DRAM timing constraints, primarily to keep the row buffer open and avoid repeated activate-precharge cycles. First-ready first-come-first-served is the standard baseline policy.
concepts.L2: For a CPU, controller policy is a fairness and throughput battleground because many threads interleave streams that thrash each other's row buffers. For an accelerator the problem largely evaporates, because the access pattern is a small number of long, statically scheduled, sequential DMA transfers.
concepts.L3: Here knowing the workload deletes a hard problem. Mutlu's memory-scheduling work exists because in a shared multicore one thread's streaming pattern can starve another's, so policies such as stall-time fair and parallelism-aware batch scheduling were needed to restore fairness. An accelerator's DMA engine issues long contiguous bursts mapping onto whole rows, so consecutive requests hit the row buffer and the controller can be simple. Attention moves to address mapping: how physical addresses interleave across channels, ranks and banks decides whether a tile's accesses spread for parallelism or collide in one bank. A tiling optimal for reuse can be pathological for interleaving.

L4.prompt_tpl: With a row-buffer hit costing {h} ns and a miss costing {m} ns, compute average latency at {r} percent hit rate, and the hit rate needed to reach {t} ns average. Answer with the average latency in nanoseconds.
L4.explanation: Row-buffer hit rate is the single most important DRAM metric and it is almost entirely determined by access pattern and address mapping, not by the DRAM parts. A sequential stream approaches 100 percent; a random-access pattern approaches the reciprocal of the row size in accesses.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain how a tile shape chosen to maximise on-chip reuse can accidentally reduce DRAM {x}, and what the fix is.
L4.answer: If the tile's stride in physical address space is a multiple of the channel or bank interleaving granularity, all of a tile's accesses land in the same channel or bank, serialising what should have been parallel. The fix is to choose tile dimensions coprime with the interleave stride, or to pad the tensor's leading dimension so successive rows fall in different channels.
L4.explanation: This is the same pathology as cache-set conflicts, one level down, and it produces the same cliff-edge behaviour: a tile one element wider runs several times faster. Padding is the standard remedy and it costs a little capacity to recover a large fraction of the memory system.

prereqs: Row buffer hits and the timing parameters

L0.body:
# A DRAM device is many independent banks. While bank 0 does its
# activate and precharge, banks 1..n-1 can be busy too.
#
#   tRC (activate to activate, SAME bank)  ~ 45 ns
#   burst transfer time on the bus         ~  2 ns
#
#   one bank: 1 access per tRC = 22 M accesses/s
#   to saturate the bus: tRC/burst = 45/2 = 23 banks in flight
#
# So bandwidth is not a property of the bus alone:
#   achievable BW = min(bus BW, banks_in_flight * burst / tRC)
#
# Little's law again: concurrency = rate x latency. A DMA engine must
# issue MANY outstanding requests across MANY banks, or HBM idles.
L0.cloze: Bandwidth requires {{c1::tRC divided by burst time}} banks busy concurrently, about 23 for representative timings. Achievable bandwidth is the minimum of bus bandwidth and {{c2::banks in flight}} times burst over tRC. This is {{c3::Little's law}} again.

concepts.L1: A DRAM device contains many independent banks, each of which can only start a new row access every tRC. Sustained bandwidth therefore requires enough concurrent bank activity to cover that recovery time.
concepts.L2: This is why an accelerator's DMA engine matters as much as the memory it talks to. A DMA that issues one large request at a time, however large, cannot saturate an HBM stack; it must have many independent transfers outstanding across banks, and the address mapping must ensure they land in different banks.
concepts.L3: State it as Little's law. To sustain rate $R$ at per-bank service time $tRC$, the banks concurrently occupied must be at least $R \cdot tRC$ over the bytes delivered per bank access. At a 45 ns row cycle and a 2 ns burst, one bank delivers $1/23$ of bus rate, so about 23 banks must be in flight. HBM helps structurally, not only through width: a stack presents many independent channels, each with its own banks. The design work is on the requester side: enough outstanding request slots, an address map scattering a tile across banks and channels, and a tile shape that does not stride into collisions. Get one wrong and measured bandwidth sits far below spec.

L4.prompt_tpl: With tRC = {trc} ns and a burst occupying the data bus for {tburst} ns, compute the number of banks that must be concurrently active to saturate the bus, and the achieved fraction with only {n} banks in flight. Answer with the number of banks needed to saturate the bus.
L4.answer: Banks needed $= tRC/\mathrm{burst}$; fraction achieved $= \min(1, n \cdot \mathrm{burst}/tRC)$. For $tRC=45$, burst $=2$: 22.5 banks needed; with 8 in flight you get $16/45 = 35.6$ percent of bus bandwidth.
L4.explanation: The result is often startling on first calculation: even a perfectly sequential stream achieves a small fraction of peak if it does not spread across banks. It is the memory-system analogue of memory-level parallelism on a CPU and it is measured the same way, by counting outstanding requests.

L4.prompt_tpl: A DMA engine achieves {p} percent of an HBM stack's rated bandwidth on a purely sequential {s} MB transfer. The compute pipeline is idle. Where do you look first?
L4.answer: At outstanding-request concurrency and address mapping, not at the compute side. Either the engine has too few request slots to keep enough banks busy, or the address interleaving maps the sequential stream onto too few channels or banks. Measure banks in flight and the channel distribution of the address stream.
L4.explanation: Sequential access guarantees row-buffer hits but not bank parallelism, and those are different properties. This is a very common accelerator bring-up finding, and it is diagnosed with performance counters on outstanding requests rather than by inspecting the kernel.

L0.body:
# Move compute to the data.
#
#   conventional : DRAM -> interface -> compute die. Every byte crosses.
#   near-memory  : logic on the HBM BASE DIE or a DIMM buffer chip, so
#                  reductions happen before the interface.
#
# Reducing R bytes to R/k: conventional crosses R, near-memory R/k,
# so interface energy and bandwidth demand fall by k.
#
# Examples (status varies, verify): Samsung HBM-PIM / AxDIMM,
# SK Hynix AiM, UPMEM DPUs on DDR4.
#
# The hard part is not the arithmetic: DRAM processes are optimised
# for capacitors, so logic there is slow and area-hungry.
L0.cloze: Near-memory compute puts logic on the {{c1::base die or buffer chip}} so a reduction from R to R/k bytes cuts interface traffic by {{c2::k}}. The obstacle is that DRAM processes are optimised for {{c3::capacitors}}, making logic there slow and area-expensive.

concepts.L1: Near-memory compute places arithmetic on the memory side of the interface, typically on an HBM base die or a DIMM buffer chip, so that data-reducing operations complete without crossing the expensive link.
concepts.L2: The wins are confined to operations with a high reduction ratio and low arithmetic complexity: embedding gathers, all-reduce, filtering, sums. General matrix multiplication is a poor fit, because it is not data-reducing at the memory boundary and the logic available on a DRAM process is far weaker than on a logic process.
concepts.L3: Understand the process constraint, because it bounds the whole idea. A DRAM process is tuned for high-aspect-ratio capacitors and very low leakage, at the cost of transistor performance and metal layers. Logic there runs at a fraction of the frequency and takes several times the area it would on a logic process, so you cannot relocate a MAC array. What you can place is simple, wide, low-frequency arithmetic exploiting the internal bandwidth already present inside a DRAM device, far higher than what escapes through the pins. That is the real asset: a row buffer is thousands of bits wide, read in full on every activation, most of it discarded. Embedding lookup is the canonical fit.

L4.prompt_tpl: An operation reads {r} MB from memory and produces {o} MB of result. Compare bytes crossing the memory interface with conventional and near-memory execution, and give the reduction factor. Answer with the reduction factor.
L4.answer: Conventional: $r$ MB cross. Near-memory: $o$ MB cross. Reduction $= r/o$. For $r=512$, $o=1$: 512x less interface traffic, which is the case for an embedding gather or a large reduction.
L4.explanation: The reduction ratio is the whole criterion for whether near-memory helps. A matmul has a ratio near 1 at the memory boundary and gains nothing; a reduction, a filter or a gather has a large ratio and gains proportionally. Compute it before considering any hardware.

L4.prompt_tpl: Which of these is the better candidate for near-memory execution: a {a} or a {b}?

b: sparse embedding table gather with reduction

options: The embedding gather: high reduction ratio and simple arithmetic
The matrix multiplication: it has the highest arithmetic intensity
Neither: near-memory compute cannot perform arithmetic, only movement
L4.answer: The embedding gather: it reads a large amount of scattered data and produces a small reduced result, so most of the traffic never needs to cross the interface, and the arithmetic required is simple addition well suited to a DRAM process.
L4.explanation: Dense matmul is compute-intensive and not data-reducing at the memory boundary, so relocating it to slow DRAM-process logic loses on every axis. The gather is the opposite on both counts, which is why commercial near-memory products target recommendation workloads.

concepts.t: In-memory compute and the ADC tax

L0.body:
# Analog in-memory MAC: a crossbar of resistive cells.
#   voltages V_j on columns, conductances G_ij store weights
#   current summed on row i is  I_i = sum_j G_ij * V_j
#   -> Ohm's law multiplies, Kirchhoff's law sums: a whole
#      matrix-vector product in one analog settling time.
#
# The catch, and it is the whole story:
#   the result is a CURRENT. You need an ADC per row.
#   ADC energy grows roughly as 2^b for b bits of resolution
#   ADC area is large next to a memory cell
#   -> ADCs commonly dominate BOTH energy and area
#
# Plus device variability, drift, limited write endurance.
L0.cloze: An analog crossbar does the multiply with {{c1::Ohm's law}} and the sum with {{c2::Kirchhoff's law}}, but the result is a current requiring an {{c3::ADC}} per row, whose energy grows roughly as 2 to the power of the bit resolution.

concepts.L1: In-memory computing performs matrix-vector multiplication inside a memory array, using cell conductance as the weight and analog current summation as the accumulation. The theoretical energy per operation is extremely low.
concepts.L2: The efficiency claims are almost always quoted for the crossbar alone. Once analog-to-digital conversion, digital-to-analog conversion, device variability compensation and periodic reprogramming are counted, the system-level advantage shrinks dramatically and can vanish for anything above very low precision.
concepts.L3: The ADC is the structural problem, not a detail. Converter energy scales roughly exponentially in resolution, so an 8-bit output costs far more than twice a 4-bit one, and you need one per crossbar row, or a shared one with a time-multiplexing penalty. Meanwhile analog precision is limited independently by conductance variation, drift, and read noise, so high resolution is often unachievable regardless of converter quality. So in-memory compute is credible at very low precision and for noise-tolerant workloads, and any published efficiency figure must be checked for whether it is a crossbar or a system figure. That is the standard way an impressive number here excludes the expensive part.

L4.prompt_tpl: A paper reports {t} TOPS per watt for an analog in-memory accelerator. What must you check before believing it applies to a deployed system?
L4.answer: Whether the figure includes the ADCs and DACs, the digital periphery, weight reprogramming and any calibration; what precision it is measured at, since ADC energy scales roughly exponentially with resolution; and whether accuracy on a real network was preserved under device variability and drift.
L4.explanation: Crossbar-only figures are common and are not wrong, merely incomplete: the multiply genuinely is nearly free. The conversion boundary is where the energy reappears, and it is the one term a system-level number must include. Asking which components are inside the measurement boundary is the general skill here.

L4.prompt_tpl: If ADC energy scales as $2^{b}$ for {b}-bit resolution and one converter serves each of {n} crossbar rows, compare total conversion energy at {b} bits against {b2} bits for one matrix-vector product. Answer with the energy ratio per conversion.
L4.answer: Ratio $= 2^{b}/2^{b2}$ per conversion, times $n$ conversions either way. For 8 versus 4 bits: $2^{8}/2^{4} = 16$ times more energy for the same number of conversions.
L4.explanation: The exponential is why in-memory designs cluster at low precision and why they suit workloads that tolerate noise. It also explains the common architectural response of splitting a high-precision operation into several low-precision passes, which trades a much cheaper converter for more passes through the array.

concepts.t: Sizing a memory system for an array

L0.body:
# The whole memory chapter as one budget, NxN int8 array at f Hz.
#
# 1. Array demand from SRAM:
#      N bytes/cycle in, N bytes/cycle out
#      N=256, f=1 GHz -> 256 GB/s each way
#
# 2. SRAM demand from DRAM, set by REUSE (tile size T):
#      bytes_dram_per_mac ~ 1/T for a well-tiled matmul
#      MACs/s = N^2 * f = 6.55e13
#      T=128 -> 5.1e11 B/s = 512 GB/s;  T=512 -> 128 GB/s
#
# 3. So the SRAM capacity that holds a T-tile SETS the DRAM bandwidth
#    you must buy. Doubling the tile halves the HBM bill.
#
# Chain: SRAM area -> tile -> reuse -> DRAM bandwidth -> cost.
L0.cloze: The chain is {{c1::SRAM area}} sets tile size, which sets reuse, which sets {{c2::DRAM bandwidth}}, which sets cost. Doubling the tile dimension {{c3::halves}} the required DRAM bandwidth.

concepts.L1: Memory system sizing is a chain: on-chip SRAM capacity determines the tile that fits, the tile determines reuse, reuse determines DRAM bytes per MAC, and that times the MAC rate is the bandwidth you must buy.
concepts.L2: The direction of causation surprises people. Bandwidth is not a parameter you choose to match a compute target; it is an output of the SRAM budget. Adding SRAM is often cheaper per unit of delivered performance than adding an HBM stack, and the comparison is computable rather than a matter of taste.
concepts.L3: Work the chain concretely. A $256 \times 256$ int8 array at 1 GHz performs $6.55 \times 10^{13}$ MACs per second. For a well-tiled matmul with square tile dimension $T$, DRAM bytes per MAC scale as roughly $1/T$, so $T = 128$ needs about $5.1 \times 10^{11}$ bytes per second, 512 GB/s, and $T = 256$ about 256 GB/s. The SRAM holding that tile, counting two input tiles at one byte and one output tile at four, is $6T^{2}$ bytes, doubled for double buffering: at $T = 256$ that is 786 KB. So roughly 786 KB of extra SRAM removes 256 GB/s of HBM demand. Price both sides at your process and packaging costs and the decision is arithmetic. This is what a performance-modelling role does daily.

L4.prompt_tpl: An {n}x{n} int8 array at {f} GHz is tiled with square tile dimension {t}. Estimate DRAM bandwidth required, and the SRAM needed to double-buffer the tiles with 4-byte accumulators. Answer with the SRAM in bytes.
L4.answer: MACs/s $= n^{2}f$; DRAM bytes/s $\approx n^{2}f/T$; SRAM $= 2(2T^{2} + 4T^{2}) = 12T^{2}$ bytes. For $n=256$, $f=1$, $T=256$: $6.55\times10^{13}$ MACs/s, 256 GB/s, and 786 KB of SRAM.
L4.explanation: Both terms move in opposite directions with $T$, which is what makes it a real optimisation rather than a preference. SRAM grows as $T^{2}$ while bandwidth demand falls as $1/T$, so there is a cost-optimal tile that depends on your relative prices for SRAM area and HBM bandwidth.

L4.prompt_tpl: You can spend a fixed budget on either {s} MB more on-chip SRAM or one more HBM stack. What determines the right answer?
options: Compare the bandwidth demand removed by the larger tile against the bandwidth the stack supplies
Always the HBM stack, since off-chip bandwidth is the binding constraint
Always the SRAM, since on-chip access energy is lower per byte
L4.answer: Compute how much the extra SRAM raises the feasible tile dimension and therefore reduces DRAM bytes per MAC; if the resulting bandwidth reduction exceeds what the extra stack would have supplied, the SRAM wins. It is an arithmetic comparison, not a preference.
L4.explanation: SRAM reduces demand, HBM increases supply, and both are expressible in bytes per second. The comparison also has second-order terms: SRAM adds no packaging risk and no power for a wide interface, while an extra stack adds capacity, which may matter independently for model size.

concepts.t: Die yield and the cost of area

L0.body:
# Poisson yield model (the teaching one):
#     Y = exp(-A * D0)   A in cm^2, D0 = defects per cm^2
# Murphy's model (closer for mature processes):
#     Y = ((1 - exp(-A*D0)) / (A*D0))^2
#
# D0 = 0.1 /cm^2, Poisson:
#     A = 100 mm^2 = 1 cm^2  -> Y = 0.905
#     A = 400 mm^2           -> Y = 0.670
#     A = 800 mm^2           -> Y = 0.449
#
# 300 mm wafer usable area = pi * 150^2 = 70,686 mm^2
#     800 mm^2 die:  88 gross,  40 good -> 31,761 mm^2 good
#     100 mm^2 die: 707 gross, 640 good -> 63,959 mm^2 good
#
# 2.01x more good silicon from the smaller die. That is the
# chiplet argument.
L0.cloze: Poisson yield is {{c1::exp(-A D0)}}. At D0 = 0.1 per square centimetre, an 800 square millimetre die yields {{c2::0.449}} against 0.905 for a 100 square millimetre one, giving about {{c3::2x}} more good silicon per wafer from small dies.

concepts.L1: Yield falls exponentially with die area under a Poisson defect model, so cost per good square millimetre rises steeply with die size. The relationship is the economic foundation of chiplet design.
concepts.L2: The exponential is only half the story; the other half is that a large die also wastes more wafer at the edges and that a single defect kills the whole part. Splitting a design into chiplets converts one exponential penalty into several much smaller ones, and lets a defective chiplet be discarded rather than a whole product.
concepts.L3: Run both numbers. At a defect density of 0.1 per square centimetre an 800 square millimetre die yields 44.9 percent, and a 300 millimetre wafer holds about 88, so 40 good dies and 31,800 square millimetres of usable silicon. The same wafer holds about 707 dies of 100 square millimetres at 90.5 percent yield: 640 good dies, 64,000 square millimetres, twice as much. Two caveats. Defect density is process- and maturity-dependent and vendors do not publish it, so treat any yield figure as illustrative. And chiplets are not free: each adds die-to-die interface area and power, packaging cost rises, and known-good-die testing becomes essential. The break-even is a real calculation.

L4.prompt_tpl: With defect density {d} per cm^2, compute Poisson yield for dies of {a1} and {a2} mm^2, and the ratio of good silicon per 300 mm wafer, ignoring edge loss. Answer with the ratio of the two yields.
L4.answer: $Y = e^{-AD_{0}}$ with $A$ in cm^2. For $D_{0}=0.1$: $Y(100) = 0.905$, $Y(800) = 0.449$. Good silicon per wafer $= 70686 \times Y$ regardless of die size, so the ratio is simply $Y_{1}/Y_{2} = 2.01$.
L4.explanation: Note the elegant simplification: ignoring edge and scribe loss, good silicon per wafer is wafer area times yield, so the ratio of good silicon is exactly the ratio of yields. Edge loss then penalises the large die further, since fewer whole dies fit near the wafer rim.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show why splitting an {a} mm^2 design into {n} equal chiplets improves good silicon per wafer under a Poisson model, and name two costs that offset it.
L4.answer: Yield goes from $e^{-AD_{0}}$ to $e^{-(A/n)D_{0}}$ per chiplet, which is much closer to 1, so the fraction of wafer area that becomes sellable rises. Offsetting costs: each chiplet needs die-to-die interface area and power, and the assembled module now requires known-good-die testing plus advanced packaging, whose yield and cost are non-trivial.
L4.explanation: The exponential means the benefit is largest exactly where it is most needed, at large die sizes. The offsetting costs are why chiplets appeared first in the largest, most expensive products, where the yield saving dominates the packaging premium.

prereqs: Sizing the matmul unit: three independent budgets

L0.body:
# Three reasons to disaggregate:
#
# 1. YIELD. Small dies yield better. Pure economics.
#
# 2. RETICLE LIMIT. Lithography exposes at most ~858 mm^2 per shot
#    (26 x 33 mm). Chiplets are how you exceed it.
#
# 3. PROCESS HETEROGENEITY. SRAM and analog/IO scale poorly on
#    advanced nodes; logic scales well. Logic on N3/N2, cache and
#    IO on a cheaper mature node.
#
# Reference: AMD's CPU + IO die split, MI300, NVIDIA
# Blackwell, Simba (Shao et al., MICRO 2019), TPU v7.
#
# You take on die-to-die PHY area and pJ/bit, packaging yield,
# and a NUMA-like non-uniformity software must see.
L0.cloze: The three reasons to use chiplets are yield, the {{c1::reticle limit}} of about 858 square millimetres, and {{c2::process heterogeneity}}. The cost includes die-to-die PHY area, packaging yield, and a {{c3::non-uniform}} memory topology software must handle.

concepts.L1: Chiplets partition a design across several dies joined in one package. The motivations are yield economics, exceeding the lithographic reticle limit, and placing each function on the process node where it is cheapest.
concepts.L2: The cost that surprises architects is not area or power but non-uniformity. A chiplet boundary is a latency and bandwidth discontinuity, so a multi-chiplet accelerator has a topology that the compiler and the collective library must model, exactly like NUMA on a multi-socket server.
concepts.L3: Take the three separately; they have different consequences. Yield-driven disaggregation replicates identical chiplets, so software sees a symmetric but non-uniform fabric. Reticle-driven disaggregation splits one logical device across two dies and aims to make the seam invisible, needing die-to-die bandwidth close to on-die crossing bandwidth; Google describes TPU v7's die-to-die interface as far faster than its inter-chip links for that reason. Heterogeneity-driven disaggregation puts different functions on different nodes and is the most economically interesting, since SRAM density improved far more slowly than logic. Once a fabric is non-uniform the mapping must be topology-aware.

L4.prompt_tpl: A monolithic design would need {a} mm^2, above the {r} mm^2 reticle limit. Split into {n} chiplets with a die-to-die PHY costing {p} mm^2 per link and {b} pJ per bit. Compute per-chiplet area and the power for {t} TB/s crossing the seams. Answer with the seam power in watts.
L4.answer: Per chiplet $= a/n$ plus PHY area. Seam power $= t \times 10^{12} \times 8 \times b \times 10^{-12}$ watts. For $t = 10$ TB/s at 0.5 pJ/bit: $10^{13} \times 8 \times 0.5 \times 10^{-12} = 40$ W just to move data across the seam.
L4.explanation: That seam power is the number people omit. At tens of terabytes per second, even sub-picojoule-per-bit interfaces cost tens of watts, which is a meaningful slice of a package budget and is why die-to-die energy per bit is the headline metric for these interfaces rather than raw bandwidth.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your accelerator's {s} MB of on-chip SRAM would consume most of a leading-edge die. What does heterogeneous integration suggest and what does it cost?
options: Put the SRAM on a cheaper node as a separate die, accepting interface energy and latency
Keep everything monolithic, since any die-to-die crossing is prohibitively slow
Replace the SRAM with HBM entirely, since off-chip DRAM is always cheaper per bit
L4.answer: Move the SRAM to a separate die on a cheaper mature node and connect it with a high-bandwidth die-to-die or 3D-stacked interface, because SRAM density scales poorly on advanced nodes so the premium buys little. The cost is interface energy, packaging complexity and added access latency.
L4.explanation: This is the clearest instance of process heterogeneity as an argument. Since SRAM barely shrinks on new nodes, paying leading-edge cost per square millimetre for it is poor value, while logic genuinely benefits. The counterweight is that the memory is now further away in both latency and energy per access.

# 2.5D: dies side by side on a fine-pitch carrier.
#
#   silicon interposer (TSMC CoWoS-S): a full silicon die, fine pitch,
#     carries the ~1024-2048 wires an HBM stack needs. Expensive and

#   organic / RDL (CoWoS-R, InFO): cheaper, coarser, less bandwidth.
