#     where fine pitch is needed.
#
# Why it is the bottleneck: an HBM accelerator CANNOT be built
# without one, packaging is a scarcer supply chain than wafers, and
# CoWoS is widely reported as the binding constraint.
L0.cloze: 2.5D places dies {{c1::side by side}} on a carrier. A silicon interposer supports the roughly 1024 to 2048 wires an {{c2::HBM}} stack needs; Intel's {{c3::EMIB}} embeds a small silicon bridge only where fine pitch is required.

concepts.L1: Advanced 2.5D packaging places multiple dies on a shared carrier that provides much finer wiring pitch than a package substrate. A silicon interposer is the highest-bandwidth option and is what makes HBM attachment possible.
concepts.L2: Packaging capacity is a distinct supply chain from wafer capacity, with different vendors, different lead times and different economics. It has been the widely reported binding constraint on accelerator production, which means an architecture that demands more interposer area is expensive in availability, not only in dollars.
concepts.L3: The trade is pitch against cost. A package substrate offers wiring pitch in the tens of micrometres, perhaps a few hundred connections across a die edge. A silicon interposer offers single-digit micrometre pitch and tens of thousands, which is what a 1024-bit HBM interface needs. Since the interposer is a silicon die it costs like one and hits the same reticle limit, so a large accelerator with many stacks may need a stitched interposer. Intel's embedded bridge is the response: fine pitch only under the seams needing it. Interposer area is therefore a budgeted resource like die area, and a design needing more may be unbuildable at volume.

L4.prompt_tpl: An HBM stack needs {w} data wires plus control. At a substrate pitch of {p1} um versus an interposer pitch of {p2} um, estimate the die-edge length required for each and say which is feasible. Answer with the die-edge length in millimetres at the interposer pitch.
L4.answer: Edge length $\approx$ wires $\times$ pitch, assuming a single row. For 1024 wires: at 40 um, 41 mm of edge, which is impossible on a die of a few tens of millimetres per side; at 4 um, 4.1 mm, which is entirely feasible. Multiple rows relax both but the ratio stands.
L4.explanation: This calculation is why HBM requires an interposer rather than merely benefiting from one: the wire count simply does not fit at substrate pitch. It also shows why die-to-die interfaces are specified in bandwidth per millimetre of shoreline, since edge length is the scarce dimension.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why packaging capacity rather than wafer capacity has been reported as the constraint on accelerator supply, and what an architect can do about it.
L4.answer: Because every HBM-equipped accelerator requires advanced 2.5D assembly, which is a separate and smaller supply chain with long lead times and few qualified providers, while leading-edge wafer capacity is comparatively broader. An architect can reduce interposer area demand: fewer, denser stacks, more on-chip SRAM to lower bandwidth needs, or bridge-based packaging instead of a full interposer.
L4.explanation: This is one of the clearest places where a supply-chain fact becomes an architectural constraint. A design that trades interposer area for SRAM area may be strictly better in delivered volume even if slightly worse on paper, which is not a consideration that appears in any performance model.

L0.body:
# 3D: dies stacked VERTICALLY, face-to-face or through TSVs.
#
#   microbump      pitch ~ 30-40 um -> ~10^3 connections per mm^2
#   hybrid bonding pitch ~ 1-10 um  -> ~10^4-10^6 per mm^2
#     (direct copper-to-copper, no solder)
#
# Why it matters: connection density rises by orders of magnitude and
# energy per bit falls with the shorter path. A vertical link becomes
# cheaper than a long on-die wire.
#
# Reference: AMD 3D V-Cache, Intel Foveros, HBM's own stack.
#
# The hard constraint is THERMAL: heat from the bottom die must cross
# the top die, a resistor in series with the spreader.
L0.cloze: Hybrid bonding replaces solder microbumps with {{c1::direct copper-to-copper}} contacts, raising connection density from about 10^3 to as much as 10^6 per square millimetre. The binding constraint on 3D stacking is {{c2::thermal}}: the top die is a thermal resistor in series with the heat spreader.

concepts.L1: 3D integration stacks dies vertically with through-silicon vias or direct bonding. Hybrid bonding eliminates solder entirely, giving connection densities orders of magnitude above microbumps and much lower energy per bit.
concepts.L2: The reason 3D has not simply replaced everything is heat, not manufacturing. Power removed from a stack must travel through the dies above it, so the achievable power density falls as you stack, and the hottest die must be closest to the cooler. That is why stacked cache shipped before stacked logic.
concepts.L3: Consider the thermal path. A processor die conducts heat upward into a lid and then a heatsink. Bond a second die on top and you insert roughly a hundred micrometres of silicon plus a bonding interface into that path, raising thermal resistance and junction temperature at the same power. Since leakage rises with temperature and generates heat, the feedback can run away if margin is thin. The resolutions: stack low-power dies on high-power ones, as stacked SRAM does; thin dies; lower the bottom die's power density, which is why some stacked-cache parts clock lower. The appeal is large: a memory die bonded above the array turns a long horizontal SRAM access into a short vertical one.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare connection density for microbumps at {p1} um pitch against hybrid bonding at {p2} um pitch, per square millimetre, and state the factor. Answer with the hybrid-bonding density per square millimetre.
L4.answer: Density $= (1000/p)^{2}$ per mm^2. At 40 um: 625. At 9 um: 12346, a factor of 20. At 1 um: 1000000, a factor of 1600.
L4.explanation: The quadratic in pitch is what makes hybrid bonding transformative rather than incremental: a nine-fold pitch improvement gives an eighty-fold density improvement. That density is what allows a vertical link to carry more bandwidth than a die edge, changing which partitions are architecturally sensible.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why stacking a low-power SRAM die on a {p}-watt logic die is far easier than stacking two logic dies, in thermal terms.
L4.answer: Heat must exit through the topmost die to the heat spreader, so the top die adds thermal resistance in series. A low-power SRAM die generates little additional heat and merely adds resistance, which can be budgeted; two high-power logic dies both generate heat and the lower one must push its heat through the upper one's own thermal load, raising junction temperature enough to trigger leakage feedback.
L4.explanation: The asymmetry explains the order in which products appeared: stacked cache first, stacked logic much later and at reduced power density. It also explains why some stacked products clock lower than their unstacked equivalents, which is a thermal concession, not a manufacturing one.

L0.body:
# UCIe (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express), an open die-to-die
# standard: a physical layer, an adapter, and a protocol layer
# carrying PCIe, CXL, or raw streaming.
#   UCIe 3.0 is current (uciexpress.org, 3 Sept 2026).
#
# Metrics that matter, in order:
#   1. energy per bit (pJ/bit) -- is the seam affordable
#   2. bandwidth per mm of edge -- shoreline is scarce
#   3. latency (ns) -- is the seam visible to software
#   4. raw bandwidth -- most quoted, least useful
#
# STANDARD package (organic, longer reach, lower density) versus
# ADVANCED (interposer, short reach, lower pJ/bit).
L0.cloze: UCIe defines a physical layer, a {{c1::die-to-die adapter}} and a protocol layer carrying PCIe, CXL or raw streaming. The metrics that matter, in order, are {{c2::energy per bit}}, bandwidth per millimetre of shoreline, latency, and only then raw bandwidth.

concepts.L1: UCIe is an open standard for connecting chiplets within a package, defining electrical, link and protocol layers so dies from different vendors can interoperate. It specifies both organic-substrate and advanced-package variants.
concepts.L2: Raw bandwidth is the least informative number for a die-to-die link. Shoreline bandwidth density decides whether the interface physically fits along the die edge, and energy per bit decides whether the seam is affordable at all; at multi-terabyte rates, a tenth of a picojoule per bit is watts.
concepts.L3: The standard solves a market problem more than a technical one. Proprietary die-to-die links already worked; what did not exist was the ability to buy a chiplet from one vendor and integrate it with another's, which turns chiplets from an internal cost optimisation into an industry structure. The technical content follows: an adapter layer for link management and retry, and mappings onto PCIe and CXL so existing stacks work unchanged across the seam. Demand three numbers from any proposal: energy per bit, bandwidth per millimetre of shoreline, added latency. If latency is small against on-die crossing, the partition is invisible to software.

L4.prompt_tpl: A die-to-die link carries {t} TB/s at {e} pJ per bit across {s} mm of shoreline. Compute the interface power and the required bandwidth density in GB/s per mm. Answer with the interface power in watts.
L4.answer: Power $= t \times 10^{12} \times 8 \times e \times 10^{-12}$ W. Density $= t \times 1000/s$ GB/s per mm. For $t=5$, $e=0.5$, $s=20$: 20 W and 250 GB/s per mm.
L4.explanation: Both numbers are constraints rather than goals. The power lands in the same package budget as the compute, and the density must be achievable by the chosen package class, since organic substrates cannot reach the densities an interposer or bridge can.

L4.prompt_tpl: A vendor advertises a die-to-die interface at {t} TB/s. Which additional figure would you ask for first?
options: Energy per bit, since interface power becomes a large share of the package budget
Maximum reach in millimetres, since longer links allow more flexible floorplans
Protocol support, since bandwidth is meaningless without CXL compatibility
L4.answer: Energy per bit, because at these rates the interface power is a significant share of the package budget and a link that is fast but inefficient may be unaffordable regardless of its bandwidth.
L4.explanation: Bandwidth alone can always be bought with more wires if shoreline and package class allow. What cannot be bought back is the power, and at multi-terabyte rates a difference between 0.25 and 1 pJ per bit is tens of watts, which is compute you no longer get to run.

L0.body:
# NVIDIA's NVLink page, checked 3 September 2026:
#   generation        6th
#   per-GPU bandwidth 3,600 GB/s bidirectional
#   links per GPU     36  -> 100 GB/s per link, 50 each direction
#   NVLink Switch     260 TB/s aggregate for NVL72
#   domain sizes      8 or 72 GPUs
#
# Cross-check: 72 * 3600 GB/s = 259.2 TB/s, i.e. the published
# 260 TB/s rounded. Do this before quoting any of them.
#
#   SCALE-UP  : one high-bandwidth domain (NVLink, TPU ICI)
#   SCALE-OUT : many domains over a commodity network
# Domain size sets the largest tensor-parallel group you can run.
L0.cloze: NVLink's sixth generation is documented at {{c1::3600}} GB/s bidirectional per GPU over 36 links, so each link carries {{c2::100}} GB/s bidirectional. For 72 GPUs that gives {{c3::259.2}} TB/s aggregate, matching the published 260 TB/s.

concepts.L1: A scale-up fabric connects a modest number of accelerators at very high bandwidth into one tightly coupled domain. Scale-out uses commodity networking between domains. The domain size is an architectural parameter with direct consequences for model parallelism.
concepts.L2: The domain boundary is what actually shapes distributed training code. Tensor parallelism demands enormous bandwidth per step and must stay inside the scale-up domain; pipeline and data parallelism tolerate less and can cross it. So the fabric's domain size determines the largest tensor-parallel degree that is practical.
concepts.L3: Check published numbers against each other; self-consistency is the cheapest verification available. Per-GPU bidirectional bandwidth of 3600 GB/s over 36 links is exactly 100 GB/s per link bidirectional, 50 each way. Multiplying 3600 GB/s by 72 GPUs gives 259.2 TB/s, the quoted 260 TB/s rounded. When vendor figures fail this check, one of them measures something else, usually unidirectional versus bidirectional. On architecture: a switched fabric gives uniform bandwidth between any pair in the domain, making arbitrary tensor-parallel layouts viable, whereas a torus gives high neighbour bandwidth and lower bisection, suiting collectives that match it. Neither is better.

L4.prompt_tpl: A fabric gives {b} GB/s bidirectional per accelerator over {l} links, in domains of {n}. Compute per-link bandwidth each direction and the aggregate domain bandwidth, then check it against a published aggregate. Answer with the aggregate domain bandwidth in GB/s.
L4.answer: Per link bidirectional $= b/l$; each direction $= b/(2l)$. Aggregate $= nb$. For $b=3600$, $l=36$, $n=72$: 100 GB/s per link bidirectional, 50 each way, and $259200$ GB/s $= 259.2$ TB/s aggregate.
L4.explanation: Doing this arithmetic is the habit to build: vendor figures mix unidirectional and bidirectional freely, and the only defence is checking whether the numbers multiply out. A mismatch by exactly two is almost always a direction convention.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must run a model with tensor-parallel degree {tp} on a fabric whose scale-up domain holds {n} accelerators. What happens and what do you change?
options: Keep tensor parallelism within the domain and use pipeline or data parallelism across domains
Increase tensor parallelism further, since more parallelism always reduces step time
Nothing changes: the fabric transparently extends the domain across the network
L4.answer: If the tensor-parallel degree exceeds the domain size, every layer's all-reduce crosses the slow scale-out network and step time collapses. Reduce tensor parallelism to fit the domain and take the remaining parallelism as pipeline or data parallelism, which tolerate lower bandwidth.
L4.explanation: Tensor parallelism communicates activations every layer, so it is the most bandwidth-hungry form and must stay inside the high-bandwidth domain. Pipeline parallelism communicates only at stage boundaries and data parallelism only at step boundaries, so both survive the cheaper network. The domain size is therefore a hard architectural parameter for the training plan.

concepts.t: Collective bandwidth as the real cluster metric

L0.body:
# Ring all-reduce, N nodes, D bytes of gradient per node:
#   bytes sent per node = 2D(N-1)/N  -> approaches 2D, independent of N
#   steps               = 2(N-1)      -> latency grows linearly in N
#
#   time = 2D(N-1)/(N * B_link) + 2(N-1) * latency
#
# D = 1 GB, N = 64, B_link = 50 GB/s, lat = 2 us
#   bandwidth term = 2 * 1e9 * 63/64 / 50e9 = 39.4 ms
#   latency term   = 126 * 2e-6             =  0.25 ms
#   -> bandwidth bound, as expected.
#
# Compare against the model's compute time per step. If all-reduce is a
# large fraction of it, you are building a network, not a chip.
L0.cloze: Ring all-reduce sends {{c1::2D(N-1)/N}} bytes per node, which approaches 2D {{c2::independent of N}}, in 2(N-1) steps so latency grows {{c3::linearly}} in N.

concepts.L1: At cluster scale, training throughput is set by how fast collective operations complete, not by per-chip peak compute. Ring all-reduce moves a fixed number of bytes per node regardless of cluster size but takes a number of steps linear in it.
concepts.L2: The bytes-per-node independence from $N$ is the property that makes large-scale data-parallel training possible at all, and it is why ring all-reduce displaced tree reductions. The linear step count is its weakness, which is why hierarchical and tree-based hybrids reappear for small messages.
concepts.L3: Do the comparison that decides a cluster design. With one gigabyte of gradients, 64 nodes and 50 GB/s per link, the bandwidth term of a ring all-reduce is about 39 ms, while the latency term at two microseconds per step is 0.25 ms. So it is bandwidth bound, and the fix is more link bandwidth or gradient compression, not lower latency. Now compare 39 milliseconds against the compute time of one training step. At 200 ms per step, communication is 20 percent overhead and overlapping it with backward-pass compute mostly hides it; at 50 ms the network dominates and adding accelerators makes throughput worse. This calculation, not the chip's TOPS, decides whether a cluster scales.

L4.prompt_tpl: A ring all-reduce over {n} nodes moves {d} GB of gradients per node on {b} GB/s links with {l} microseconds per step. Compute the bandwidth and latency terms and say which dominates. Answer with the bandwidth term in seconds.
L4.answer: Bandwidth term $= 2D(N-1)/(NB)$; latency term $= 2(N-1)l$. For $N=64$, $D=1$ GB, $B=50$ GB/s, $l=2$ us: 39.4 ms versus 0.25 ms, so bandwidth dominates by more than 150 times.
L4.explanation: Large models are always bandwidth bound in all-reduce, which is why gradient compression, bf16 or fp8 gradients, and overlapping communication with backward-pass compute are the standard remedies. Latency only matters for small messages, where tree algorithms beat rings.

L4.prompt_tpl: Show why ring all-reduce's bytes per node is independent of node count, and derive the point at which it stops being bandwidth bound for a message of {d} MB.
L4.answer: Each node sends $D/N$ bytes in each of $2(N-1)$ steps, giving $2D(N-1)/N$ bytes, which tends to $2D$ as $N$ grows. It stops being bandwidth bound when $2D(N-1)/(NB) < 2(N-1)l$, i.e. when $D/N < Bl$: for $B=50$ GB/s and $l=2$ us, when the per-step chunk falls below 100 KB.
L4.explanation: The crossover condition is a clean statement of when to switch algorithms: once each step's chunk is smaller than the bandwidth-delay product of a single hop, the ring's step count dominates and a logarithmic-depth algorithm wins. This is why collective libraries select algorithms by message size.

sections.note: One equation and its consequences: everything else in this section is downstream of alpha C V squared f.

L0.body:
# Charge a capacitance C from 0 to V through a pull-up:
#   supply delivers      = C*V^2
#   stored on the cap    = 0.5*C*V^2
#   dissipated in PMOS   = 0.5*C*V^2
# Discharge through the NMOS: the stored half is dissipated too.
#
#   -> one full 0->1->0 cycle dissipates exactly C*V^2, ALL heat.
#
# For alpha transitions per clock at frequency f:
#   P_dyn = alpha * C * V^2 * f
#
# alpha is the ACTIVITY FACTOR: 1.0 for a clock pin, ~0.1-0.2 for data.
# C*V^2 is per full cycle and alpha counts cycles, so there is no
# stray factor of 1/2 to argue about.
L0.cloze: One full charge-discharge cycle dissipates {{c1::C V squared}}, half in the pull-up and half in the pull-down. With activity factor {{c2::alpha}} at frequency f, dynamic power is {{c3::alpha C V^2 f}}. A clock pin has alpha = 1.

concepts.L1: Dynamic power is the energy dissipated charging and discharging node capacitances. A full transition cycle costs $CV^{2}$ regardless of transistor sizing, so power is $P = \alpha C V^{2} f$ with $\alpha$ the transitions per clock.
concepts.L2: The dissipation is independent of the resistance through which the capacitor charges. Making transistors stronger changes how fast the transition happens, not how much energy it costs, which is why you cannot reduce switching energy by improving drive strength, only by reducing $C$, $V$ or $\alpha$.
concepts.L3: Do the derivation once, because it explains why the equation has no adjustable constant. Charging $C$ to $V$ draws charge $Q = CV$ from a supply held at $V$, so the supply delivers $CV^{2}$. Only $\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$ is stored; the other half is dissipated in the charging path, and integrating $i^{2}R$ over the transient confirms this independently of $R$. On discharge the stored half goes into the pull-down, so a cycle costs $CV^{2}$. Multiply by $\alpha f$. Three levers follow, and they are the only ones: cut $C$ with shorter wires and smaller devices, cut $V$ (quadratic), cut $\alpha$ by clock gating and by not computing what you discard.

L4.prompt_tpl: Derive $P = \alpha C V^{{2}} f$ from charging a capacitance {c} through a resistance, showing why the dissipated energy does not depend on the resistance.
L4.answer: Charging draws $Q = CV$ from a supply at $V$, delivering $CV^{2}$; $\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$ is stored and $\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$ dissipated, since $\int i^{2}R\,dt$ evaluates to $\frac{1}{2}CV^{2}$ for any $R$. Discharging dissipates the stored half. A full cycle costs $CV^{2}$; multiplying by $\alpha f$ transitions per second gives the result.
L4.explanation: The resistance independence is the surprising and important part: a stronger driver switches faster but dissipates the same energy per transition. That is why the design levers are capacitance, voltage and activity, and why sizing transistors up buys speed at the cost of more capacitance, not less energy per switch.

L4.prompt_tpl: A block has {n} million switching nodes of {c} fF each, activity factor {a}, at {v} V and {f} GHz. Compute dynamic power, and the power if voltage drops to {v2} V. Answer with the dynamic power in watts at v.
L4.explanation: The quadratic in voltage is why voltage is the first lever anyone reaches for and why every low-power technique that can be expressed as a voltage reduction is preferred. Note that lowering voltage also lowers the maximum frequency, so the comparison is only fair at matched throughput.

concepts.t: Leakage and the end of Dennard scaling

L0.body:
# Static power flows when nothing switches. Components:
#   subthreshold: I_sub ~ exp((V_gs - V_th) / (n * kT/q))
#   gate leakage (oxide tunnelling), junction leakage
#
# The subthreshold exponential is the whole problem:
#   drop V_th to keep speed at lower V_dd -> leakage rises EXPONENTIALLY
#   raise temperature -> leakage rises -> more heat -> RUNAWAY
#
# Dennard scaling (1974): shrink dimensions by k and V by k, power
# density stays CONSTANT. Held to ~2005. This is why multicore.
L0.cloze: Subthreshold leakage grows {{c1::exponentially}} as threshold voltage falls, which is why supply voltage stopped scaling around {{c2::2005}} and Dennard scaling ended. Leakage also rises with temperature, giving a {{c3::thermal runaway}} feedback path.

concepts.L1: Static power is current that flows without any switching, dominated by subthreshold conduction which depends exponentially on the gap between supply and threshold voltage. It is why supply voltage stopped scaling and therefore why frequency stopped scaling.
concepts.L2: The temperature coupling is what makes leakage qualitatively different from dynamic power. Leakage generates heat, heat raises leakage, and the loop has positive gain, so a design with inadequate thermal margin can fail catastrophically rather than merely running slowly.
concepts.L3: State Dennard's argument to see what broke. Shrink all dimensions and the supply voltage by a factor $k$: capacitance falls by $k$, voltage squared by $k^{2}$, frequency rises by $k$, so power per device falls by $k^{2}$ while density rises by $k^{2}$, leaving power density constant. Every term held except one. Reducing supply voltage requires reducing threshold voltage to preserve drive current, and subthreshold leakage depends exponentially on that threshold. By the mid 2000s leakage was a large fraction of total power, threshold voltage could fall no further, supply voltage stopped falling, and power density began rising each generation. Frequency scaling stopped with it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain precisely which term of Dennard's scaling argument failed and why that specific failure produced {c} rather than continued frequency scaling.
L4.answer: Supply voltage stopped scaling, because reducing it requires reducing threshold voltage and subthreshold leakage depends exponentially on that. With voltage fixed, power per device stopped falling while density kept rising, so power density rose. Frequency could no longer be increased within a fixed thermal budget, so the extra transistors were spent on parallelism instead of speed.
L4.explanation: The chain from one exponential to the entire structure of modern computing is worth being able to state from memory. It also frames why specialisation followed multicore: once parallelism alone stopped paying, the remaining lever was doing less work per useful result, which is what a domain-specific datapath does.

L4.prompt_tpl: Subthreshold current varies roughly as $10^{{\Delta V/S}}$, where $\Delta V$ is the gate overdrive and $S = {s}$ mV per decade is the subthreshold swing. Compute the leakage change from lowering the threshold voltage by {dv} mV, and from a temperature rise that raises $S$ to {s2} mV per decade. Answer with the leakage multiplier from lowering the threshold.
L4.answer: Leakage multiplies by $10^{\Delta V/S}$. For $\Delta V = 100$ mV at $S = 80$: $10^{1.25} = 17.8$ times. A rise in $S$ from 80 to 100 mV per decade flattens the turn-off, raising off-state current for the same $V_{th}$ by a further $10^{V_{th}(1/80 - 1/100)}$, which for $V_{th} = 400$ mV is $10^{1.0} = 10$ times.
L4.explanation: Subthreshold swing has a physical floor near 60 mV per decade at room temperature for a conventional MOSFET, and it worsens with temperature. Those two facts together are why the leakage problem is not an engineering oversight but a device-physics limit, and why FinFET and gate-all-around structures exist.

L0.body:
# Above threshold, max frequency scales roughly linearly with V.
#
#   P = alpha*C*V^2*f,  and f ~ V   ->   P ~ V^3 ~ f^3
#
# Halve both voltage and frequency:
#   power                 = 0.5 * 0.5^2 = 0.125  (1/8)
#   time for fixed work   = 2x
#   ENERGY for fixed work = 0.125 * 2   = 0.25   (1/4)
#
# SLOWER AND WIDER at lower voltage is a 4x energy win at the same
# throughput. This is why accelerators are wide and slow, and why
# race-to-idle is often wrong for throughput work.
#
# The floor: not below threshold plus margin, and leakage x time
# starts to dominate as you slow down.
L0.cloze: With frequency roughly proportional to voltage, power scales as {{c1::V cubed}}. Halving both gives {{c2::1/8}} the power and, for fixed work, {{c3::1/4}} the energy. The floor is set by threshold voltage and by leakage times elapsed time.

concepts.L1: Because maximum frequency scales roughly with supply voltage, dynamic power scales with roughly the cube of frequency. Reducing both voltage and frequency while widening the datapath to preserve throughput is therefore a large energy win.
concepts.L2: Race-to-idle is the right strategy only when the idle state is genuinely cheap and the work is bursty. For a sustained throughput workload the opposite holds: running wide and slow at low voltage beats running narrow and fast, by a factor close to the square of the frequency reduction.
concepts.L3: Work it exactly. Take a design at $V$ and $f$ doing work $W$ in time $T$. Halve both: power becomes $\alpha C (V/2)^{2}(f/2) = P/8$, the work takes $2T$, so energy is $PT/4$. To keep throughput, double the width: $C$ doubles, power returns to $P/4$ at the original throughput, energy still $PT/4$. So a design twice as wide at half the frequency gives the same performance for a quarter of the energy, before leakage. That is the whole argument for wide, slow accelerator datapaths, and why a TPU-class array clocks below a gigahertz while a CPU clocks above four. The limit: voltage cannot fall below threshold plus noise margin, and leakage over a longer runtime eventually dominates.

L4.prompt_tpl: A block runs at {v} V and {f} GHz. Scale to {v2} V and {f2} GHz and compute the power ratio, the time ratio for fixed work, and the energy ratio. Then give the width multiplier needed to restore throughput and the resulting energy. Answer with the power ratio.
L4.answer: Power ratio $= (V_{2}/V_{1})^{2}(f_{2}/f_{1})$; time ratio $= f_{1}/f_{2}$; energy ratio is their product. For 1.0 V, 2 GHz to 0.5 V, 1 GHz: power $0.25 \times 0.5 = 0.125$, time $2$, energy $0.25$. Doubling width restores throughput at power $0.25$ and energy $0.25$.
L4.explanation: The energy ratio equals the voltage ratio squared, which is the clean way to remember it: energy per operation depends only on voltage, and frequency only sets how fast you spend it. Widening then converts the time penalty back into throughput at no energy cost.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a sustained inference serving workload at {u} percent utilisation, is race-to-idle or run-slow-and-wide the better strategy?
options: Run slow and wide, since energy per operation falls with voltage squared and there is little idle time
Race to idle, since finishing sooner always saves energy
Neither matters: at high utilisation power is dominated by leakage
L4.answer: Run slow and wide: at high sustained utilisation there is little idle time to race into, and energy per operation falls with the square of voltage, so lowering voltage and widening the datapath is a large win.
L4.explanation: Race-to-idle wins only when the idle state is much cheaper than the active state and the duty cycle is low, which describes a phone, not a serving fleet. At high utilisation the machine is essentially always active, so the metric is energy per operation, which is minimised at low voltage.

L0.body:
# CLOCK GATING: stop the clock to idle logic. Attacks alpha and f.
#   ICG cell: enable latched on the opposite clock phase, then ANDed
#   with the clock, so the gated clock can never glitch.
#
#     always_ff @(posedge clk) if (en) q <= d;   // infers an ICG
#
#   Wake-up 1 cycle. Leakage untouched. Essentially free.
#
# POWER GATING: cut the supply with a header/footer switch. Kills
#   leakage AND dynamic power, but:
#     - state is LOST unless retention flops are used (area)
#     - wake-up costs 10s-1000s of cycles and a current surge
#
# Clock gate everything; power gate deliberately.
L0.cloze: Clock gating removes {{c1::dynamic}} power including the clock tree share, wakes in one cycle and leaves leakage untouched. Power gating removes {{c2::leakage}} too but loses state, costs tens to thousands of cycles to wake, and adds {{c3::series resistance}} in the active path.

concepts.L1: Clock gating suppresses the clock to idle logic, eliminating its dynamic power at negligible cost. Power gating disconnects the supply, eliminating leakage as well, at the cost of state loss and a long wake-up.
concepts.L2: Clock gating is the highest-leverage single technique in digital design because it attacks the clock tree, whose activity factor is 1 by construction and which is a large share of core dynamic power. Synthesis infers it from a guarded register assignment, so your RTL style decides how much of it you get.
concepts.L3: The distinction that matters in practice is break-even time. Clock gating has essentially no overhead: the ICG cell adds one latch and one gate, wake-up is a single cycle, and the tool inserts it wherever a register has an enable. So gate everything, by writing enables explicitly rather than feeding registers a multiplexer that recirculates the old value, which looks like unconditional writing to the tool. Power gating has a real break-even: the sleep transistor must be large enough not to limit active current, costing area and voltage drop. It pays only for regions idle far longer than the wake-up cost: an unused precision path, not a MAC array under load.

L4.prompt_tpl: An RTL author writes a register as `q <= en ? d : q;` instead of `if (en) q <= d;` and finds the design misses its power target by {p} percent. Explain.
L4.answer: The recirculating multiplexer form writes the register every cycle, so synthesis sees no enable condition and infers no clock gate. The clock reaches every flop unconditionally, so the clock tree and flop internal power are spent whether or not the data changes. The guarded form lets the tool insert an integrated clock gating cell.
L4.explanation: The two forms are logically identical and physically very different, which makes this a favourite interview question and a real source of missed power targets. Lint rules and power-aware synthesis reports exist to catch it; the habit is to write enables as conditions, never as recirculation.

L4.prompt_tpl: A region draws {d} W dynamic and {s} W leakage and is idle {i} percent of the time. Compute the saving from clock gating alone and from power gating, ignoring wake-up cost, then state when power gating is not worth it. Answer with the power-gating saving in watts.
L4.answer: Clock gating saves $i \times d$; power gating saves $i \times (d+s)$. For $d=12$, $s=2$, $i=0.9$: 10.8 W versus 12.6 W. Power gating adds only $i \times s = 1.8$ W of saving, so it is not worth it unless idle periods are long compared to the wake-up cost and leakage is a large share.
L4.explanation: The marginal benefit of power gating over clock gating is exactly the leakage term, which is often small on a mature node and large on an advanced one. That is why power gating became standard as leakage grew, and why the decision is node-dependent rather than universal.

concepts.t: Thermal design, TDP and dark silicon

L0.body:
# TDP is a COOLING SPECIFICATION, not a power measurement: the
# sustained heat the cooler must remove. Peak power exceeds it; the
# chip throttles to hold the average.
#
# The thermal chain as a resistor network:
#   T_junction = T_ambient + P * (R_jc + R_cs + R_sa)
#
#   P = 300 W, R_th = 0.15 C/W, T_amb = 35 C -> T_j = 80 C.  Fine.
#   Same cooler at 700 W                     -> T_j = 140 C. Not fine.
#
# DARK SILICON: the die fraction that can switch at full frequency
# FALLS each node. Specialisation is nearly free in area.
L0.cloze: TDP is a {{c1::cooling specification}}, not a power measurement. Junction temperature is ambient plus power times total {{c2::thermal resistance}}. Dark silicon means the fraction of the die that can switch at once {{c3::falls}} each node, which makes specialised blocks nearly free in area.

concepts.L1: Thermal design power specifies the sustained heat a cooling solution must remove; junction temperature follows from power times the thermal resistance of the path to ambient. Dark silicon is the consequence of power density rising while area kept growing.
concepts.L2: Dark silicon inverts the usual area intuition. If you cannot power all your transistors simultaneously anyway, adding a fixed-function block that is idle most of the time costs almost nothing in the currency that binds, and it may replace a general-purpose computation that would have cost far more energy.
concepts.L3: Model the thermal path as resistances in series: junction to case, case to heatsink, heatsink to ambient, giving $T_{a} + P \sum R$. At 300 watts through 0.15 degrees per watt from a 35 degree ambient the junction sits at 80 degrees; at 700 watts the same cooler gives 140, which is not viable. Hence liquid cooling: the only way to cut the resistance term enough. Dark silicon follows from the power side. Density kept rising after voltage scaling stopped, so the power to switch everything at full frequency grew faster than the coolable budget. The consequence: area is no longer binding, energy is, so the answer is many specialised blocks each used occasionally.

L4.prompt_tpl: A package dissipates {p} W with junction-to-case {rjc}, case-to-sink {rcs} and sink-to-ambient {rsa} degrees per watt, at {ta} C ambient. Compute junction temperature and the maximum power for a {tmax} C limit. Answer with the junction temperature in degrees C.
L4.explanation: The linear model is crude but it is the right first calculation and it makes the leverage obvious: halving thermal resistance doubles the power budget at the same junction temperature, which is why cooling technology, not silicon, often sets the achievable design point.

L4.prompt_tpl: Dark silicon means you cannot power all transistors at once. A team proposes adding {n} specialised fixed-function blocks each used in under {u} percent of workloads. Assess.
options: Reasonable: area is in surplus under dark silicon, and specialised blocks win on energy per task
Unreasonable: die area is always the scarcest resource and idle blocks waste it
Unreasonable: fixed-function blocks increase leakage proportionally to their area regardless of use
L4.answer: Reasonable: area is not the binding constraint when much of the die cannot be powered simultaneously anyway, and a specialised block performing its task at a fraction of the energy of a general-purpose implementation is a good trade against a resource you already have in surplus.
L4.explanation: This is the standard justification for heterogeneous SoCs, and it is a genuine consequence of dark silicon rather than a rationalisation. The real costs are verification effort, software support and the risk that the block goes unused, which are engineering and product costs rather than silicon ones.

concepts.t: PPA as one space, and performance per watt as the currency

L0.body:
# PPA = Power, Performance, Area. No design is 'better'; it is a POINT.
#
# Normalised metrics that make comparison possible:
#   TOPS        peak throughput, says almost nothing alone
#   TOPS/W      energy efficiency  <- the deployment constraint
#   TOPS/mm^2   area efficiency    <- manufacturing cost proxy
#   TOPS/W/mm^2 rarely useful; usually cherry-picking
#
# A datacentre is provisioned in megawatts, not square millimetres.
#
# Report EFFECTIVE TOPS/W on a real workload at a stated batch size
# and precision, not peak. The gap is where every claim lives.
L0.cloze: PPA has no single winner, only {{c1::points}} in a space. The metric that binds for ML deployment is {{c2::TOPS per watt}}, because datacentres are provisioned in megawatts. The honest form quotes {{c3::effective}} rather than peak, at a stated workload, batch size and precision.

concepts.L1: Power, performance and area form a single tradeoff space in which every design is a point and no design dominates. Normalised metrics such as throughput per watt and throughput per square millimetre are what make two points comparable at all.
concepts.L2: Performance per watt is the binding metric because the constraint at deployment is a facility's power and cooling, not its floor space. Once a rack is power-limited, doubling a chip's throughput at double the power buys nothing, which is why efficiency claims and not peak claims decide purchasing.
concepts.L3: Insist on the qualifiers, because they are where the number is made. Peak throughput per watt is computed from a MAC count, a clock and a power specification, and no real workload achieves it. Effective throughput per watt requires stating the network, the batch size, the precision, whether sparsity was used, and whether power is measured at the chip, the board or the wall. Two chips quoted at the same peak can differ by an order of magnitude on a real workload, through utilisation and memory traffic, both mapping properties. Convert every claim into a question: at what batch size, what precision, measured where, at what fraction of peak.

L4.prompt_tpl: Chip A delivers {a} TOPS at {pa} W; chip B delivers {b} TOPS at {pb} W. Compute TOPS per watt for each, then recompute if A achieves {ua} percent utilisation and B achieves {ub} percent on your workload. Answer with chip A's effective TOPS per watt.
L4.answer: Peak efficiency $= \mathrm{TOPS}/W$; effective $= \mathrm{TOPS} \times u / W$. For A at 800 TOPS, 400 W, 25 percent: peak 2.0, effective 0.5. For B at 200 TOPS, 150 W, 80 percent: peak 1.33, effective 1.07. B wins on the real workload despite losing on both peak numbers.
L4.explanation: This reversal is the entire reason to insist on effective figures. Utilisation is a property of the mapping and the memory system, and it varies more between designs than peak does, so peak rankings routinely invert once real workloads are run.

L4.prompt_tpl: A vendor claims {t} TOPS per watt. List the questions you must ask before the number means anything.
L4.answer: At what precision; peak or effective; on which network and at what batch size; with or without structured sparsity counted; whether the throughput counts a multiply-accumulate as one operation or two; and where power was measured, at the die, the module or the wall, and whether memory power is included.
L4.explanation: Each question can move the number by a factor of two or more, and several apply at once, so the compound uncertainty is easily an order of magnitude. Being able to ask this list quickly is one of the most transferable skills in architecture analysis, and it applies to your own numbers as much as anyone else's.

concepts.t: Synthesis: RTL to a gate netlist

L0.body:
# Synthesis maps RTL onto a standard cell library under a timing
# constraint YOU supply. It optimises for that and nothing else.
#
#   yosys -p 'read_verilog top.v; synth -top top; \
#             dfflibmap -liberty sky130.lib; \
#             abc -liberty sky130.lib; \
#             stat; write_verilog out.v'
#
# A .lib gives per cell: area, input capacitance, and a delay TABLE
# indexed by (input transition, output load).
#
#   1. 'it synthesises' says nothing about quality
#   2. a tighter constraint buys speed with AREA
#   3. an unconstrained path is not optimised badly: it is IGNORED
L0.cloze: Synthesis optimises only against the {{c1::timing constraint you supply}}. A Liberty file gives per-cell area, pin capacitance and a delay table indexed by {{c2::input transition and output load}}. An unconstrained path is {{c3::ignored}}, not optimised.

concepts.L1: Synthesis translates RTL into a netlist of standard cells from a specific library, choosing cell types and drive strengths to meet a timing constraint. The constraint is an input you write, not something the tool infers.
concepts.L2: The most common failure is not a bad result but an unconstrained one. Paths without a timing constraint are not optimised badly; they are not optimised at all, so a design that reports zero violations may simply have told the tool to ignore its critical path.
concepts.L3: The delay model explains why results are so constraint-sensitive. Each cell's delay is a table lookup on input transition time and output load, so enlarging a driven cell both speeds the path it drives and slows its own driver by adding input capacitance. Synthesis is a global optimisation with coupled costs, and it stops the moment it meets your constraint. Ask for 500 MHz and you get a small netlist; ask for 1 GHz and it inserts larger cells, duplicates logic and restructures arithmetic; ask for 5 GHz and it burns hours failing. So read area and power alongside timing, and check every clock and I/O delay is declared: the paths you forgot are the ones that fail on silicon.

L4.prompt_tpl: A design reports zero timing violations at {f} MHz but fails on the bench. The SDC file declares `create_clock` but no `set_input_delay` or `set_output_delay`. Diagnose.
L4.answer: Input and output paths are unconstrained, so the tool never analysed or optimised them. Timing is clean only for register-to-register paths inside the block; the interface paths could have arbitrary delay and will fail against whatever drives or receives them. The fix is to declare input and output delays for every port.
L4.explanation: Unconstrained equals unanalysed is the rule to remember. A clean timing report is a statement about the constraints you wrote, not about the design. This is why constraint review is a distinct signoff step and why tools have specific reports listing unconstrained endpoints.

L4.prompt_tpl: The same RTL is synthesised at {f1} MHz and at {f2} MHz. Predict qualitatively what happens to cell count, area and power, and explain the mechanism from the Liberty delay model.
L4.answer: At the tighter constraint, area and power rise, typically substantially: the tool selects higher drive-strength cells, duplicates logic to cut fanout, and restructures arithmetic into faster wider forms. Delay is a table lookup on transition and load, so speeding a path means bigger drivers, which means more capacitance and more switching energy.
L4.explanation: Frequency is purchased with area and power, and the exchange rate worsens as you approach the library's limit. This is the concrete form of the PPA trade at the implementation level and the reason a synthesis run should always be reported as a triple, never as a frequency alone.

L0.body:
# STA checks every path exhaustively, with no stimulus.
#
# SETUP (does the data arrive in time?):
#   arrival  = T_launch + T_clk2q + T_logic
#   required = T_capture + T_period - T_setup - T_uncertainty
#   slack    = required - arrival, must be >= 0
#
# HOLD (does the data stay stable long enough?):
#   slack = (T_launch + T_clk2q + T_logic_min) - (T_capture + T_hold)
#
#   setup failure -> SLOW THE CLOCK. Recoverable.
#   hold failure  -> frequency-INDEPENDENT. The chip is dead.
#
# period 2.0, clk2q 0.1, logic 1.6, setup 0.1, skew 0.05 ns:
#   arrival 1.7; required 1.85; slack +0.15 ns.
L0.cloze: Setup slack is {{c1::required minus arrival}} and a setup failure is fixed by {{c2::slowing the clock}}. A hold failure is {{c3::frequency-independent}} and can only be fixed by adding delay, which means a new layout.

concepts.L1: Static timing analysis computes, for every register-to-register path, whether data arrives early enough for setup and late enough for hold. It is exhaustive and requires no stimulus, which is why it is the signoff method rather than simulation.
concepts.L2: The setup and hold asymmetry is the fact that shapes schedules. A setup violation found late costs you frequency; a hold violation found late costs you a respin, because no clock frequency fixes it and the repair is physical insertion of delay cells.
concepts.L3: Work through why hold is frequency-independent. The hold check compares the fastest possible data arrival at a capture register against the clock edge that must not yet have sampled it. Both sides reference the same clock edge, so the period cancels: the check is a race between a fast data path and clock skew, not about cycle time. If the launch register's clock arrives earlier than the capture register's by more than the minimum data delay, new data overwrites old before capture, at any frequency including one hertz. Repair means inserting buffers into the fast path, perturbing every other path. Skew is known only after clock tree synthesis, so hold problems appear late.

L4.prompt_tpl: Clock period {p} ns, clock-to-Q {q} ns, combinational delay {d} ns, setup time {s} ns, clock uncertainty {u} ns. Compute setup slack and the maximum frequency. Answer with the setup slack in nanoseconds.
L4.answer: Slack $= P - (q + d + s + u)$. Max period $= q+d+s+u$. For $P=2.0$, $q=0.1$, $d=1.6$, $s=0.1$, $u=0.05$: slack $= 2.0 - 1.85 = +0.15$ ns; minimum period 1.85 ns, so 541 MHz.
L4.explanation: Note that the maximum frequency is set by the worst path only, so improving anything else changes nothing. This is why timing reports are read as a ranked list of critical paths and why fixing the top one simply promotes the next.

L4.prompt_tpl: Post-layout analysis shows {n} hold violations and {m} setup violations. Which do you treat as the emergency?
options: Hold: it is frequency-independent, so no clock setting makes the chip work
Setup: violations there directly reduce achievable frequency, which is the product spec
Whichever is more numerous, since fix effort scales with violation count
L4.answer: The hold violations: they are frequency-independent, so the chip is non-functional at any clock rate, and repair requires inserting delay cells in layout. Setup violations can be tolerated by shipping at a lower clock frequency while you fix them.
L4.explanation: This ranking is counterintuitive because setup violations are usually more numerous and more visible in reports. The decisive property is that a setup failure has a workaround that costs performance while a hold failure has none, and hold repair perturbs the layout that all the setup fixes depend on.

concepts.t: Floorplanning: where wires set your clock

L0.body:
# The floorplan places macros (SRAMs, IP blocks) and defines where
# standard cells may sit. BEFORE placement, and it decides more
# about frequency than synthesis does.
#
# On-chip wire delay: 100-300 ps per mm unrepeatered; with optimal
# repeaters delay is LINEAR in length, still tens of ps per mm.
#
#   die 10 mm across at 1 GHz -> 1000 ps per cycle
#   corner-to-corner at 150 ps/mm costs ~2100 ps: THREE cycles of
#   pure wire, before any logic.
#
# SRAM banks --------> PE array
#   a buffer 4 mm from the array edge is a pipeline stage you did
#   not design, and it changes the dataflow.
L0.cloze: Global wire delay is roughly {{c1::100-300}} ps per millimetre, so a corner-to-corner path on a 10 mm die can cost {{c2::three}} clock cycles at 1 GHz before any logic. The distance from {{c3::SRAM banks}} to the PE array is the accelerator floorplan question.

concepts.L1: Floorplanning fixes the physical position of memory macros and the regions available to logic. Because wire delay is proportional to distance and does not improve with process scaling the way gate delay does, the floorplan largely determines achievable frequency.
concepts.L2: This is where an elegant dataflow meets physics. A mapping that assumes any PE can read any SRAM bank in one cycle is describing a chip whose buffer is adjacent to every PE, which is geometrically impossible past a certain array size, so the dataflow must be revised or the design gains pipeline stages nobody planned.
concepts.L3: The relevant scaling fact is that gate delay has fallen with each node while wire delay per unit length has not, so the number of gate delays a signal can travel in one cycle has shrunk steadily. On a large die at a gigahertz, a corner-to-corner traversal is multiple cycles. For a systolic array this is mostly benign, since communication is neighbour-to-neighbour and short by construction. It becomes acute at the array boundary: operands come from SRAM banks that are physically somewhere, and if they are millimetres away the fetch is pipelined, changing the compiler's schedule. Co-design floorplan and dataflow, banking the buffer so each bank sits beside the PEs it feeds.

L4.prompt_tpl: On a {d} mm die at {f} GHz with global wire delay of {w} ps per mm, compute how far a signal can travel in one cycle and how many cycles a corner-to-corner traversal costs. Answer with the distance per cycle in millimetres.
L4.answer: Distance per cycle $= 1000/(f \times w)$ mm with $f$ in GHz. Diagonal $= d\sqrt{2}$. For $d=10$, $f=1$, $w=150$: 6.67 mm per cycle, diagonal 14.1 mm, so 2.1 cycles, i.e. 3 pipeline stages of pure wire.
L4.explanation: The number of cycles is what turns into pipeline registers in the implementation, which turns into latency in the architecture. Doing this calculation early is how you find out whether a proposed global structure is physically realisable at your target frequency.

L4.prompt_tpl: An accelerator's dataflow assumes any PE can read any of {n} SRAM banks in one cycle. Explain why this may be unimplementable and what the standard fix is.
L4.answer: The banks and the PEs occupy physical area, so some pairs are millimetres apart and cannot be traversed in one cycle at the target frequency. The standard fix is to bank the buffer spatially, giving each group of PEs a nearby bank and restricting the dataflow to local access, or to pipeline the fetch and expose the extra latency to the compiler's schedule.
L4.explanation: Both fixes change the architecture, which is the point: the floorplan is not an implementation detail applied afterwards. Spatial banking is what real accelerators do, and it is why their dataflows describe local buffers per PE row rather than one monolithic memory.

concepts.t: Placement, clock tree synthesis and routing

L0.body:
# The back end, in order, and what each can still ruin:
#
# 1. PLACEMENT  assign every cell an (x,y). Global, then detailed.
#      fails as CONGESTION: too many nets want one channel
# 2. CTS        build the clock distribution network.
#      minimise SKEW and INSERTION DELAY
#      HOLD violations are born here, because skew appears here
# 3. ROUTING    assign every net real metal on real layers.
#      fails as unroutable -> rip up, re-place, repeat
# 4. SIGNOFF STA on extracted parasitics, not estimates.
#
# The loop is iterative and slow: hours to days, not seconds.
L0.cloze: The back-end order is placement, {{c1::clock tree synthesis}}, routing, then signoff timing on {{c2::extracted parasitics}}. CTS is where {{c3::hold}} violations are created, because clock skew first becomes real there.

concepts.L1: After synthesis the flow places cells, builds a clock distribution network, routes every net in metal, and re-runs timing on parasitics extracted from the actual layout. Each stage can invalidate the previous one's assumptions.
concepts.L2: Clock tree synthesis is the stage architects should understand best, because it is where hold violations are born. Before CTS the tool assumes an ideal zero-skew clock; afterwards skew is real, and every fast path that was previously fine may now lose its race against it.
concepts.L3: The flow iterates rather than proceeding linearly because each stage's cost model approximates the next stage's reality. Synthesis estimates wire load statistically; placement makes those wires real but does not know their routing; routing makes them metal but changes their capacitance, changing delay, possibly breaking timing placement had met. Extraction after routing gives the first accurate resistance and capacitance, and numbers move there. Congestion is the other driver: a timing-optimal placement may pack cells so densely the router cannot fit the wires, forcing re-placement that costs timing. For a software reader: a compiler with a very expensive, very late verification step.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why hold violations typically appear after clock tree synthesis rather than after synthesis, and why that timing in the flow is expensive.
L4.answer: Before CTS the clock is treated as ideal with zero skew, so the hold check compares data delay against nothing. CTS builds a real network with real arrival differences, and any path whose minimum data delay is less than the skew now fails. It is expensive because the fix is inserting delay cells into the layout, which perturbs placement and routing and can break setup paths that were already closed.
L4.explanation: The general pattern is that each stage reveals a class of problem the previous stage could not see, and later fixes are more disruptive. It is why flows front-load pessimism, using conservative uncertainty margins early so that late-stage reality rarely surprises them.

L4.prompt_tpl: A design closes timing after placement but the router reports {n} thousand unroutable nets in one region. What happened and what is the fix?
L4.answer: Placement optimised for timing packed heavily connected cells together, creating routing congestion that exceeds the available metal tracks in that region. The fix is to re-place with congestion-aware weighting, spread the cells, or restructure the RTL to reduce the fanin of the congested logic, accepting some timing cost.
L4.explanation: Congestion is a wiring-resource problem, not a timing one, and the tools optimise them separately, which is why the conflict appears. Highly connected structures such as crossbars and large multiplexers are the usual culprits, which is another argument for local, regular interconnect in accelerator design.

L0.body:
# DRC (Design Rule Check): does the layout obey the foundry's
#   geometric rules? Width, spacing, enclosure, density (metal fill is
#   REQUIRED for CMP planarity), antenna rules (etch charge can
#   destroy a gate oxide).
#   -> manufacturability. Violations: the fab will not run it.
#
# LVS (Layout Versus Schematic): does the netlist extracted from the
#   layout match the one you intended, device by device?
#   -> correctness. Clean DRC with failing LVS means you built
#      something, just not your design.
#
# Open tools: Magic or KLayout (DRC), Netgen (LVS), on SKY130 or IHP.
L0.cloze: DRC is a {{c1::manufacturability}} check against foundry geometric rules; LVS is a {{c2::correctness}} check that the layout's extracted netlist matches the intended one. Metal fill for planarity and {{c3::antenna}} rules are DRC requirements, not options.

concepts.L1: Design rule checking verifies that a layout obeys the foundry's geometric manufacturing rules. Layout versus schematic verifies that the layout implements the intended netlist. Both are pass-fail gates before any mask is made.
concepts.L2: The rules that surprise newcomers are the ones with no logical content: metal density minimums exist because chemical-mechanical polishing needs uniform density to planarise, and antenna rules exist because charge accumulated on a long metal segment during plasma etch can destroy a gate oxide before the chip is ever powered.
concepts.L3: Both checks are absolute, unlike almost everything else in engineering. A single spacing violation means the foundry declines the tapeout, because it invalidates their yield model. A single LVS mismatch means the manufactured device is not the one that was verified, so every simulation result about it is void. The consequence for a learner is that these are the checks you can genuinely run yourself: Magic or KLayout for DRC, Netgen for LVS, against an open PDK, free, producing exactly the reports a commercial flow does. Working one small block to DRC and LVS clean, then reading the layout, is the highest-value week of physical-design education available.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why {r} is a design rule at all, given that it has nothing to do with whether the circuit is logically correct.
L4.answer: Metal density: chemical-mechanical polishing removes material at a rate depending on local pattern density, so sparse regions dish and dense ones remain proud, breaking planarity for subsequent layers. Antenna rules: during plasma etch a long metal segment connected to a gate accumulates charge with no discharge path, and the resulting voltage can rupture the gate oxide before the chip is ever powered.
L4.explanation: Both rules are about the manufacturing process rather than the circuit, which is why they cannot be reasoned about from the schematic and why fill insertion and antenna diodes are automated flow steps rather than design decisions.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your layout is DRC clean but LVS reports {n} mismatched nets. Can you tape out?
options: No: LVS failure means the manufactured circuit is not the verified netlist
Yes, if the mismatches are on non-critical nets and DRC is clean
Yes: LVS is advisory, DRC is the actual foundry gate
L4.answer: No. DRC clean only means the fab can manufacture it; LVS mismatches mean the manufactured circuit is not the netlist that was verified, so all functional verification is void regardless of how few mismatches there are.
L4.explanation: The two checks answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other. A DRC-clean, LVS-failing layout will yield perfectly good silicon implementing something you did not design and did not simulate. There is no threshold below which mismatches are acceptable.

prereqs: Placement, clock tree synthesis and routing

L0.body:
# Between 'my RTL works in simulation' and 'chips arrive':
#
#   RTL freeze -> synthesis -> floorplan -> place -> CTS -> route
#   -> parasitic extraction -> signoff STA at MULTIPLE CORNERS
#      (process x voltage x temperature: slow/typ/fast x Vmin/Vmax
#       x -40C/125C -> dozens of corners, all must pass)
#   -> IR drop and electromigration
#   -> DFT: scan, ATPG, MBIST (~5-15% area)
#   -> DRC, LVS, antenna, density
#   -> GDSII -> masks -> fab -> test -> package
#
# Fab is 6-9 months on a mature-node shuttle. Masks: tens of
# thousands of dollars at 180-130nm, USD 10M+ at 5nm.
L0.cloze: Signoff requires timing to pass at {{c1::multiple process, voltage and temperature corners}}, plus IR drop, electromigration, and DFT insertion costing roughly {{c2::5-15}} percent area. Fab alone takes {{c3::6-9}} months on a mature node.

concepts.L1: A tapeout is the handoff of a GDSII layout for mask making, and it follows a long signoff sequence: multi-corner timing, power integrity, test insertion and physical verification. The feedback loop from freeze to silicon is measured in months to a year.
concepts.L2: The multi-corner requirement is what makes signoff so much larger than a single timing run. The design must meet setup at the slow corner and hold at the fast corner simultaneously, across voltage and temperature ranges, and those are opposing optimisation targets on the same paths.
concepts.L3: Understand why the corners oppose each other. At the slow process corner, low voltage and high temperature, gates are slow, so setup is hard and hold is easy. At the fast corner, high voltage and low temperature, gates are fast, so hold is hard and setup easy. A fix for one worsens the other, which is why closure is iterative and margin is added early. Design for test adds its own tax: scan chains stitch every flip-flop into shift registers so the chip can be tested at the wafer, costing area and some timing, non-negotiable because an untested die is assumed dead. Then economics: the mask set is the fixed cost, which is why multi-project shuttles exist at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why setup and hold must be verified at {c} different process-voltage-temperature corners and why fixing one can break the other.
L4.answer: Setup is worst at the slow corner, low voltage and high temperature, where logic delay is greatest; hold is worst at the fast corner, high voltage and low temperature, where minimum data delay is smallest relative to clock skew. Adding buffers to fix hold increases delay and can break setup at the slow corner, so closure requires satisfying both simultaneously.
L4.explanation: This opposition is why timing closure is iterative rather than a single optimisation, and why designs carry explicit margin. It also explains why late hold fixes are so disruptive: each inserted buffer must be re-checked against the setup corner on the same path.

L4.prompt_tpl: A project freezes RTL and needs {m} months of signoff, then a shuttle with {f} months of fabrication, then {t} months of packaging and test. Compute total time to working silicon and state what that implies for the engineering process.
L4.answer: Total $= m + f + t$ months. For 4, 9 and 3: 16 months from RTL freeze to a board. There is no fast iteration, so verification must be exhaustive before freeze and the design must include enough observability and configurability to work around bugs found in silicon.
L4.explanation: The arithmetic is trivial and the consequence is the entire culture: verification consumes most of the engineering headcount, formal methods are used routinely, and designs include fuses, spare gates and configuration registers specifically so that a bug found in silicon can sometimes be bypassed rather than respun.

# SCALE-Sim v3 (github.com/scalesim-project/scale-sim-v3; v3 paper
# arXiv:2504.15377). Cycle-accurate systolic array simulator. Give it
# array dimensions, dataflow and a topology CSV; get cycles,
# utilisation and SRAM/DRAM traffic.
#
#   # topology CSV: Layer, M, N, K (or conv dims)
#   # config: ArrayHeight, ArrayWidth, IfmapSramSzkB,
#   #         FilterSramSzkB, OfmapSramSzkB, Dataflow = ws|os|is
#   python3 scalesim/scale.py -c my.cfg -t net.csv
#
# The afternoon that teaches most: sweep Dataflow over {ws,os,is}
# x ArrayHeight over {16..256}; plot cycles and DRAM bytes.
L0.cloze: SCALE-Sim takes {{c1::array dimensions, dataflow and a layer topology}} and returns cycles, utilisation and memory traffic. The highest-value first experiment is sweeping {{c2::dataflow and array size}} for one real network and plotting cycles against DRAM bytes.

concepts.L1: SCALE-Sim is a cycle-accurate simulator for systolic arrays that takes array geometry, dataflow and a network topology and reports cycles, utilisation and SRAM and DRAM traffic per layer. It is the fastest way to make dataflow arguments concrete.
concepts.L2: Its value is not accuracy but turnaround. A design-space sweep that would take weeks in RTL runs in minutes, so you can answer questions like where output-stationary overtakes weight-stationary for your workload by measurement rather than by argument.
concepts.L3: Run the experiments that reproduce this section's arithmetic: agreement validates your understanding, disagreement reveals an assumption you had wrong. Sweep array height at fixed work and watch utilisation fall as fill and drain grow, which is the $M/(M+2N-2)$ curve appearing empirically. Sweep dataflow across a network with both convolutional and fully connected layers and watch the winner change per layer, which is why fixed-dataflow accelerators leave performance on the table. Sweep SRAM size and watch DRAM traffic fall then plateau; the plateau names the tile size beyond which more buffer buys nothing.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have one afternoon and want to understand dataflow tradeoffs for a {n}-layer network. Which experiment do you run?
options: Sweep dataflow and array size across the whole network and plot cycles and DRAM bytes
Simulate the largest layer at the largest array size for maximum fidelity
Write RTL for one processing element and measure its Fmax
L4.answer: Sweep dataflow across weight, output and input stationary at several array sizes for the real network, and plot cycles and DRAM bytes per layer. That single sweep exposes fill and drain cost, the per-layer dataflow crossover, and the point where the array outruns its SRAM.
L4.explanation: Simulating one configuration teaches almost nothing, because the interesting content is entirely in how the metrics move with the parameters. A sweep with plots is also the shape of a real design-space exploration, so the habit transfers directly to the job.

L4.prompt_tpl: SCALE-Sim reports {c} cycles for a layer whose ideal MAC count is {m} million on a {n}x{n} array. Compute utilisation and compare against the fill-drain prediction for {p} passes. Answer with the utilisation.
L4.answer: Utilisation $= \mathrm{MACs}/(n^{2} \times \mathrm{cycles})$. For $m = 800$ million, $n = 256$, $c = 20000$: $8\times10^{8}/(65536 \times 20000) = 61.0$ percent. Fill-drain alone predicts $16000/(16000+510) = 96.9$ percent, so the extra loss is memory stalls, not pipeline fill.
L4.explanation: Comparing the measured utilisation against the fill-drain bound separates two causes: geometry and memory. If they agree, the array is running at its structural limit; if measured is much lower, the SRAM or DRAM is not keeping up and the fix is in the memory system, not the array.

concepts.t: Timeloop and Accelergy: the mapspace, searched

L0.body:
# Timeloop (github.com/NVlabs/timeloop, Parashar et al. ISPASS 2019):
#   describe an ARCHITECTURE as a memory hierarchy with capacities,
#   bandwidths and spatial fanouts; describe a PROBLEM as a tensor
#   loop nest; it SEARCHES the mapspace and returns the best mapping
#   plus exact access counts at every level.
#
# Accelergy (Wu, Sze, Emer, ICCAD 2019) turns access counts into
#   energy and area via plug-in estimators (CACTI for SRAM).
#
# Labs: github.com/Accelergy-Project/timeloop-accelergy-exercises
#
# Analytical, not simulated -- hence 10^11 mappings are searchable.
L0.cloze: Timeloop searches the {{c1::mapspace}} for a given architecture and problem and returns exact {{c2::access counts}} per memory level; Accelergy converts those into energy and area. It is {{c3::analytical}}, not simulated, which is why the search is tractable.

concepts.L1: Timeloop models an accelerator as a memory hierarchy with capacities, bandwidths and spatial fanouts, searches the space of loop-nest mappings for a tensor problem, and reports exact per-level access counts. Accelergy converts those counts into energy and area estimates.
concepts.L2: The key property is that it is analytical rather than simulated. Because the loop nest fully determines access counts, no execution is needed, so a search over an enormous mapspace becomes feasible and comparisons between architectures can be made under each one's own best mapping.
concepts.L3: The methodological discipline is the reason to learn this rather than build a spreadsheet. A fair architecture comparison requires each candidate to be evaluated under its own optimal mapping, found with equal search effort, or you are measuring which architecture you tuned harder. Timeloop makes that a mechanical step. It also forces you to write the architecture down explicitly, every buffer capacity, bandwidth and fanout, surfacing assumptions that stay implicit in prose; Accelergy then requires an energy model per component, surfacing a second set. The free MIT 6.5930 lab material is a genuine two-to-three week project producing exactly the artifact a modelling role wants to see.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why Timeloop can search on the order of {n} mappings without simulating any of them, and what that implies for comparing two architectures.
L4.answer: Because a loop nest fully determines how many times each tensor is accessed at each memory level: a tensor is refetched at a level whenever a loop it does not depend on sits outside a loop it does. Access counts are therefore computed in closed form from the mapping, with no execution. The implication is that architectures must be compared under their own separately optimised mappings, since finding those is cheap and using a shared mapping biases the result.
L4.explanation: The closed-form property is what separates analytical modelling from simulation and it is the reason this tool exists. It also bounds its fidelity: anything not captured by access counts, such as bank conflicts, arbitration or DRAM timing, is outside the model and must be checked elsewhere.

L4.prompt_tpl: You compare architecture A and architecture B on a network using the {m} mapping for both, and A wins by {p} percent. Is that a valid result?
options: No: each architecture must be evaluated under its own optimal mapping
Yes: using one mapping for both is the fairest possible controlled comparison
Yes, provided the mapping was chosen to be optimal for architecture B
L4.answer: No. Each architecture has a different optimal mapping, so a shared mapping measures how well that mapping suits each design rather than the designs themselves. Both must be evaluated under their own optimal mapping found with equal search effort.
L4.explanation: This is the most common methodological error in accelerator evaluation and it can invert conclusions, since mapping quality routinely changes energy by an order of magnitude. It is also why Timeloop's mapper is as important a contribution as its model.

prereqs: Loop nests, tiling and the mapspace
Reuse arithmetic: bytes moved per MAC

L0.body:
# gem5 (gem5.org): full-system cycle-level CPU/memory simulator.
#   CPU models AtomicSimple..O3, configurable caches, Ruby for
#   coherence protocols, boots Linux. Long build, slow runs.
#
# Ramulator 2 (github.com/CMU-SAFARI/ramulator2, Mutlu's group):
#   cycle-accurate modular DRAM simulator: DDR/LPDDR/HBM/GDDR,
#   scheduling, refresh, RowHammer. arXiv:2308.11030.
#
# Which tool:
#   coherence protocol cost          -> gem5/Ruby
#   DMA pattern vs bank parallelism  -> Ramulator
#   which dataflow for my array      -> Timeloop
#   does my RTL work                 -> Verilator
L0.cloze: gem5 provides {{c1::full-system cycle-level}} CPU and memory simulation including detailed coherence through Ruby; Ramulator 2 is a modular {{c2::DRAM}} simulator covering DDR, LPDDR, HBM and GDDR. Pick the tool by the question: coherence cost, {{c3::bank parallelism}}, dataflow, or RTL correctness.

concepts.L1: gem5 simulates complete systems at cycle level, including detailed cache coherence protocols. Ramulator 2 simulates DRAM devices in detail, covering timing parameters, scheduling policies and refresh across current memory standards.
concepts.L2: The mistake is picking a simulator by reputation rather than by question. gem5's fidelity is wasted and its cost is real if the question is which dataflow to use, and Timeloop cannot answer whether your DMA pattern achieves bank parallelism. Choose the least detailed tool that can answer the question.
concepts.L3: Match tool to question and the answer comes quickly. Coherence protocol cost, memory consistency behaviour and full-system effects such as OS interference need gem5, because they involve interactions no analytical model captures; Ruby exists precisely to model coherence protocols in detail. DRAM behaviour under a given access stream, including row-buffer hit rate, bank parallelism and refresh interference, needs Ramulator, which models the timing constraints exactly and is fast enough for long traces. Mapping questions need Timeloop, which is analytical and fastest. And your own RTL under Verilator is often the most accurate model of your own accelerator: the design is the model.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to know whether your accelerator's DMA access pattern achieves adequate {x} on an HBM stack. Which tool?
options: Ramulator 2, which models DRAM bank state, timing and scheduling exactly
Timeloop, since it reports DRAM access counts per mapping
gem5 with the AtomicSimple CPU, since full-system fidelity is always preferable
L4.answer: Ramulator 2: it models DRAM timing constraints, bank state, scheduling and refresh exactly, which is what determines bank parallelism and row-buffer hit rate. gem5 would work but is far heavier, and Timeloop does not model DRAM timing at all.
L4.explanation: The general rule is to pick the least detailed tool that captures the mechanism you are asking about. Bank state and timing are outside Timeloop's analytical model entirely, so it cannot answer this regardless of effort, while gem5 answers it at much greater cost.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain why your own RTL under Verilator is often a better model of your accelerator than a {t} simulator, and where that stops being true.
L4.answer: Because the RTL is the design: it is exact by construction, needs no calibration, and captures every structural hazard and stall your implementation actually has. It stops being true when you need to explore designs you have not written, when you need full-system context such as an operating system or a host CPU, or when simulation speed makes the experiment infeasible.
L4.explanation: This reframing matters for someone with a software background: writing the thing and measuring it is often cheaper than modelling it, provided the design space you are exploring is small. Analytical models earn their place exactly when the space is large.

concepts.L1: Chipyard is a Berkeley RISC-V SoC generator framework in Chisel containing in-order and out-of-order cores, vector units, and Gemmini, a configurable systolic array accelerator with an accompanying software stack.
concepts.L2: Gemmini is the reference design worth studying because it is complete rather than illustrative: it has a compiler path, a driver, a real integration with a core, and configurable dataflow. Reading it before building your own array is far more efficient than reading it afterwards to discover what you missed.
concepts.L3: What makes this uniquely valuable to one person is that it closes the whole loop. Change Gemmini's array dimensions or switch its dataflow between weight and output stationary, rebuild, run a real quantised network on a real RISC-V core under Verilator, measure cycles and memory traffic, then take the same design through synthesis and place-and-route for area and timing. That is the industrial co-design loop, free, on a laptop-plus-patience budget. The costs are honest: Scala and Chisel, a long build, a machine with substantial memory. Read Gemmini's Chisel for structure, run it unmodified for a baseline, then change one parameter and measure.

L4.prompt_tpl: You have written your own {n}x{n} systolic array in SystemVerilog and want to know whether it is any good. What is the most informative next step?
options: Configure Gemmini identically and compare cycles, traffic, area and timing
Increase your array to 256x256 and report the peak TOPS figure
Port the design to a different FPGA to check that it is portable
L4.answer: Configure Gemmini to the same dimensions, dataflow and precision, run both on the same network, and compare cycles, memory traffic and post-synthesis area and timing. A like-for-like comparison against a mature reference is the only way to know whether your numbers are good or merely numbers.
L4.explanation: Absolute numbers from your own design are uninterpretable without a reference point. Gemmini is the right reference precisely because it is parameterisable to match your configuration, and a written comparison including where you lose is more credible than one where you win.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain what the loop from Gemmini configuration through Verilator to an ASIC flow gives you that {a} alone does not.
L4.answer: It closes the loop between architectural choice and physical cost. An analytical model gives cycles and estimated energy but no timing closure or real area; an FPGA gives cycles and resource usage but its area and frequency do not translate to silicon. Running the same configuration through synthesis and place-and-route yields area, achievable frequency and power for a real cell library, so an architectural change can be priced in the currency that matters.
L4.explanation: This is the specific gap that makes most hobby accelerator projects unpersuasive: they report a working design without a cost. Pricing your architectural choices in area and timing is what turns a project into evidence of engineering judgement.
